When Andy Burnham told the Labour conference that he wanted to start a debate on a new relationship with the EU, because Brexit had done more harm than good, he raised the possibility that this could lead to Labour proposing to rejoin at some point after the next election.

But some ministers and Labour MPs are deeply unhappy about that prospect, believing that there would have to be a referendum and that this would be deeply divisive, and there are some signs that Burnham (who is on record as saying he would like the UK to rejoin in his lifetime) is starting to scale back his ambitions.

I don’t believe Brexit and the deal that they got has been good enough for Britain. I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years.

And actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016.

People’s jobs depend on working together and collaborating.

And that’s our approach, and it will always be our approach. People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are.

Look, here’s my starting point. My constituents, people across the country, voted for a range of reasons for Brexit, but one of them was one of the biggest, certainly for my constituents, was to make our economy better, positive economic change. We haven’t had that. The economy has got worse. And nobody really thinks this Brexit deal is a good deal.

title: Russian tennis sensation claims historic WTA Finals title (VIDEO, PHOTO)
content:
Mirra Andreeva defeated Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina to become the first Russian player to win the season-ending tournament in 22 years

Russian tennis star Mirra Andreeva has won a WTA Finals singles title, defeating Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina in straight sets in California.

The 19-year-old has secured a career-high world No. 2 ranking and has become the first Russian woman to lift the trophy since her compatriot Maria Sharapova defeated American Serena Williams in 2004.

Andreeva beat Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 in Sunday’s final at Indian Wells, claiming the biggest title of her career without dropping a set throughout the competition.

The Russian briefly stumbled while serving for the opening set at 5-4, handing Svitolina a break with two double faults and two unforced errors. She immediately broke back, however, and regained control to take the set 7-5 before sealing victory in the second.

Svitolina refused to shake hands with Andreeva or pose for the traditional joint photograph after the match, continuing her practice of snubbing Russian and Belarusian opponents since 2022. The Ukrainian also left the stage after her runner-up speech, taking a seat courtside rather than remaining alongside the champion, although she nodded when Andreeva congratulated her on her tournament performance and season.

Russian athletes have faced widespread bans and restrictions in international sport since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. While Russian tennis players have been allowed to compete individually under neutral status, Russia remains barred from international team competitions, including the Billie Jean King Cup and Davis Cup. Wimbledon also excluded Russian and Belarusian players in 2022 before reversing the ban the following year.

Read more

Andreeva’s victory placed her among the youngest players to win the WTA Finals on their debut, following Chris Evert and Sharapova. She also completed the tournament without losing a set, joining an exclusive group of champions that includes Serena Williams and Iga Swiatek.

The Russian swept through the group stage before defeating American Jessica Pegula 6-3, 6-4 in the semifinals. The triumph capped a remarkable season in which she also won the French Open at Roland Garros and claimed titles in Adelaide, Australia and Linz, Austria.

Andreeva will finish the year as world No. 2 for the first time in her career, having recorded 55 match victories this season. Her latest triumph was her fourth title of 2026 and seventh on the WTA Tour.

Along with the trophy and prize money, Andreeva received a new Mercedes, prompting an amusing exchange with tennis legend Billie Jean King. Asked whether she could drive, the Russian admitted she had yet to obtain a license, joking that the prize was an “amazing motivation” to get one and that she could otherwise remain a “passenger princess for life.”

title: Why The Times of India sees value in focusing on an ‘Adult Renaissance’
content:
By Joon-Nie Lau

“Old has gold” Jain proclaimed before going on to elaborate on why an “Adult Renaissance” is taking place and why print is still alive in some parts of the world, particularly in India.

Citing a World Economic Forum survey during question period following his keynote at WAN-IFRA’s Asian Media Leaders Summit in Singapore in October, Jain said, “A Gen X spends about US$ 84,000 in the US and Gen Z spends half that,” emphasising the high disposable income that this demographic at the peak of their careers has.

The AI of distribution

For this media powerhouse that prints the world’s largest English language daily, The Times of India (TOI), and world’s second most widely read English business newspaper, The Economic Times, the acronym “AI” takes on a whole new meaning.

“The most significant part is where are we selling,” said Jain, explaining TOI’s concept of the “AI” (Affluence and Influence) of Distribution that sells nearly three million print copies a day.

“Let’s say Mumbai. While we may have an 81 percent market share of the brand audience, we have 90 percent market share in a city like Mumbai of the premium audience, like the people who are making a change in society—the top 1 or 2 percent of the whole demographic.”

This approach is replicated across key cities like New Delhi, Bangalore and Chennai where TOI’s relative share in affluent areas ranges from 67 to 90 percent, even though its market share vis-à-vis competitors ranges from 51 to 81 percent.

Bridging video, podcasts and print

To attract younger readers and drive stickiness, there are 43 city editions of Times of India Metro Supplements (TIMS) such as the Delhi Times, Bombay Times and Hyderabad Times, packed with food, fashion, fitness, family, travel and Bollywood happenings. It’s a trendy metro lifestyle franchise that attracts over 2.6 million daily readers and 6 million followers on social media.

Jain highlighted TIMS’ new multimedia extension launched last year – the popular Bombay Times Lounge celebrity video and podcast talk show which bridges the print coverage of the Bombay Times city supplement with digital and social storytelling for omnichannel distribution.

For TIMS, this is a major revenue diversification initiative, allowing brand partners and sponsors to integrate into premium editorial entertainment content across print and digital platforms.

On the digital front, TOI runs one of the world’s largest digital news platforms. Its own first-party Google Analytics clocks over 300 million monthly active users (MAU), about 25 percent of whom are international, with readers from the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom among its largest foreign audiences.

Trust at scale in the Age of AI

While TOI uses AI for both content generation (transcription, translation, research, summarisation, tagging) and distribution (language adaptation, story formatting and repurposing, algorithmic recommendations) with human editors controlling what gets published, Jain highlighted how TOI uses AI to strengthen reader retention by improving tele-sales conversations, among its various AI initiatives improve customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning.

Its 85 telesales callers handle 200,000 subscription renewals calls a month and are responsible for 28 percent of order bookings. The sheer volume makes call auditing, quality control and continuous training a challenge.

Now, an easy-to-use in-house AI tool, Call AIQ (Agent Interaction Quality), can audit every call, provide real-time 24/7 coaching whenever tele-sales staff need it, automatically create scorecards and leaderboards, award badges and highlight best performing calls as case studies for shared peer learning. The result: calls are now handled faster and more efficiently.

Turning to its partnerships with AI platforms — with Google for five years and Open AI more recently — Jain noted, “Yes, it is difficult to reach an agreement. It is difficult to have that negotiation in terms of how much we want and how much they want to give: where is the sweet spot. But once it’s done and dusted, in the last five years, we didn’t have to look back to chase for payments or the fulfilment of contract.”

He added that the relationships so far have been dispute-free, based on fairness, professionalism and mutual respect.

10x ambition

At BCCL, management executives are challenged to come up with ideas that produce 10 times the results, not incremental change.

“The way of working with senior leaders is to see how we can think of ideas which don’t give us 10 percent improvement, but 10x like,” said Jain, “Because, unless the idea is crazy, it will not be interesting to even implement!”

Jain offered numerous big examples of editorial innovation, product innovation and business model innovation over the years, citing TOI’s low cover price of just six US cents as the biggest innovation in the print world.

This invitation pricing approach — made possible by strong advertising support – was introduced by TOI in the 1990s to protect reach and audience in an extremely competitive market.

“Content is king. Distribution is god,” he reminded the room, emphasising TOI’s strong belief in its own product, its “Project Sunrise” commitment to deliver 80 percent of copies by 6:30 am, and the power of its editorial platforms to elevate a low-cost newspaper into an indispensable cultural and civic institution in the world’s most populous country.

Moderator Chris Janz, left, speaking with Mohit Jain during Asian Media Leaders Summit in Singapore. 

Decades of editorial and social impact campaigns such as “Aman ki Asha” (Hope for Peace) together with Pakistan’s Jang Group in 2010 to promote peace between the two countries, “Lead India” (2007-2008) and “Lost Votes” (2019) which encouraged new political engagement, have helped build emotional equity, command premium advertising rates, and generate globally recognised, award-winning creative work at Cannes and other competitions.

During question period with moderator Chris Janz, Jain said smaller news publishers could think of themselves as providers of branded information services as they decided on the content that they provide, continue to protect journalism and build audiences, while staying attuned to their readers’ evolving lifestyles and purchasing power.

About the writer: Joon-Nie Lau is a Director of Singapore Press Club Ltd and former Director of WAN-IFRA Asia (2018-2022). In the past three years, she has parlayed her experience as a law and technology reporter into ‘live’ journalism, running the 2,000-attendee TechLaw.Fest in Singapore.

content:

  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.

title: The Legal Path to Autocracy
content:
UK-based Zimbabweans protest against the Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Bill outside the Zimbabwe Embassy in London, UK, on 18 April 2026. Credit: Maynard Manyowa/News Images/NurPhoto via AFP

By Inés M. Pousadela
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay, Nov 16 2026 (IPS)

Zimbabwe’s President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who took over when a miliary coup ended Robert Mugabe’s 37 years in power, has made clear he has no intention of limiting himself to a decade at the top. In July, he signed a constitutional amendment that lengthened the terms of the sitting president and parliament from five to seven years and pushed the next general election back from 2028 to 2030.

Zimbabwe is not alone. In several African countries and beyond, presidents are using constitutional amendments, courts and parliaments to stay in power beyond the original limits. They are extending terms, abolishing term and age limits, writing rivals out of the race and, in the boldest cases, removing voters from the equation altogether, while repressing those who stand up for democracy. These moves can achieve much the same outcome as a coup, but their legal veneer spares those behind them the consequences. A military takeover can get a country suspended from the African Union (AU), while presidents who rewrite the rules have so far faced no penalties at all.

Limits erased

In Djibouti, President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh has ruled since 1999. In October 2025, parliament voted unanimously to scrap the presidential age limit of 75, which Guelleh had already exceeded. In April 2026, he claimed a sixth term on an implausible 97.8 per cent in an election most opposition parties boycotted.

In Chad, where Mahamat Idriss Déby took power in 2021 after his father’s death and won a disputed election in 2024, parliament abolished presidential term limits in October 2025 and lengthened terms from five to seven years. The Republic of the Congo shows where this road leads. A decade after a referendum removed term and age limits that would have stopped Denis Sassou Nguesso running again, the 82-year-old claimed a fifth term in March 2026, on an official 94.82 per cent.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) may be next. President Félix Tshisekedi is constitutionally barred from a third term, but he has floated a constitutional revision and a possible delay to the 2028 election. On 23 October, the National Assembly passed a law allowing a referendum to be triggered by a ‘major dysfunction’ of state institutions and sent it to the Senate. The constitution still forbids any change to term limits, but civil society and the opposition see this law as a step towards indefinite rule.

Africa has no monopoly on this tactic. In El Salvador, Nayib Bukele used his party’s supermajority to purge the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber, whose new judges reinterpreted the constitutional ban on consecutive re-election to clear his way to a second term in 2024. In July 2025, the Legislative Assembly abolished presidential term limits altogether.

Rivals off the ballot

Once limits are out of the way, rivals are next. In Côte d’Ivoire, President Alassane Ouattara argued that the 2016 constitution had reset his term count to zero. The Constitutional Council agreed, clearing him for a fourth term at 83, and struck several challengers off the ballot seven weeks before the October 2025 vote. With no viable contenders left, he won with around 90 per cent.

In Nicaragua, Daniel Ortega jailed every viable challenger ahead of the 2021 election. In July, he declared that the country would hold no more elections, and now he’s writing political exclusion into the constitution. An amendment approved on first reading in September, pending a second vote in January 2027, would permanently bar anyone accused of being a ‘traitor to the homeland’ or of supporting foreign sanctions from standing for public office.

Voters written out

The ultimate way to entrench power is to deprive voters of their say. Once Zimbabwe’s amendment has kept the 84-year-old Mnangagwa in office until 2030, a parliament his party dominates could renew his mandate indefinitely, without voters having any say.

In Cameroon, President Paul Biya, 93 and in power since 1982, claimed an eighth term in October 2025. In April, parliament voted 200 to 18 to reintroduce the vice-presidency, a post the president appoints and dismisses, whose holder would serve out any unfinished term, even though the constitution requires a fresh election. The law effectively hands Biya the power to choose his own successor. Opposition leader Maurice Kamto called it a ‘constitutional coup’.

Ongoing repression

Legal manipulation relies on repression. In Zimbabwe, police shut down the inaugural meeting of the Constitutional Defenders Forum and Human Rights Watch documented seven attacks on student leaders campaigning against the amendment, some of whom were abducted, tortured and handed to police. Ruling-party loyalists trapped journalists covering parliamentary hearings and forced them to delete footage of violence against activists.

In Chad, opposition leader Succès Masra was sentenced to 20 years in prison two months before term limits were removed. In Côte d’Ivoire, authorities banned protests and public meetings other than campaign events. In the DRC, police fired teargas at people marching against the referendum law and arrested dozens, and clashes in Kinshasa left an opposition politician dead.

An outdated rulebook

When soldiers removed Gabon’s president in August 2023, the AU suspended the country the next day. None of the presidents rewriting the rules to stay in power have faced anything comparable. The AU has the tools. Its African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance provides for sanctions when governments amend constitutions or legal instruments to stay in power, just as it does for a coup.

Yet the AU has only ever suspended states after military takeovers or, as in Côte d’Ivoire in 2010, when a defeated incumbent refused to leave, and never for rewriting a constitution. It did not even suspend Chad in 2021, when the army installed the younger Déby in breach of succession rules, the first step in a process that ended with the abolition of term limits.

Each manoeuvre that goes unanswered lowers the cost of the next one. As long as rewriting the rules brings no consequences, presidents determined to stay will keep doing it, and those who resist will keep paying the price.

Inés M. Pousadela is CIVICUS Head of Research and Analysis, co-director and writer for CIVICUS Lens and co-author of the State of Civil Society Report. She is also a Professor of Comparative Politics at Universidad ORT Uruguay.

For interviews or more information, please contact research@civicus.org.

title: Russia says its air defenses intercept over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in massive aerial attack
content:
Russian air defenses intercepted 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Monday, in what appeared to be Kyiv’s biggest aerial attack since Moscow’s all-out invasion of its neighbor nearly five years ago.

Ukraine has scaled up its long-range aerial assaults on Russia, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black and the Azov seas, with more than 1,000 drones used in some attacks in recent months.

Russia, meanwhile, has battered Ukrainian civilian areas with relentless strikes that seek to make normal daily life impossible and break public morale, especially through strikes on the power grid, as well as choking the economy.

The war has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of Ukrainian civilians, Western analysts and officials say.

Six people were wounded in an attack on Russia's southern Krasnodar region, according to local authorities. The town is home to the Ilsky oil refinery, a frequent target of Ukrainian drone attacks.

In the Rostov region near the border with Ukraine, three people in the city of Azov, where two oil depots are located, were wounded by drones, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said.

Around 600 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Most were downed far away, while 191 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital, he said.

Ukraine pushes back against Russia with long-range strikes

The strikes on Russia serve multiple purposes for Ukraine.

They have repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, which are an economic mainstay for Moscow. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed late Sunday that Ukrainian attacks have disabled more than 55% of Russia’s oil refining capacity.

Russian officials didn’t comment on that claim, and independent verification wasn’t possible. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact, President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product.

Ukrainian officials are keen, too, to make Russians feel the war at home, while mid-range strikes are disrupting Russia’s front-line supply routes and hampering Moscow’s efforts to get momentum on the battlefield, analysts say.

Kyiv says newly imposed speed limits on the U.S.-made Starshield system, which is SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, have weakened Ukraine's air defenses. Ukrainian forces say they are adapting to that by launching pre-emptive attacks that hit Russian weapons production plants and sites that Russia uses to launch drone and missile attacks.

Kyiv also wants to show its supporters that it is still in the fight, as Moscow tries to depict its victory in Ukraine as inevitable and U.S.-mediated talks make no impact on the war.

There was no clear picture of the extent of damage caused by Ukrainian strikes in Russia. Moscow-based and local officials rarely provide details.

Zelenskyy says Russian strikes on Ukraine are ‘brutal’

Ukrainians are bracing for what could be the hardest winter since the war began, as Russia repeatedly batters the power grid and denies civilians heat, light and running water.

Russian strikes on power lines and substations in the southern Zaporizhzhia and central Dnipropetrovsk regions left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Monday.

Zelenskyy says the Russian strategy is to bombard specific areas for days, flattening energy infrastructure.

Since the start of September, for example, the central Dnipro region has endured 131 strikes, while the Kyiv region around the capital has witnessed 125, he said.

One person was killed and three were injured in a Monday morning strike on Dnipro, local officials said.

Just over the past week, Russia has launched more than 2,300 attack drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine, according to Zelenskyy.

They are "brutal strikes that are difficult to counter,” he said on social media.

Four people were killed and three more injured in Russian shelling of towns and villages in the Donetsk region over the past day, said Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk Regional Military Administration.

title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
content:
Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.

title: Paris bans protests near schools and universities
content:
The students’ union has slammed the order as “a clear attack on freedom of assembly” and demanded its immediate lifting

Paris police have banned unauthorized gatherings near ten secondary schools and five university campuses in the French capital in an attempt to counter continued blockades and violence at educational institutions across the country.

Any unauthorized gatherings within 100 meters of the listed venues will be banned for five days, from November 16 to 20, Paris police chief Patrice Faure said in a statement on Sunday.

The order followed a call on Friday by mayors of eight Parisian districts for measures to “secure the entrances and exits” to schools amid ongoing protests.

French students began blocking schools in September, demanding better learning conditions, including more teachers and greater funding for education. The demonstrations have drawn support from unions and Yellow Vest activists, growing into wider, often violent protests against the rising cost of living, which have seen hundreds of thousands taking to the streets.

Read more

According to Faure, the restrictions on gatherings are needed due to “numerous disruptions and blockades” of schools and universities, which led to damage to public property, fires, “significant violence against members of the educational community as well as clashes with the police.”

A total of 1,548 people have been arrested since the start of the student protests, he said. According to government data, some 360 students and 240 education staff, including 81 school principals and deputy principals, have been injured during the period.

The police chief noted that blockades are being carried out by “a minority of students,” but undermine the right to education for all their peers.

They also “anger parents of some students who want those disruptions to end, which has resulted in tensions,” Faure added.

Read more

The National Union of Students of France (UNEF) said later in the day that the ban was a “clear attack on… the freedom of assembly” and demanded it be lifted immediately.

“The order does not define what a gathering is,” leaving all the decisions in the hands of the police on the ground, it said. The absence of clear criteria “paves the way for checks, searches, fines and mass arrests,” UNEF stressed.

November 14 marked the fifth Saturday in a row when people took to the streets across France. The latest protest, which drew fewer participants than previous demonstrations, saw some 106,000 people taking part, including 24,000 in Paris. The demonstrations were again marred by clashes, with 219 people arrested nationwide.

title: Canary Islands migrant arrivals hit record high
content:
More than 1,500 people reached the Spanish archipelago in a single day, prompting opposition calls for naval intervention

Migrant arrivals in Spain’s Canary Islands have reached their highest daily level in 32 years, with 1,580 people arriving on Saturday as opposition politicians called for naval intervention to stem the influx.

Another 1,261 migrants reached El Hierro on Sunday, bringing the three-day total across the archipelago to 3,684, according to Spanish news agency EFE. The island, home to around 12,000 people, has received more than 8,000 migrants since the beginning of November.

The surge has placed additional pressure on the small island, prompting demands for emergency assistance from the government and renewed criticism of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s handling of illegal immigration ahead of Spain’s November 29 general election.

Spain has been grappling with a migration crisis since late July, when around 80,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into its North African exclave of Ceuta, according to Spanish government estimates. Although most subsequently returned to Morocco, thousands remained, many living in makeshift camps along beaches, prompting protests by local residents demanding government action.

The migrants arrived in the Canary Islands aboard 15 boats on Saturday, including 173 minors among the passengers, EFE reported, citing provisional figures from rescue services.

Read more

Many of the migrants departed from Senegal, Gambia, and Mauritania, spending between four and seven days at sea along one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. Most were rescued off El Hierro.

Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo accused the central government of failing to act quickly enough, demanding the immediate implementation of promised emergency measures.

Spanish Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres visited the island on Sunday, pledging additional rescue and medical resources. The government has also committed over €16 million ($17.6 million) in emergency aid.

Xavier Garcia Albiol, the mayor of Badalona and a parliamentary candidate for the conservative People’s Party (PP), urged the government to deploy the Spanish Navy to prevent migrant boats from reaching the archipelago.

“This is unbearable,” Albiol said, describing it as an “invasion of irregular immigration.” He accused criminal networks of using larger vessels to transport smaller migrant boats toward Spanish waters.

“Spain cannot continue to be the gateway for irregular immigration into Europe,” he added.

Read more

Basque regional president Imanol Pradales also urged Sanchez to address the emergency and avoid repeating the mistakes made during the Ceuta crisis.

The latest arrivals come just two weeks before Spain’s snap general election on November 29, called after Sanchez’s left-wing coalition suffered parliamentary defeats over housing reforms.

The government has faced nationwide protests over soaring housing costs. A general strike last Wednesday drew more than 3 million participants, according to unions, with clashes in Madrid and Barcelona resulting in 115 arrests nationwide, Reuters reported.

The record arrivals come despite the EU’s efforts to curb irregular migration through tighter border controls and agreements with African countries. In 2024, Brussels announced €210 million in support for Mauritania, including measures to combat migrant smuggling.

The EU has since approved rules allowing member states to establish deportation centers outside the bloc. Five countries, including Germany and Austria, are now preparing a deal to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, Reuters reported on Monday. Spain is not part of the initiative.

title: UN-backed talks consider possible rules on lethal autonomous weapons
content:
Killer robots and drones come up for a reckoning this week as government envoys rev up a discussion and could decide whether to launch negotiations toward setting rules for use of the deadly machines — or not.

Pope Leo XIV, the U.N. chief and advocacy groups cast the issue as an existential debate: Whether robots can be allowed to kill and whether humans must maintain some control of and accountability for use of lethal autonomous weapon systems.

Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones like Ukraine and the Middle East, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Scary would-be scenarios, like armed drones flying amok and gunning down civilians with pinpoint precision, have peppered years of discussions about killer robots. But those talks haven't produced any international restrictions.

The United States and Russia, longtime rivals, want to limit any curbs on their abilities to develop and roll out powerful new tools for the high-tech arms race — just as AI is gaining steam and changing battle plans.

UN meeting comes after 7 countries seek negotiations

The issue comes to a head at U.N. offices in Geneva, where a 7th review conference about the awkwardly named Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons will consider whether to start talks on regulation of killer robots.

Supporters of an accord acknowledge powerful forces are in the way, but point to precedent: Governments have already struck a deal to regulate blinding lasers.

Most countries support reining them in. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ deadline this year for the launch of talks toward regulation has given the issue urgency, but some top military powers are hesitant.

Last month, seven countries -- Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand, and Panama -- submitted a proposal to launch negotiations of a new legally binding agreement on autonomous weapons at the conference.

The various sides have been gearing up for the diplomatic standoff.

On Friday, International Committee of the Red Cross president Mirjana Spoljaric said in a statement: “States must act to ensure the future of warfare is not handed over to machines.”

Stop Killer Robots, an advocacy group, says 130 countries support new international rules on the weapons systems.

Activists began running advertisements in the streets and subways of Berlin, London and Paris touting public support for reining in killer robots.

Russia says talks on restrictions are ‘premature’

In his first encyclical in May, the pope denounced a “culture of power” driving the AI race, especially in developing ever more sophisticated methods of remote warfare, and said it's not permissible to entrust decisions about life and death to remote AI systems.

The U.N. human rights chief, Volker Türk, called Monday for nations to “urgently” agree on binding rules on lethal autonomous weapons systems.

“The international community has critical choices to make, right now, about the future of armed conflicts and the role of human beings in decisions over the use of force," he said.

Under the convention’s rules, decisions must be made by consensus. That means that any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any such deal is likely to be based on a low common denominator. Another sticking point is how long negotiators might be given to try to agree on language.

In the run-up to this week’s conference, humanitarians and activist groups said Russia looked ready to deploy tactics to slow or even stall progress toward launching formal negotiations.

“Russia attaches great importance to the successful outcome of the conference and to reaching mutually acceptable agreements that will help strengthen the Inhumane Weapons Convention and further its universalization,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters on Wednesday.

Moscow wants “organizational matters” to be ironed out first and see a process “free from politicization,” she said.

Most tellingly, Zakharova said: “We consider it premature to argue that the time has supposedly come to develop restrictive or prohibitive measures concerning such systems.”

title: How Western Europe’s NATO-first approach is getting in the way of a Ukraine deal
content:
From Abu Dhabi to Dublin, Western Europe is still searching for a common position

A week of diplomacy over Ukraine, from Abu Dhabi to Dublin, has brought the question of Western Europe’s role into focus. Its leaders want a seat at the negotiating table, but what do they intend to do with it?

The delegation the EU and UK have assembled gives a fair picture of its divisions, given its members have yet to agree on what they want to discuss, let alone what they hope to achieve. As things stand, the delegation can do little more than create confusion and make it harder for the other participants to reach an agreement.

That reflects the position Western Europe has taken on the war as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas have made it clear that they see no need to reconsider the security arrangements that took shape after the Cold War. EU leaders refuse to discuss what Moscow calls the ‘root causes’ of the conflict because as they see it, Russia’s objections are Moscow’s problem, and the European security order is theirs to decide.

Read more

Do they really believe that order can survive? It suited Western Europe for a long time, which explains the reluctance to admit that it has outlived its usefulness, but after years of insisting that the system needs no revision, the bloc’s leaders have turned a matter for negotiation into a test of their own political judgement. Any change now looks like an admission of failure, which is why they will defend NATO’s primacy to the end.

Western Europe’s immediate objective is clear: It wants a ceasefire along the current front lines. That calculation is sound enough, but Russia’s position on the battlefield is its strongest argument at the negotiating table, and Moscow retains that leverage as long as the campaign continues. Once the fighting stops, the ‘free world’ can go on the diplomatic offensive and try to recover as much as possible of what the Russian Army has gained.

How much it can recover will depend on the circumstances, but history offers plenty of examples of governments giving up at the negotiating table what their armies won in the field. An immediate ceasefire makes sense from Western Europe’s point of view, but Moscow has equally good reason to resist it. Washington appears to recognize that the dispute over Europe’s security arrangements needs to be addressed. Whether the Americans can persuade the Western Europeans to engage with it is another question, and it’s equally unclear whether the issue is important enough to Washington to make the effort.

title: Time to Home
content:
After a flood or other disaster, finding a safe home can take years. At COP31, we should commit to measuring – and shortening – that wait.

By Amy Pope and Anacláudia Rossbach
UNITED NATIONS, Nov 16 2026 (IPS)

Somewhere tonight, a family that lost its home to the water is asleep in a school gymnasium. The tent, the blankets and the first meal arrived within hours. But a secure home will take years. Every climate disaster ends with the same question, and few climate budgets have a line for it: where will we sleep tonight?

Amy Pope, Director General of IOM, at COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye. Credit: IOM

Humanity has always adapted by moving, and moving is often the most humane adaptation we have. What has changed is the arriving. Families displaced by disasters often seek safety in cities already struggling to provide adequate housing. Globally, about 1.16 billion people live in slums and informal settlements.1  With integrated planning, housing, infrastructure and basic services, cities receiving displaced people can turn arrival into resilience rather than risk.

The scale is no longer in doubt. In 2025, disasters caused 29.9 million internal displacements – 13% above the ten-year average. Almost 13.6 million people were living in displacement caused by disasters at year’s end, 37% more than a year earlier.2  Climate is rarely the only force at work, and conflict and violence triggered more displacements than disasters last year.3  However, climate can deepen these pressures – and people displaced for any reason need somewhere safe to live. We track emissions and estimate disaster losses. But we need a clearer picture of how long families wait for a safe home.

Anacláudia Rossbach, Executive Director, UN-Habitat, speaking at a High level Dialogue in COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye. Credit: UN-Habitat

Two clocks start running after every disaster. The first counts hours and days: rescue, tents, water, food. The second counts months and years: land, permits, finance, construction, tenure. It is slow, and too often no one is accountable for it. Yet the second clock is set in the first weeks. Where a site is placed, whether people have secure rights to occupy the land, whether a shelter can be upgraded rather than replaced: these early choices help determine whether a family is on a path home or into years of limbo. Without sustained support, temporary shelter can become a long-term settlement exposed to the next flood. That gap can deepen poverty and undermine adaptation.

We propose to give that gap a name and a number: time to home. It is the time between the day a family is displaced and the day it is living in a safe, affordable home with secure tenure – meaning protection against forced eviction – whether it chooses to return, settle where it is, or live elsewhere. Building on existing work on durable solutions to internal displacement, this measure would track one essential part of recovery. The idea is simple to grasp: make the wait visible, understand what prolongs it, and work to shorten it. Measuring that wait would bring together the expertise of our two organizations. IOM knows where people go and what they face on the way and where they first find shelter, as the agency that tracks displacement and co-leads the global Shelter, Land and Site Coordination Cluster. UN-Habitat knows what the land, the law and the city allow when they arrive. Working with governments and communities, we can build a clearer picture of the gap and what would help shorten it.

Behind the number lies a conviction we share. A safe home is a foundation for adapting to a changing climate and living with dignity. Without stable housing, people can face greater barriers to enrolling children in school, finding work, opening a bank account, or accessing support. Helping people stay safely, move safely, and find a secure home requires connected policies and investment.

At COP31 in Antalya, we ask governments for three commitments:

    1. Put housing into adaptation plans. Include housing and secure tenure for people who stay and those who move in national adaptation plans and in the implementation of their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, and adopt or pilot time to home among their indicators of progress. Where relocation is necessary, measure whether people have freely made informed decisions and can access safe housing, essential services and work.

    2. Fund the transition to a safe home. Bring adaptation finance and funding for loss and damage together with recovery and development finance to bridge the gap between emergency shelter and long-term housing. Work with local governments and community organizations, including in cities receiving displaced people, so that shelter is a first step toward a secure home. Track how this funding improves people’s housing and safety.

    3. Plan for safe homes before a crisis. Where climate risks are known, identify suitable land and agree with communities on access, tenure and services. Prepare cities to receive people who need to move, so that they have safe options and support before a crisis forces them to leave. Invest in upgrading informal settlements, affordable housing and resilient infrastructure to help people stay safely wherever possible. Throughout these efforts, protect people against forced eviction.

We will not ask of others what we are not prepared to do ourselves. IOM and UN-Habitat are ready to work together to put time to home into practice: drawing on IOM’s displacement tracking and shelter operations and UN-Habitat’s urban and land data, we will work to measure it, and what each month of waiting costs, in selected cities and settlements, and to share what we learn openly, including whether land and tenure, rather than construction, are the longest part of the wait. We invite every government, city and partner that wants to shorten the wait to join us in Antalya.

As climate risks grow, people will continue to adapt where they live, and some will need to move. Everyone should have the chance to build a safe future wherever they live. Climate adaptation has an address. Let us make sure that everyone has one.

Notes and sources

    1.- UN-Habitat estimate for 2024: about 1.16 billion people, or 24.8% of the global urban population, live in slums and informal settlements. UN-Habitat, Transforming informal settlements: Data, standards and practice, session summary, 13th World Urban Forum, Baku, May 2026.

    2.- Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC), Global Report on Internal Displacement 2026: summary, May 2026. In 2025: 29.9 million disaster displacements, 13% above the decadal average; almost 13.6 million people displaced by disasters at year end, 37% more than at the end of 2024. The 13.6 million figure includes people displaced in earlier years who were still displaced at the end of 2025. The 29.9 million figure counts displacements (movements), which can include the same person more than once. Both figures cover all disasters, including geophysical hazards such as earthquakes, not only climate-related events. Full report: doi.org/10.55363/IDMC.ETWG8973.

    3.- IDMC, Global Report on Internal Displacement 2026 (same source). In 2025, conflict and violence triggered a record 32.3 million displacements, more than the 29.9 million caused by disasters, the first time on record. IDMC counts displacements (movements), not distinct individuals.

Amy Pope is the Director General of the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Anacláudia Rossbach is the Executive Director of UN-Habitat.

IPS UN Bureau

title: A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
content:
A fire burned through a building in southern Thailand early Monday, killing 11 people, authorities said.

The fire started around 2 a.m. in the building in Phuket that has a motorcycle rental shop on the ground floor and residences on the upper floors, officials of the local government said. It took firefighters about an hour to bring the fire under control.

There were 17 other people who were slightly injured.

Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but initial investigations found an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started.

Phuket Gov. Chodnarin Koedsom said the rental shop had about 100 motorcycles, along with stored gas, engine oil, plastic materials and tires. He said these combustible materials may have contributed to the rapid spread of the fire and the thick, toxic smoke.

He said the victims appeared to try to escape the fire to the higher floors. One body was found on the third floor and 10 others were found on the fifth floor.

Phuket is on an island in southern Thailand and a popular tourist destination.

title: Trump’s Asia reset: Deals in Manila and Shenzhen, then a rare nuclear summit with Xi and Putin
content:
President Donald Trump is preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington.

Trump’s departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days, even as a nationwide ground stop snarled air traffic and the administration faced tough questions on its handling of the situation.

His trip to Asia, which begins in Manila then continues to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, gives Trump the opportunity to change the narrative from his domestic woes, including the air travel problems and fallout from the November midterm election where his party lost both chambers of Congress.

The controversy over tech powerhouse and chipmaker Nvidia is also certain to hang over Trump’s visit to China, despite efforts by administration officials to downplay the president’s close ties to Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent.

Beijing has said it was not involved. Trump had no plans to raise the issue with Chinese President Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet, said U.S. officials who briefed reporters anonymously about the president’s Asia trip under ground rules set by the White House.

Huang accompanied Trump on Air Force One during the president’s last trip to China in May, and he has been a sporadic presence around Trump at the White House while speaking to him frequently. Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on artificial intelligence, and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition.

Scrutiny of the Trump administration’s actions as they relate to Nvidia has been growing, including on the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to a company led by the alleged Chinese spy with whom Huang had the affair.

Asked about the matter in an interview that aired Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will “leave the internal workings of the Commerce Department to the Commerce Department.

“I think what’s more important here, Larry, is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions ... and at what level?” Bessent told Fox News anchor Larry Kudlow.

He added: “I think we’re going to see answers.”

“Jensen Huang is an incredible innovator, but that does not abrogate their duties of compliance,” Bessent said.

Among the travelers on the Asia trip with Trump will be Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is shaping up to be a top investigative target of the incoming Democratic majority in Congress.

In the Philippines, Trump will meet with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing’s aggression in the region. He plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, the White House said.

Then he heads to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit — and at the end of the trip, the first-ever three-way talks with China's Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss nuclear stockpiles.

Trump and U.S. officials have indicated that the meeting with Putin and Xi will focus on nuclear weapons and that topics of discussion would not include Russia's war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Still, the president has recently played up chances for a settlement to the conflict.

The three-way meeting will also put in the spotlight the ongoing U.S. war with Iran, a country which has often allied with China and Russia. The war has been widely blamed for the Republican Party’s steep losses in the midterms, and while Trump has tried to play down the chances he will order a resumption of major strikes against Iran, he also has said he does not see the need for talks.

China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Monday that the trilateral talks would be of “groundbreaking significance” and that China aimed to have in-depth exchanges about safeguarding world peace and promoting stability.

“Under the current circumstances, the three countries shoulder an important responsibility to work together in addressing global challenges,” she said in a regular briefing in Beijing.

title: Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
content:
Britain's Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since Catherine was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

The royal couple will begin their visit in Mumbai and attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. Founded by William, the environmental initiative awards five winners $1.3 million each to expand solutions addressing climate change.

The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established in 2020, will feature several prominent guests including Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That making its debut performance in India.

“India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country,” William posted on social media.

Shortly after their arrival, the royal couple took part in a game of street cricket in an alley in Ballard Estate, a neighborhood in Mumbai. A common sight across the city, street cricket is an integral part of everyday life in Mumbai.

The couple also will attend events highlighting India’s cricket, fashion and film industries before traveling to New Delhi, where they are scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.

The couple met with Modi on their previous trip to India 10 years ago before William, the eldest son of King Charles III, became the heir to the British throne.

The trip marks a significant return to overseas royal engagements for Catherine, who announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for cancer following major abdominal surgery. Kate, as she is commonly known, disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties.

She traveled to Italy without her husband in May, marking her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.

title: Israel arrests AFP journalist
content:
Israeli troops detained Palestinian videographer Mohammad Ateeq during an overnight raid on his West Bank home

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has arrested a Palestinian journalist working for AFP during an overnight raid in the occupied West Bank, accusing him of links to Hamas without publicly presenting evidence.

Mohammad Ateeq, a videographer who has contributed to the French news agency for three years, was taken into custody at his home in the town of Burqin, near Jenin, early on Sunday.

His wife Ansam, who is eight months pregnant with their first child, said Israeli soldiers arrived at around 1:30 AM and broke down the front door.

“Despite Mohammad calling out, ‘I’ll open!’, they continued to smash the door until it was forced off its hinges. More than 10 soldiers stormed inside to search the premises, while others remained stationed outside,” she told AFP.

The soldiers blindfolded Ateeq, confiscated his two phones, and threw his AFP video camera onto a balcony, according to his wife. She said they also refused to let him put on a winter coat before taking him away.

Read more

The IDF confirmed the arrest, saying Ateeq was “suspected of ties with Hamas,” but provided no further details. His whereabouts were not immediately known.

AFP said it was “very concerned” about Ateeq’s detention and demanded an explanation from the Israeli authorities.

“We demand the Israeli authorities explain clearly why he is being detained and provide evidence. Failure to do this should lead to his immediate release,” the agency said.

Read more

In August, Israeli forces arrested another AFP contributor, Mohammed Awad, near Ramallah. The IDF accused him of operating on behalf of Hamas and advancing terrorist attacks, without publicly providing evidence. He remains in custody.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) has documented 114 arrests of journalists and media workers by Israeli authorities since the Gaza war began on October 7, 2023. Thirty-six journalists remained in detention as of November 11, according to the watchdog.

In October 2024, the IDF accused six Gaza-based Al Jazeera journalists of belonging to Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad, citing what it described as internal militant documents. The Qatar-based network rejected the allegations as based on “fabricated evidence.” Israel had banned Al Jazeera from operating in the country in May that year.

Israeli strikes have also killed several journalists in Gaza and Lebanon this year, including Al Jazeera correspondent Mohammed Samir Washah in April and Al-Manar reporter Ali Shoaib in March. Israel accused Washah of Hamas membership, which he and Al Jazeera denied, and alleged that Shoaib was a Hezbollah intelligence operative. Two other journalists were killed alongside Shoaib, while three Palestinian journalists died in an Israeli strike in Gaza in January.

title: Netanyahu’s office probed over alleged election fraud hoax – media
content:
Israeli authorities are reportedly investigating whether the prime minister’s aides fabricated an Arab vote-buying scandal to discredit the polling

Israel’s police and attorney general are reportedly investigating whether Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office planted false allegations of Arab vote-buying to undermine last month’s parliamentary election, which cost his governing bloc its majority.

The inquiry centers on the arrests of three activists from the Ra’am party on October 27, election day, following allegations that they had offered voters money to boost turnout. All three were subsequently released without charges, raising questions about whether the accusations had been deliberately manufactured.

According to an investigation aired by Israel’s Channel 12 on Sunday, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, contacted the office of Police Commissioner Daniel Levy on the eve of the vote to report suspected vote-buying by Ra’am activists in southern Israel.

Norden also allegedly directed police to an intelligence source who could substantiate the accusations. The source, whom investigators contacted before the arrests, was a former employee of the Prime Minister’s Office, the broadcaster reported.

Read more

Hours later, 14 police officers raided the homes of three Bedouin activists without search warrants. Police announced that they had discovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash.

However, officers found nothing at the home of one suspect, Saef Abu Reash, a doctor from Rahat, who was nevertheless detained for six days before a court ordered his unconditional release and criticized the investigation.

The other two suspects were also released without charges or restrictions. Both denied attempting to buy votes, saying the money recovered from their homes was intended for charity.

Netanyahu and his Likud party repeatedly cited the arrests as evidence of electoral wrongdoing, accusing Arab parties of stealing the election.

Channel 12 reported that Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara and the police’s Investigations and Intelligence Division were now examining whether the information had been deliberately planted to trigger the arrests and provide ammunition for challenging the election’s legitimacy.

Netanyahu’s office dismissed the allegations as “another false report wrapped in dramatic music,” insisting that Norden had merely passed information about suspected criminal activity to police.

Any suggestion of further involvement was “false and grounds for libel,” it said, denying that Norden had contacted police intelligence officials or investigators.

The controversy follows an election in which Arab voter turnout reached nearly 80%, helping Arab parties win 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset. Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats, while the opposition bloc led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot won 48, leaving neither with the majority needed to govern.

Addressing parliament on November 10, Netanyahu accused Arab lawmakers of seeking “the destruction of the Jewish state” and warned against forming a government dependent on their support.  Eisenkot responded by accusing Netanyahu of fueling a “violent and racist” campaign against Arab citizens for political gain.

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

title: Wall Street Review: Stocks Log Weekly Gains Despite Nvidia Concerns, Rising Bond Yields
content:
By Panos Mourdoukoutas

U.S. stocks posted their best week since August as strong results from CoreWeave rekindled investor interest in AI shares, offsetting a late-week tech sell-off triggered by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation.

The S&P 500 rose 2.51 percent for the week to 7,561, outpacing the other major indexes. The Nasdaq Composite gained 2.27 percent to 25,136, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 2.07 percent to 52,347. The small-cap Russell 2000 rose 1.32 percent.

The CBOE Volatility Index, known as Wall Street’s fear gauge, fell 24.73 percent to 19.30.

Yet the week ended on a sour note. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note reached 5.15 percent on Friday, up from about 4.88 percent at the start of the week, after hotter-than-expected inflation data bolstered expectations that the Federal Reserve will resume raising interest rates.

Nvidia Shake-Up

Investors were also unsettled by the resignation of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, which triggered a selloff Thursday in the chip giant and its suppliers.

“Jensen Huang’s resignation is the worst-case scenario during this entire saga, as he was not just a leader, but a visionary for the company,” Michael Landsberg, chief investment officer of Punta Gorda, Florida-based Landsberg Bennett Private Wealth Management, told The Epoch Times.

Huang left days after Nvidia began investigating him following reports that a foreign intelligence operation had targeted him.

Landsberg said there are “big questions” about how Nvidia’s innovation will evolve under Chief Financial Officer and interim CEO Colette Kress, whom he called highly capable and respected.

Nvidia shares fell 12.75 percent for the week. Landsberg said he expects the stock to stay under pressure for some time as it prices in a “leadership discount.”

Lior Prosor, cofounder and managing partner at Deep33 Ventures, was more upbeat.

He said Nvidia’s engineering depth, established ecosystem, and demand that continues to outpace supply have not changed. Still, he noted that investors will want clarity on permanent leadership and several quarters of evidence that the company is executing on its roadmap.

The damage was largely contained to Nvidia and its suppliers. Rivals Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom gained, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF finished Thursday nearly flat. On Friday, however, the ETF fell 3.67 percent, pulling the Nasdaq down 0.91 percent.

Inflation Reignites Rate Worries

The Labor Department’s consumer-price index for October exceeded forecasts, fueling the rise in yields. Headline CPI rose 0.4 percent from September, slower than the prior month’s 0.6 percent gain but above economists’ expectations of 0.3 percent. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, versus expectations of 0.2 percent.

“Tuesday’s CPI was stronger-than-expected, which sets the stage for another rate hike in December,” Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer of Dallas-based Regan Capital, told The Epoch Times. He said voters expressed frustration with inflation in the midterm elections, leaving the Federal Reserve little choice but to follow through.

The 10-year yield climbed above 5 percent on Tuesday, well above the nearly two-month low of 4.84 percent set Nov. 5. Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst at eToro, told The Epoch Times that the yield had retreated for five straight weeks from multidecade highs near 5.4 percent before the inflation report threatened to snap that streak.

He said the shorter end of the curve could be even more sensitive to shifts in Fed expectations.

Stocks fell Tuesday on the data, with the Nasdaq down 0.74 percent, the Russell 2000 off 0.68 percent, the S&P 500 down 0.38 percent and the Dow down 0.30 percent.

CoreWeave Revives AI Trade

Earlier in the week, a strong earnings report from CoreWeave had reignited enthusiasm for artificial-intelligence stocks. The cloud-services provider reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, topping the Zacks consensus estimate of $3.55 billion. It raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $13 billion to $13.3 billion and lifted its adjusted operating income forecast to $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion, a 26 percent increase at the midpoint.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF gained 6 percent Wednesday, helping lift the Nasdaq 1.60 percent. The S&P 500, Dow and Russell 2000 rose 1.31 percent, 0.49 percent and 0.88 percent, respectively. The Treasury market was closed for Veterans Day.

The AI rebound had begun Monday, when chip stocks that had been sold off the prior week led a broad rally. The semiconductor ETF jumped 7.49 percent despite Nvidia’s decline, while the Nasdaq, S&P 500 and Dow rose 2.74 percent, 2.35 percent and 2.15 percent, respectively. The Russell 2000 gained 3.15 percent.

Oil Swings

Energy prices also moved markets. Brent crude settled at $92.57 a barrel on Monday, its lowest since Aug. 31, extending the prior week’s 13.3 percent drop on growing hopes for a diplomatic resolution to the U.S.-Iran conflict. Prices bottomed near $91.50 on Tuesday before rebounding to about $96 on Thursday, amid speculation that Washington no longer needs an agreement with Iran. Rising oil prices and yields weighed on small-cap shares, with the Russell 2000 falling 1.66 percent Thursday.

Outlook

Despite Friday’s declines, with the S&P 500 down 0.40 percent and the Russell 2000 off 0.31 percent while the Dow edged up 0.10 percent, the broader market recovered from steeper early losses.

Weinand said investors have rotated out of AI plays and into more defensive sectors such as healthcare, rattling some leveraged funds and momentum traders. He expects earnings to keep benefiting from heavy government and corporate spending.

“While it would be hard to repeat the earnings growth the market has seen over the past two quarters, 15–20% earnings growth should equate to continued double-digit stock market returns,” he said.

title: Trump Addresses FAA Ground Stop, Wants Congress to Act
content:
By Jack Phillips

President Donald Trump on Nov. 15 said that Congress needs to provide more funding to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) following an outage on Nov. 13 that snarled airline traffic over the weekend.

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old – RIDICULOUS!”

In another post, Trump said that his administration needs Congress to give the money to the FAA “fast.”

“We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems,” he wrote, adding that the “FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.”

The posts from Trump on Nov. 15 are the first comments he has made about the outage, which affected thousands of flights across the country.

Starting just before 4 p.m. on Nov. 13, the FAA announced a ground stop for all commercial airplanes in the United States. The agency canceled it at 8:15 p.m. that night.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, whose department leads the FAA, told CBS News on Nov. 15 that there are “some delays in the airspace right now” but that full service should return by Nov. 16.

Duffy said on Nov. 13 that outdated and analog technology was to blame for the stop and added that intermittent telecom outages affected the stability of communications and radar systems used by air traffic control.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Duffy said, noting that he and the president have been talking about it for the past two years, and that the president had for a year been asking Congress to fund a full rebuild of the control system.

Before the ground stop was declared, FAA switches and routers “got overloaded with data” and forced the shutdown, Duffy said.

“I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump and our new IP switches did not go down,” he said. “It’s the old hardware that went down.”

Also on Nov. 15, Trump criticized the previous administration, writing on Truth Social that “big money” that was allocated to the federal government was “spent unwisely,” making “an old and broken system worse than when they began.”

In 2021, President Joe Biden signed into law a massive infrastructure bill, which set aside $25 billion for the FAA to improve airports and its traffic control towers, to redevelop airport terminals, and to “upgrade the foundation” of the air traffic control system, according to the FAA.

Then last year, the Republican-controlled Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA as part of the party’s sweeping tax cut package. Duffy has repeatedly described that funding as a down payment on a broader overhaul of the aging system.

In a post on X, Duffy said he spoke with the CEO of aerospace and defense contractor L3Harris, which is also the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure contractor. He said the company has now secured two routers in Texas and Arkansas facilities and “is now conducting deep diagnostics testing at their headquarters in Florida.”

Duffy said in a Nov. 15 interview with NBC News that L3Harris got the contract “decades ago” and owns the network that allows communication for the FAA.

“Which is why I’m asking for billions of dollars from Congress to build a brand-new architecture of a network by the best companies in the world including AT&T, Verizon, and Lumens,” he said.

Also on Nov. 15, Duffy wrote on X that there is no indication that a foreign cyberattack was behind the outage. The incident is under investigation, he said.

In an emailed statement to The Epoch Times on Nov. 15, the FAA pointed to a “questions and answers” section on the agency’s website.
