title: SpaceX Successfully Returns Starship to Launch Pad
content:
By T.J. Muscaro

SpaceX’s first attempt to return Starship to the launch tower was a success.

After a 22 1/2-hour mission, the Starship upper stage dropped through the clouds over Starbase, Texas. A crowd of hundreds on-site erupted in celebration as Starship 42 fired its Raptor engines, slowed to a hover, and eased itself into the catching arms of the tower, known as Mechazilla.

Chants of “USA! USA!” could be heard in the background as the engines cut off and sealed a new chapter of spaceflight history. SpaceX’s Starship has become the first rocket to prove that it can make a controlled return to the launch pad in its entirety, with each half returning successfully—albeit on two separate flights.

No recovery teams off in some distant corner of the globe. No time lost in the additional travel time needed to return the spacecraft from its landing site back to the spaceport. SpaceX has demonstrated that the world’s largest rocket in operation can lift off a launch pad, place the super-heavy booster back on that same launch pad through a controlled automated return maneuver, and have the second half return as well to be caught by the tower. Ultimately, those tower arms would place the Starship back on the booster for another flight.

This 15th Starship mission began on the evening of Nov. 13. Immediately after launch, the super-heavy booster was also supposed to return for a catch back at the launch pad. However, during its return, its automated systems found it off course and aborted the return, opting for a soft splashdown just off the coast. The booster has completed a successful “catch” and return on previous missions.

Starship’s journey home began about 21 hours and 35 minutes after liftoff, when mission controllers reignited one of its Raptor engines for a de-orbit burn. This maneuver slowed Starship enough to pull it out of orbit and undertake a controlled, gradual fall back to Southeast Texas.

The spacecraft began re-entering the Earth’s atmosphere just past the 22-hour mark of the flight. The black-and-silver hull glowed a bright purple as it penetrated the layers of gases and used the pressure to slow down.

Three separate checkpoints were added into the 14-orbit flight plan to allow Starship to make an early return back to Earth, and it passed all three with flying colors. After the de-orbit burn, flight controllers held a final Go/No-Go for Starship’s return to the launch pad. If a No-Go had been issued, Starship would have been set up for another ditch into the ocean.

Starship passed over land, from the Pacific, over northern Mexico, back toward Starbase, Texas, and out over the Gulf of America before making one final “swoop” maneuver to line up for a final approach. Just as it came back over the Gulf, on-board autonomous systems had time for one final evaluation and to make the call to ditch into the water instead. But all systems remained nominal.

What was once only the subject of computer-animated renderings is now reality. Both Starship’s super-heavy booster and upper stage have demonstrated that they can return to their launch point, ready for reuse.

It marks a major development milestone for what is promised to be the world’s first entirely reusable launch vehicle, and it comes at a very fast-moving point in U.S. spaceflight. Work continues to make the Kennedy Space Center fit to handle Starship. A SpaceX Gigabay is under construction near NASA’s Vehicle Assembly Building, with plans to build a facility similar to Starbase’s Starfactory in development, and modifications are being made to historic Launch Pad 39A.

A SpaceX Starship will launch from Florida’s Space Coast as part of NASA’s Artemis III mission in 2027.

title: The driverless taxis, robots and tech companies in APEC host city Shenzhen show China's ambitions
content:
The app showed one minute until the taxi’s arrival. Not far from the pickup spot, the blue and white SUV with a small robot graphic on its sides approached through the light traffic. It looked like any other car, except that no one was behind the wheel.

Welcome to Shenzhen, a hub of technological development in China, where some of the latest advancements are taking shape, from artificial intelligence and robotics to electric and autonomous vehicles.

While some of these innovations can now be seen in other Chinese cities, Shenzhen has long been considered one of the country’s leading technology centers and is home to some of its best-known companies, like the telecommunication firm Huawei, electric vehicle maker BYD and internet and gaming giant Tencent.

The city will draw more attention as it hosts this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Chinese President Xi Jinping will welcome representatives from APEC’s 21 members, including U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia’s leader Vladimir Putin.

The gathering comes as China and the U.S. compete for leadership in technologies such as artificial intelligence in a rivalry intertwined with disputes over tariffs and access to critical minerals, and as a trade truce was recently extended until January.

Shenzhen’s transformation from a testing ground for market-oriented reforms into a tech center reflects China’s rise as a global economic competitor.

“Shenzhen is one of the most important symbols of China’s reform and opening up through its strong global role in trade, manufacturing, and innovation,” said Gary Ng, senior economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.

From a fishing town to a special economic zone

The city's transformation dates to 1980, when China was opening up its economy. Then-leader Deng Xiaoping declared the former fishing village as one of China's first special economic zones, where the Communist Party would allow free enterprise. That opened the door to foreign investment and manufacturing for export until it also became a place for companies to develop their own technologies.

Shenzhen is now a metropolis of more than 18 million people. From the observation deck of China’s second-tallest building, the 600-meter (1,968-foot) Ping An tower, people can see a city of glass towers amid green spaces, with mountains rising through parts of it.

This is a city known as a place to see driverless taxis, robots and electric vehicles, though some of the technologies aren't visible everywhere.

Drone deliveries only serve specific locations, while driverless taxis or robotaxis begin at designated pickup spots on the western side of the city. And some restrictions were imposed ahead of the APEC summit, being held Wednesday and Thursday. Drone deliveries were suspended, and robotaxi services were reduced.

A ride without a driver

Pony.ai is one of the companies providing driverless taxis, with a fleet of almost 2,000 SUVs painted in blue and white, the image of a small robot named “Popo” on their sides. Founded in 2016, the company operates in Shenzhen and three other Chinese cities: Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou.

But the robotaxis cannot go anywhere you want. Trips are limited to designated pickup and drop-off points within approved service areas.

One of the few places where passengers could take a robotaxi a week before the summit was in front of Tencent, the company behind the messaging and payment app WeChat.

Three AP journalists took a trip to one of the available destinations, a hotel 7.6 kilometers (4.7 miles) away.

The app warned that passengers had less than 60 seconds to get in. Once inside the car, an Arcfox, a screen displayed “Popo” giving safety instructions and asking customers to fasten their seatbelts.

For 24 minutes, the car crossed several streets, slowing down at corners and stopping completely for people and red lights. Near a corner where it needed to turn left, it switched on its turn signal and waited. When the traffic light turned green and traffic began moving, another driver let it through.

The ride was smooth — and the cost was 12.7 yuan ($1.90), cheaper than a regular taxi because of a first-trip discount.

Cong Lin, Pony.ai's public affairs representative, said the cars use 34 sensors and are able to perceive 360 degrees with a range of up to 650 meters (about 2,132.5 feet). The robotaxis averaged about 23 and 25 trips each day in February, she said.

Does the company envision a day when all taxis in Shenzhen are driverless? “We don’t see robotaxis as a replacement for regular cars or regular taxis,” Lin said. “We see ourselves as just one more option for the riders to choose from.”

Companies say Shenzhen offers policy support and suppliers at hand

When China marked 40 years of Shenzhen as special economic zone, in 2020, Xi described the city as “a miracle in the world development history.”

Government support is among the factors that have helped shape its growth and attracted migrants and entrepreneurs from other cities.

“The more flexible and open government policies have enabled experimentation different from the rest of China. At the same time, the proximity to Hong Kong is important for attracting capital, developing commercial expertise, and accessing world markets,” said Ng, from Natixis.

Cong, from Pony.ai, said Shenzhen offers “policy clarity (and) government support, so there’s a very clear pathway for autonomous driving companies like us to follow, from the testing with a safety operator on board to a commercial service with a safety operator on board to fully driverless.”

Shenzhen is also home to Pudu robotics, which makes service robots that deliver meals in restaurants, clean floors and guide shoppers to products. The company, founded here in 2016, develops humanoid robots and wheeled robots with arms, focusing on specific tasks such as picking up and delivering items in office buildings and packing goods in warehouses.

Guo Cong, chief technology officer and co-founder of Pudu, said the city provides what the company needs, from suppliers of hardware and mechanical parts to software and businesses putting their robots to work.

He added that supply chain support can arrive within half a day, while customers are close so engineers can visit within an hour or two.

“Shenzhen shows Chinese speed, and also shows Chinese strategy for efficiency and innovation to the global world,” he said. “Shenzhen is a pioneer part of China that really shows this kind of spirit to the world.”

A city that keeps drawing new people

People from across China have been moving to Shenzhen for decades. While some neighborhoods resemble other Chinese cities, some residents see it as a place with a distinctive energy.

“My impression of Shenzhen is that it’s a vibrant, youthful city, and its residents are well-mannered,” said Zhong Luqin, a kindergarten teacher who moved to Shenzhen from Zhanjiang, another city in Guangdong province.

“There is a broadly-used comment to describe Shenzhen: ‘workers with a hustle mentality’,” she added minutes after taking a selfie with an APEC summit sign in the background. “It captures the city’s very fast pace of life.”

___

Associated Press video producer Olivia Zhang and writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

___

This story corrects that the range of Pony.ai’s robotaxi sensors is 650 meters, not 615 meters, and also the public affairs officer title.

title: Guatemala Decrees State of Emergency in Two Departments After Lawmaker Killed in Attack
content:
By Reuters

GUATEMALA CITY—Guatemalan authorities on Saturday decreed a state of emergency in the eastern departments of Zacapa and Izabal, banning gatherings and boosting powers for security forces, a week after a lawmaker and three police officers were killed in an attack.

The decree limits outdoor gatherings and allows security officials to disperse groups by force, as well as to make arrests and enter residences without a warrant. It is effective immediately and through the next 30 days.

The two neighboring departments span an area roughly the size of Qatar.

The announcement follows a series of armed attacks in Zacapa, including the shooting of lawmaker Julio Cesar Portillo in Rio Hondo on November 6. Portillo was taken to a hospital but later died of his injuries. Three police officers were also killed in the attack, President Bernardo Arevalo later announced.

Authorities did not identify who was responsible, but the attack occurred amid heightened concerns over the influence of organized crime. Washington this week designated several crime groups operating in Zacapa as terrorist organizations and has accused them of ties to Mexican drug trafficking cartels.

“The Government of Guatemala remains committed to protecting the lives, safety, and peace of Guatemalan families,” the government said in a statement, adding the state of emergency aimed to protect the local population.

title: Fetterman Suggests He Could Leave Democrats If Next Senate Leader Hostile to Israel
content:
By Jack Phillips

Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) suggested he may leave the Democratic Party if Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) becomes the next Senate majority leader amid a leadership battle in the upper congressional chamber.

“It would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being very anti-hostile to Israel,” Fetterman said in a Fox News interview, released Saturday, when asked whether there is a “red line” that would make him “walk away” from the Democratic Party.

Fetterman’s comments were made after Van Hollen announced Thursday that he would challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to be the Senate Democratic leader.

In a post on X, Van Hollen wrote that in the midterms, voters “called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption.”

“To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call,” he wrote.

Fetterman, who is up for reelection in 2028, has consistently broken with some Democrats on supporting Israel and other issues. However, he has said he doesn’t plan on becoming a Republican.

Responding to the Pennsylvania senator, Van Hollen told “Fox News Sunday” that “it’s widely known that Sen. Fetterman is worried about a Democratic primary in his state of Pennsylvania, and so may be looking for an exit ramp.”

Van Hollen said that his position on Israel is that taxpayers “should not be providing a blank check to Israel, or any government.” He also criticized Israel’s government for backing settlers in the West Bank.

“First of all, I hope Sen. Fetterman will stay true to his economic populist message, and that’s something that I would support,” Van Hollen also remarked.

Weeks before the midterm elections, during which Democrats took significant majorities in both the House and Senate to recapture Congress, President Donald Trump welcomed the idea of Fetterman becoming a Republican.

“I’d love to see him as a Republican,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in October. “He does better as a Republican than he does as a Democrat.”

Previously, Fetterman had rejected the idea of switching parties, writing in a Washington Post opinion article published in May that voters would consider him a “terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats.”

“It wasn’t long ago when Democrats wanted a secure border,” he also wrote. “I voted on an immigration bill in 2024 to make sure an influx the size of Pittsburgh doesn’t come through the border like it did under the previous administration. I have co-sponsored legislation to stop the flow of fentanyl.”

His relationship with fellow Democrats became more tenuous after he recorded a video for the Republican midterm convention in September that praised Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), suggesting there were extremists in his party.

“I’m always going to stand with America,” Fetterman said in the video. “I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life.”

In a statement on Nov. 12, Schumer said that he has enough votes in the Senate to remain majority leader during the next Congress.

“I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” he wrote, adding that he welcomes “any discussion about the future of our caucus.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Houthis tighten grip on key Red Sea shipping route (VIDEOS)
content:
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have abandoned positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait as the rebels advance toward Aden

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have withdrawn from positions overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, giving the Iran-backed Houthi rebels greater control over the strategic waterway.

The strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, is a vital shipping route between Asia and Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal. Its importance has grown as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted by the US-Israeli war against Iran. The withdrawal could give the Houthis additional leverage over commercial shipping and further complicate Gulf oil producers’ access to key export routes.

The Southern Armed Forces, allied with the internationally recognized Yemeni government, announced on Sunday that they were redeploying from Dhubab Airport and positions near Bab el-Mandeb, west of Taiz Governorate, to reinforce defenses around Aden, where the government is based. The move follows Houthi advances into neighboring Lahj Governorate, bringing the group closer to the southern port city.

“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats,” the Southern Armed Forces said in a statement.

Saudi-backed forces have RETREATED from Bab el-Mandeb, leaving the Houthis in control of a strategic gateway to the Red Sea. THE SAUDIS ARE IN RETREAT. THE HOUTHIS REMAIN LOCKED AND LOADED. https://t.co/ioqoXOAcT5

— Steve Hanke (@steve_hanke) November 15, 2026

Military spokesman Majid Al-Nazili also appealed to the international community to help restore government control over Bab el-Mandeb and the western coast, citing the strait’s importance for international shipping and trade.

Saudi Air Force fighter jets accidentally bombed a large column of their own PLC/Southern Forces who were trying to escape the incoming Ansarallah encirclement near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, reportedly results in dozens of casualties. https://t.co/x1fncjaRQw

— AMK Mapping 🇳🇿 (@AMK_Mapping_) November 15, 2026

Fighting has threatened the Kharaz refugee camp in Lahj Governorate, home to around 9,600 displaced people, according to the United Nations. UNHCR said insecurity and nearby shelling had disrupted essential services and prompted families to flee. Yemen’s Human Rights Ministry reported that a Somali refugee woman was killed when the camp was shelled on Thursday.

Humanitarian conditions are also worsening in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where fighting has blocked aid deliveries and prevented civilians from leaving. The city is sheltering roughly 150,000 people displaced by the latest escalation.

Read more

The Houthis, a Shiite armed movement, have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, since 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in the civil war in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

Fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but erupted again in July after Yemeni government forces struck Sanaa International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The plane was diverted to Houthi-controlled Hodeidah, while the rebels blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack.

The rebels launched a major offensive in September, capturing the strategic port city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, including Perim, Zuqar and the Hanish archipelago. Government forces subsequently recaptured some coastal positions before announcing Sunday’s withdrawal. The Houthis have also stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and energy facilities.

On Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition reported intercepting two Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh and three drones over the Mecca and Medina regions. The Houthis had previously denied targeting Mecca, one of Islam’s holiest cities.

title: Meta fined nearly $900 million in Facebook photo privacy ruling
content:
Italy’s watchdog says the app accessed Android users’ pictures and videos without specific, informed consent

Italy’s privacy watchdog has fined Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, €805 million ($887 million). Facebook, it claims, accesses users’ photos and videos on Android devices without obtaining informed consent.

In a statement on Saturday, the Italian Data Protection Authority said it had launched an investigation in July 2025 into a Facebook feature that suggests photos and videos from users’ phone galleries for posting on the platform.

According to the regulator, the feature is enabled by default through a single permission covering multiple functions. The authorization notice, which asks users to consent to “enable other features,” fails to make clear that they are also allowing Facebook to suggest content from their galleries, the watchdog said.

Once full permission is granted, the app can continuously access the device’s entire photo and video archive, with users and regulators unable to verify what information is actually being accessed or used, according to the regulator.

The watchdog gave Meta 60 days to change how its Facebook app requests consent for the feature and explicitly inform users about its purpose, while keeping it disabled by default unless they provide separate, informed consent.

The authority said the breach potentially affected a significant number of people, noting that Italy has an estimated 20 million Android users. It also accused Meta of failing to cooperate with the investigation.

The regulator said it may separately investigate a feature introduced earlier this year that allows cloud processing of Facebook users’ gallery content.

A Meta spokesperson said the company would appeal the “disproportionate” fine.

Read more

“This is a simple feature that helps people share photos and videos on Facebook. Users must grant permission on their device before the feature can operate, and they can change that permission at any time in their settings,” Meta said.

Last month, a court in New Mexico ordered Mark Zuckerberg’s company to pay $25 billion in civil penalties for violating the US state’s Unfair Practices Act. The New Mexico Department of Justice described the verdict as a “landmark victory,” saying it “has secured one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.”

The case followed the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which the British political consulting firm obtained personal data from tens of millions of Facebook users without their consent and used it to target voters with political messaging, including during Donald Trump’s successful 2016 US presidential campaign. The New Mexico case also involved broader allegations that Facebook misled users about its privacy practices, third-party access to personal data, and content moderation.

Meta also faces a potential fine of up to 6% of its worldwide annual turnover after European Union regulators preliminarily found that the US tech giant had failed to adequately assess and mitigate risks to Facebook and Instagram users’ wellbeing from features that encourage compulsive use. These include autoplay, infinite scroll, push notifications, and highly personalized recommendation systems.

A final decision has yet to be made, with Meta rejecting the allegations.

title: NATO cancels 2027 leaders’ summit
content:
The US-led military bloc will not hold a top-level meeting in Tirana in 2027, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has said

NATO has dropped plans to hold a leaders’ summit in 2027, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has said. The summit was supposed to be held in the Albanian capital of Tirana. The decision comes as tensions between Washington and its European NATO allies continue to mount.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized Washington’s European NATO allies over their defense spending and refusal to support the US military campaign against Iran.

Speaking on Thursday, Rama said that “there is not yet a common position on when the [NATO] summit will happen, for sure not in 2027.” He added that “in 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana.”

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, meanwhile, played down the change, telling the Associated Press that the military bloc is “flexible” with its summits and will convene one “when a necessity is there.”

The declaration adopted at NATO’s 2025 summit in The Hague stated that the leaders looked “forward to our next meeting in Türkiye in 2026 followed by a meeting in Albania.” However, any mention of the Balkan nation was conspicuously absent from a similar document issued after this year’s gathering in Ankara.

In April, Reuters reported, citing several officials speaking anonymously, that NATO members were considering holding fewer summits, breaking with the recent practice of annual gatherings. Some of the sources cited a desire to avoid confrontations with Trump.

Read more

Moreover, NATO has throttled back its ministerial meetings, canceling the customary October gathering of defense chiefs this year, with none scheduled for 2027 either. The number of foreign ministers’ get-togethers has likewise been reduced from two to one for next year.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have either not attended or left early during some of the previous meetings.

Earlier this year, US envoy to NATO Matthew Whitaker said that Europe only ranked fourth among Washington’s global security priorities, taking a back seat to the “defense of the homeland,” as well as the situation in the Western Hemisphere and the Pacific.

“For 77 years our NATO allies have taken advantage of the United States’ strength,” Whitaker told Newsmax in August.

Whitaker's remarks followed a Bloomberg report claiming that Washington was intending to make continued military support for European NATO member states contingent on whether they had “been publicly supportive” of US foreign-policy initiatives, including those in the Middle East and Western Hemisphere.

Ahead of the July summit in Ankara, Trump told reporters that he was “very disappointed with NATO,” suggesting that Washington could further scale back its military footprint in Europe.

“I just want loyalty. You know, we’re so loyal to them. We are always fighting for them,” the US president said earlier.

Hegseth previously accused European NATO members of
denying Washington predictable access to their bases and airspace during the US military campaign against Iran, an apparent reference to France, Spain, and Italy. He concluded that NATO had degenerated into a “paper tiger and a one-way street” following the end of the Cold War.

title: Boris Johnson’s vodka ‘punishment’ claim gets a sobering response from Moscow
content:
The former British prime minister claims Sergey Lavrov forced him to drink heavily beside a blazing fireplace during a 2017 visit to Moscow

Moscow has poured cold water on former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s claim that he was forced to drink vodka during a visit to Russia, saying he willingly embraced Russian hospitality and repeatedly asked for refills.

Johnson complained earlier this week that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov had subjected him to a grueling vodka-drinking session beside a blazing fireplace during a December 2017 visit to Moscow, when he was Britain’s foreign secretary.

Speaking to former Colombian President Ivan Duque on his Tres Respuestas podcast about his failed attempt to reset relations with Russia at the time, Johnson called Lavrov a “ghastly man” who had made him drink a “huge amount of vodka.”

“He made me drink a huge amount of vodka in front of a very hot fire,” Johnson recalled. “It was literally like a sort of Victorian public school punishment. It was terrible.”

Instead he then met with Lavrov, and this terrible man got him drunk on vodka in front of a hot fireplace 🙈🤦‍♂️🤣 pic.twitter.com/K2idv4HkDn

— Roberto (@UniqueMongolia) November 15, 2026

Johnson’s account, however, was disputed by Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, who was also present at the alleged vodka marathon.

Read more

“He could have chosen the wine that was right in front of him. But he chose to indulge himself,” Zakharova told Komsomolskaya Pravda on Sunday. “I remember that lunch. Johnson kept asking for more.”

Johnson’s vodka horror story also failed to convince one of his own countrymen. Former British diplomat Ian Proud, who served at the UK Embassy in Moscow at the time, dismissed it as a “gross exaggeration.” According to Proud, the visit involved an official meeting followed by lunch. He said met Johnson immediately afterward, witnessing no vodka-induced catastrophe.

READ MORE: How Britain built a war network around Russia

“He was absolutely not drunk nor showing signs of having consumed vast amounts of vodka,” Proud wrote on X.

@BorisJohnson is lying. For the record, when he visited Moscow in December 2017, the plan was never for him to meet President Putin. The plan was only and always for Johnson to meet Lavrov. At this time the UK had had practically no face to face ministerial contact with Russia since before the Ukraine started, except for a brief visit by David Lidington in December 2015. While Putin would meet some visiting Foreign Ministers - e.g. John Kerry and Lex Rillerson - there was absolutely no way he would see us, at the bottom of the EU pile behind Germany and France. The fireside vodka tale is also a gross exaggeration. There was a meeting with officials present followed by a lunch after which he departed with the whole entourage. Yes alcohol was being served but the idea that Lavrov plied him with vast amounts of Vodka is simply untrue. I greeted Johnson at Plekhanov Economic University immediately after he departed the Foreign Ministry and spent the whole time there with him - he was absolutely not drunk nor showing signs of having consumed vast amounts of vodka. In late 2017 UK-Russia relations were in their best shape for some time. In the run up to the Johson visit , Junior Minister Alan Duncan had visited (two visits in the space of a month was unprecedented) to discuss world cup preparations and agree a new diplomatic visa handover. The Archbishop of Canterbury had just visited. Plans were afoot for Prince William to attend the England v Belgium game in the FIFA World Cup of 2018. Yes Salisbury happened and everything went down the toilet. But the idea that everything was terrible is simply untrue.

— Ian Proud (@proud_diplomat) November 14, 2026

Interestingly, during that same visit, Johnson, now one of Britain’s most outspoken Russia hawks, declared himself a “convinced Russophile.” However, his professed affection for Moscow proved short-lived. During his premiership, he became one of Kiev’s staunchest Western backers and a vocal advocate of confronting Russia. His April 2022 visit to Kiev later stirred controversy, with Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia accusing Johnson of helping derail peace negotiations in Istanbul that could have brought the Ukraine conflict to an early end.

READ MORE: Moscow has stopped calling Britain ‘Great.’ Here’s why

Johnson’s supposed vodka ordeal is particularly curious given his famously warm relationship with alcohol. In 2019, he told Politico he had enjoyed a “long and happy relationship” with drinking. His fondness for a tipple later acquired political consequences during the notorious Partygate scandal, which saw police investigate lockdown-breaching gatherings in Downing Street during the Covid-19 pandemic. Johnson was fined for attending a gathering held to mark his birthday in June 2020, when Covid restrictions were in force.

title: Pope Leo visits Peru's Amazon to spotlight threats to Indigenous communities
content:
The plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the Amazon take center stage Sunday as Pope Leo XIV travels across Peru to visit communities high in the Andes and deep in the rainforest.

On the penultimate day of his visit to his adopted homeland, Leo is expected to echo Pope Francis, emphasizing Catholic teaching that links care for the most vulnerable with care for Gods creation.

He travels first to Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, before flying to the Amazonian city of Pucallpa, where illegal mining, deforestation and threats to Indigenous communities will be central concerns.

The church in Peru perceives the continuity of his commitment to accompany Indigenous peoples in the defense of life and the care of the territory, which is increasingly threatened by deforestation and illegal mining, Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, president of the Amazon bishops conference, told The Associated Press.

Leo is clearing the path laid out by Francis on environmental protection and human rights, Barreto said. He added that the pope would hear about violence affecting children and young people.

From the Andes to the Amazon

The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, will test the stamina of the pope, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery.

His schedule begins at the historic Sacsayhuamn fortress, where he will speak about local religious devotion. In the Plaza de Armas, he will present a shroud from the Holy See for the image of the Lord of the Earthquakes, a focus of devotion in a country prone to seismic activity. He will then deliver a message to the sick before leaving for Pucallpa.

In the rainforest city of 434,000 people, Leo is expected to reinforce Francis teachings on protecting the environment and Indigenous communities threatened by illegal mining and other forms of exploitation.

The Rev. Luca Zanta, one of the visits organizers, said Leo would primarily listen to the Amazonian Indigenous peoples, including the Shipibo, Ashninka, and Kukama communities gathered beside Lake Yarinacocha.

Zanta said Leo would lead a symbolic planting of a shihuahuaco, a native rainforest tree that can live for more than 1,000 years and grow dozens of meters tall.

That is a symbol of how we want our common house to be. We want the Catholic Church to live long, protect those who need it and see its values and beauty admired by generations and generations, Zanta told local radio Saturday.

Indigenous communities face mounting threats

The Rev. Peter Hughes, an 84-year-old Irish priest who has lived in Peru for more than six decades, said the visit reflects the churchs concern for the poor.

In Latin American terms, the Indigenous peoples, or what is left of them, are the most important collective representing the truly poor, he said. That is what makes leaders like Pope Francis and Pope Leo speak the language of the Gospel in very human terms, putting a premium on justice and peace. In the Christian sense of justice, the most important people are the poor, the marginalized, and those who have no voice.

Illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Miners use makeshift suction dredges and mercury, a toxic metal, to extract gold.

This global context of war and conflict has contributed to gold prices rising to historic highs, and the direct impact of this is that gold which is present in all Amazonian rivers can be extracted using mercury, particularly if you want to do this on a large scale, said Raphael Hoetmer, Western Amazon program director at Amazon Watch.

Its causing pollution, health issues, and environmental degradation, he said.

On Saturday, police reported three operations against illegal mining in Madre de Dios, one of the countrys most biodiverse regions. They said they destroyed extraction equipment, including rafts and motors, valued at $4.1 million.

Illegal mining also drives deforestation and encroaches on Indigenous territories, threatening ancestral lands and exposing communities to violence and organized crime.

Isolated peoples are especially vulnerable

Leo is also expected to address sexual violence against women and girls. Barreto said the pope would likely pay particular attention to a recent case in Condorcanqui province in the northern Amazon, where teachers sexually abused Indigenous Awajn and Wampis girls.

There is particular concern in Peru for Indigenous peoples living in isolation, including the Mashco Piro in the forests of southeastern Madre de Dios.

Images released by Survival International in 2024 showed dozens of Mashco Piro people near logging concessions. Clashes between Indigenous people and loggers that year left at least two loggers dead.

Concerns also extend to Kakataibo communities living in isolation or initial contact.

They have reservations that should protect them. But the Peruvian government is increasingly unwilling to acknowledge the existence of these peoples, Hoetmer said. And their reserves are also being invaded by drug cartels because, of course, theyre ideal places for them to operate since no one can get in.

title: Israel kills senior Hamas commander in Gaza two months after killing his predecessor as ceasefire stagnates
content:
Israel killed a senior Hamas commander involved in planning the October 7 attacks only two months after killing his predecessor, a fresh sign of how the Gaza conflict remains active despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in place.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) killed Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, the commander of Hamas Rafah Brigade, in a strike in southern Gaza overnight Saturday, both Hamas and the IDF said.

Abu Younis, who was a long-time member of the brigade, had replaced Nael Abu Obeid, the previous commander who was killed in a strike in September. And Abu Obeid himself replaced Mohammad Sabaneh, another commander of the Rafah Brigade who was killed in May 2025.

The strike comes just days after an Israeli attack on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in what the IDF said was an attempt to kill another Hamas commander.

In a statement, Hamas military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, acknowledged the death of Abu Younis, saying he had joined the brigade in 1991 and was among the most prominent commanders who participated in planning and overseeing the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023.

The IDF continues to eliminate Hamas leaders in Gaza, and another one joins his predecessors in the depths of hell, said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. The offensive policy that I am leading together with the Prime Minister and the IDF in Gaza will continue until Gaza is demilitarized and there is no Hamas.

The killing of Abu Younis underscores an emerging pattern in Gaza. Despite a nominal ceasefire that went into effect more than one year ago, Israel has continued to carry out strikes targeting members of Hamas, particularly senior commanders. But those commanders are quickly replaced as Hamas entrenches its own grip on power over the half of Gaza not occupied by Israel.

Meanwhile, the Board of Peace, a body created by the Trump administration with United Nations backing to oversee the Gaza ceasefire plan, remains sidelined, unable to make any substantive progress on the 20-point plan agreed to in October 2025.

On Friday, the board said it had held very constructive discussions with 17 countries about a civilian Gaza police force under the authority of a Palestinian technocratic committee that was supposed to run Gaza. But that committee has yet to enter the enclave, and an international security force meant to stabilize Gaza has yet to materialize.

The IDF strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza last week killed at least six people, including a doctor and a child, according to Palestinian officials. The strike hit the hospitals surgery unit, killing Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira and a 13-year-old boy who was awaiting surgery. A total of 40 others were injured in the strike, including two doctors who were in critical condition, officials said.

In a statement, the IDF said it had targeted the commander of Hamas Khan Younis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, as well as additional terrorists who were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis. But when pressed on whether Abu Ismail was killed in the strike, the IDF did not answer.

Doctors Without Borders (Mdicins Sans Frontires, or MSF) condemned the strike, saying: It is unconscionable that patients and medical staff are once again being killed and injured inside a hospital, a place where lives should be saved, not taken. MSF withdrew its own staff from the hospital in January because of the presence of armed men inside, as well as concerns over the hospitals neutrality and management. Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected, MSF said.

The Board of Peace also urged both Israel and Hamas to uphold their commitments under the Comprehensive Peace Plan and protect civilians.

According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 people have been killed in near-daily Israeli strikes in Gaza since the ceasefire was signed one year ago.

The shattered territory also faces an unfolding humanitarian crisis ahead of the onset of winter. Last week, seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, where nearly two million Palestinians remain displaced.

Israel said that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but it has refused to allow in the heavy equipment needed for large-scale clean-up and rubble removal efforts.

The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms, said Israels Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories.

title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
content:
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.

The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.

The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.

“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.”

Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.

Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.

“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.”

The government apparently wants to rush the bill through Parliament

The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings.

Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others.

“We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading.

Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.”

Babiš has opposed other EU policies

Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom.

He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves.

Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion.

His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry.

"While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said.

___

Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report.

title: Zelenskyy warns Starshield restrictions threaten Ukraine’s energy defenses ahead of winter
content:
Restrictions on Ukraines Starshield satellite communications system are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.

He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musks SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraines energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.

Ukraines interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 kph (100 mph) along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said.

We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted, he wrote on social media. The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the Presidents Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX. It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine.

Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control.

Outages after Russian strike on power facility

Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraines Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram.

The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire.

The strike hit a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks, temporarily leaving about 41,000 customers without power, Kiper said.

Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a 2-year-old boy, Ukraines State Emergency Service said Sunday.

Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian attack kills 1 in Russia's Rostov region

Ukrainian drone strikes damaged two electrical substations in Russias Rostov region, killing a chief engineer, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Sunday.

Four people were injured when drone debris fell on their cars, Slyusar wrote on social media. A fifth person was wounded when debris struck a production facility in the village of Troitskoye, he said.

Ukrainian forces also targeted Russias Tatarstan region, officials said. Radmir Belyaev, mayor of Nizhnekamsk, the regions third-largest city, said a large-scale and prolonged attack damaged its industrial zone.

Six people were injured, and heating and hot water supplies were disrupted in parts of the city, he said.

Russias Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.

Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a 2-year-old boy, Ukraines State Emergency Service said Sunday.

Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian attack kills 1 in Russia's Rostov region

Ukrainian drone strikes damaged two electrical substations in Russias Rostov region, killing a chief engineer, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Sunday.

Four people were injured when drone debris fell on their cars, Slyusar wrote on social media. A fifth person was wounded when debris struck a production facility in the village of Troitskoye, he said.

Ukrainian forces also targeted Russias Tatarstan region, officials said. Radmir Belyaev, mayor of Nizhnekamsk, the regions third-largest city, said a large-scale and prolonged attack damaged its industrial zone.

Six people were injured, and heating and hot water supplies were disrupted in parts of the city, he said.

Russias Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.

title: UK must be ready to strike Russian Arctic – ex-PM
content:
Moscow says it has never threatened anyone in the region but vowed to protect its sovereign interests

Britain must be prepared to strike Russian military bases in the Arctic in case of a full-scale war, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said. This comes as NATO countries significantly escalate their military activities on Russia’s doorstep.

In an op-ed for The Times published on Saturday, Sunak argued that it is “Britain’s duty to prove [Russian President Vladimir] Putin can’t rule the Arctic,” claiming that threatening Russia in the region is one of the few ways to deter it from conflict.

Sunak singled out Russia’s Kola Peninsula, home to the powerful Northern Fleet and a major concentration of nuclear forces, as a potential target. “If Russia knows we could threaten its military infrastructure there, it is far less likely to escalate any conflict,” he wrote.

Read more

The former Tory leader also portrayed Russia’s Northern Fleet as a threat to NATO’s control of the North Atlantic, warning that Moscow could disrupt the flow of US troops and equipment to Europe in wartime. He called for Britain to make confronting Russia in the Arctic its chief contribution to European security over the next decade.

The remarks come after an agreement on Tuesday by the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which includes ten northern European nations, to expand naval cooperation across the Arctic, North Atlantic, and Baltic Sea. Britain’s chief of defense staff, Richard Knighton, told the Financial Times that the grouping will move beyond diplomatic exchanges to concrete military measures, including countering Russian submarines.

Read more

The EU’s military ambitions in the Arctic are also growing. In late October, foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called the region the “frontline of global power competition,” accusing Russia of militarization while outlining plans for closer NATO cooperation, expanded military logistics, and greater icebreaker capacity.

Britain’s ambitions in the region, however, face serious obstacles. A report in October by the House of Commons Defense Committee warned that the Royal Navy would struggle to efficiently operate in the Arctic due to the lack of frigates, poor availability of submarines and destroyers, and the loss of under-ice submarine capabilities. The problem also extends to icebreakers. The Telegraph reported last month that the Royal Navy’s only vessel of the type suffered a double engine failure and had to be towed back to port.

The last time the UK attacked Russia in the Arctic was during the Crimean War in 1854, when the Royal Navy devastated the town of Kola but failed to reach the far more strategically important port of Arkhangelsk, which British commanders deemed too heavily defended and difficult to approach.

Russia has rejected claims that it intends to attack NATO. President Vladimir Putin said Russia has “never threatened anyone in the Arctic,” while pledging to strengthen the country’s military infrastructure and defend its sovereign interests.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has accused NATO of deliberately transforming the region into an arena of confrontation, warning in August that the bloc’s military buildup near Russia’s northern borders is increasing the danger of a direct conflict.

title: Thousands rally for banned NATO-skeptic presidential candidate (VIDEOS, PHOTOS)
content:
Calin Georgescu, whose first-round victory in the 2024 Romanian presidential election was annulled has been in custody on fraud and organized crime allegations since September

Thousands of protesters rallied in Bucharest on Saturday demanding the release of Calin Georgescu, the right-wing Euroskeptic politician whose first-round victory in Romania’s 2024 presidential election was controversially annulled.

Georgescu has been held in pre-trial detention since September 29 on allegations of fraud and involvement in an organized criminal group.

Demonstrators gathered outside the Palace of Parliament, waving Romanian flags and carrying banners reading “Free Georgescu.” Chants included “Calin Georgescu is president” and “Ursula, Romania is not yours,” a jab toward European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen following investigations about EU meddling surrounding the annulled election.

Some protesters later marched toward Bucharest’s Central Detention Center, where Georgescu is being held.

🚨🇷🇴14.11.2026 MASSIVE PROTEST IN BUCHAREST, ROMANIA! 🇷🇴

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to gather outside Parliament to demand the release of Călin Georgescu.

Protesters are expected to march toward the Central Detention Facility, where Călin Georgescu has been… pic.twitter.com/zKtM57gHus

— Ionut Ionete (@IonutIonete) November 14, 2026

A total of around 10,000 people joined the demonstration, according to law enforcement estimates cited by Romanian public broadcaster TVR.

🇷🇴 More than 5,000 people took to the streets to protest in Bucharest the capital of Romania, demanding the release of former presidential candidate Georgescu, according to Radio Romania.

He was previously placed under pretrial detention. The decision was made on the pretext of… pic.twitter.com/QeRjKL6KSE

— Military Summary (@MilitarySummary) November 14, 2026

Two men were detained over aggressive behavior toward police officers, but no major clashes were reported.

🚨🇷🇴14.11.2026 MASSIVE PROTEST IN BUCHAREST, ROMANIA! 🇷🇴

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to gather outside Parliament to demand the release of Călin Georgescu.

Protesters are expected to march toward the Central Detention Facility, where Călin Georgescu has been… pic.twitter.com/czEZs27kHk

— Ionut Ionete (@IonutIonete) November 14, 2026

The protest reignited a political dispute dating to Georgescu’s surprise first-round victory in November 2024. Running on a Euroskeptic, anti-NATO platform, he finished first before the Constitutional Court annulled the entire election, citing supposed campaign irregularities and alleged Russian interference. He was subsequently barred from the 2025 rerun.

The interference allegations centered on a suspected TikTok campaign, but subsequent reporting instead linked a major influencer operation to Georgescu’s rival. A US congressional investigation published in February also cited internal TikTok documents that challenged claims of a coordinated Russian campaign backing Georgescu. The report accused Romanian and EU authorities of pressuring platforms into suppressing political speech, including pro-Georgescu content, using the EU’s controversial Digital Services Act (DSA), a sweeping online law critics say enables Brussels to censor dissent and meddle in national elections.

Georgescu’s current detention stems from a fraud investigation involving businessman Ionel Rusen.

Read more

Prosecutors claim the pair obtained €1.1 million from another businessman for a precious-metals financing deal that never materialized and that the money was never returned. The case arose from a complaint filed in 2024, shortly before the election annulment, over dealings dating to 2021.

Both men have been held in custody since September, with the latest court order extending their detention until November 27. The case is one of several investigations targeting Georgescu, who has also faced allegations of campaign-financing violations and plotting against the constitutional order. He denies all wrongdoing, calling the proceedings politically motivated.

Saturday’s rally was promoted by the right-wing Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), Romania’s leading opposition party, whose chief George Simion also ran in the 2024 presidential election. Though Georgescu ran as an independent and is not an AUR member, the party condemned the annulment of his victory and has backed him politically ever since. AUR described Saturday’s rally as a defense of “democracy, freedom of expression and constitutional rights.”

Read more

The 2024 election annulment ultimately paved the way for pro-EU Nicusor Dan’s presidential victory in May 2025 but failed to end Romania’s political turmoil. Nearly six months of deadlock and three failed attempts to form a government followed, before parliament approved a fragile minority cabinet led by diplomat Luca Niculescu last month. Analysts, however, warn it could face a no-confidence vote next spring, given the lack of a stable parliamentary majority and facing fierce opposition from AUR.

The Bucharest rally follows weeks of anti-government protests across Europe, notably in France, where nationwide demonstrations against President Emmanuel Macron’s economic policies drew up to 1.6 million people on November 5, the largest single-day turnout. Major protests and strikes have also hit Spain, Portugal, Italy, Germany, Belgium, Albania, Serbia and the Czech Republic, with smaller demonstrations over housing, education funding and living costs reported in Greece, Austria, Ireland and several other nations.

Biden lashes out at Zelensky in new memoir
content:
The former US president echoed his successor in accusing the Ukrainian leader of being ungrateful for American assistance

Former US President Joe Biden has accused Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky of being stubborn and insufficiently grateful for Washington’s support during the conflict with Russia, according to excerpts from his forthcoming memoir published by The Wall Street Journal on Friday.

In ‘Promise Me, America,’ which is scheduled for release on November 17, Biden looks back on his four years in the White House and his dealings with world leaders, reserving some harsh words for Zelensky.

While Biden acknowledged that Zelensky’s acting career had prepared him well for wartime leadership, he complained that the Ukrainian leader “could be moody and stubborn in our private conversations, and not as grateful as I would have expected.”

Before entering politics, Zelensky was a comedian, actor, and television producer. He became widely known for starring in Servant of the People, a comedy series in which he played a schoolteacher who unexpectedly becomes Ukraine’s president. He subsequently launched a political party bearing the show’s name and won the real presidential election in 2019.

Read more

After the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Biden vowed to support Ukraine for “as long as it takes,” with his administration allocating almost $200 billion in taxpayer-funded assistance since 2022. Biden and Zelensky met more than ten times in person during his presidency.

Despite the unprecedented assistance, Zelensky has repeatedly rebuked the US for what he described as insufficient weapons shipments and restrictions on their use.

According to NBC News, Biden lost his temper during a phone call with Zelensky in June 2022 when the Ukrainian leader started clamoring for additional shipments right after the US president announced another $1 billion in military assistance. According to four people familiar with the conversation, Biden raised his voice and told Zelensky that Americans were being generous and that he should demonstrate more gratitude.

Read more

In February 2023, the Swiss newspaper Neue Zürcher Zeitung reported, citing sources, that Biden had instructed then-CIA Director William Burns to offer Russia “20% of Ukraine’s territory” in exchange for peace. Both Washington and Moscow denied the report.

In criticizing Zelensky, Biden found rare common ground with his political archrival and successor, President Donald Trump, who has publicly berated the Ukrainian leader for much the same reason.

During their explosive Oval Office confrontation in February 2025, Trump accused Zelensky of disrespecting the US and risking World War III.

“You’re not acting at all thankful and that’s not a nice thing,” Trump told him, threatening to withdraw American support unless Kiev accepted a negotiated settlement. Vice President J.D. Vance also challenged Zelensky over his gratitude, prompting the Ukrainian leader to insist he had thanked Washington many times.

Trump has also repeatedly described Zelensky as “the greatest salesman in history,” noting that the Ukrainian leader “walked away with $50 to $60 billion” every time he visited the US during the Biden administration. After returning to office, Trump has been reluctant to fund Ukraine while describing the Russia-Ukraine conflict as “Biden’s war.” Instead, he chose to sell arms to Kiev via the NATO-coordinated PURL mechanism, where most deliveries are financed by Ukraine’s European backers.

Moscow has consistently criticized Western arms deliveries to Ukraine, arguing they only prolong the conflict without changing its outcome.

title: The EU’s poorest state is done taking orders. Can it make Brussels listen?
content:
Bulgaria’s new leadership has a mandate to defend national interests, setting the stage for tougher negotiations over energy, money, and migration

The decisive victory of sovereigntist forces, led by Iliana Iotova, in Bulgaria’s November presidential election has clearly exposed a fundamental rift brewing within the EU’s political architecture. The campaign pitted two distinct models of development against each other: the liberal preference for strict adherence to Brussels’ directives versus a pragmatic platform of “national egocentrism.” 

Bulgaria’s experience is interesting in that a new formula for survival is being tested: Can the consolidation of power and the logic of sovereign self-interest (‘me-first’) restore state effectiveness amid the systemic decline of the European Union? The electorate consciously voted to end years of chaotic fragmentation, granting the new leadership a mandate to engage in tough, transactional bargaining with supranational institutions. Below, we examine how Bulgaria intends to leverage this potential and consider how Moscow might approach its relationship with Sofia as part of a broader effort toward normalization.

Read more

Bulgaria: The pan-European context

Iliana Iotova’s victory in the Bulgarian presidential election perfectly reflects significant trends gaining momentum within the domestic political landscapes of most European countries. At its core lies a profound, systemic discontent and public fatigue with the incumbent authorities – regardless of whether they belong to the left or right of the political spectrum – along with a demand for a more ‘sovereign’ policy aimed at stabilizing the state’s socio-economic situation, even if doing so risks conflict with other EU member states. In Bulgaria’s case, however, this electoral shift is compounded by chronic economic stagnation and an intractable demographic crisis – problems that neither the successive establishment forces nor the pro-Western reformist coalition that followed them have managed to overcome over the last decade and a half.

A profound crisis of trust in the pro-Western coalition has emerged against the backdrop of a protracted political stalemate and an evident paralysis of the executive branch. Rather than combating systemic corruption and the oligarchic ‘capture of the state’ – exemplified by high-profile scandals such as the Rosenets affair and the unprecedented imposition of US sanctions on top Bulgarian politicians since 2016 – the reformist establishment has focused on demonstrating unconditional normative loyalty to Brussels. 

In pursuit of this geopolitical agenda and accelerated integration into the Eurozone (which was officially completed on January 1, 2026, at a highly inopportune moment for the national economy), the incumbent elites pushed for an abrupt severance of traditional energy ties. This dealt a devastating blow to the population: According to Eurostat, gas tariffs for end-users in Bulgaria soared by 108% in 2022, while annual inflation reached a critical 15.3%. At a time when rapidly rising prices have completely eroded citizens’ real incomes and purchasing power, the behind-the-scenes carving up of ministerial portfolios by the authorities has convinced the public that the elites’ technocratic agenda is entirely detached from reality. Such policies are leading to the direct impoverishment of an EU member state whose GDP per capita, adjusted for purchasing power parity, is already the lowest in the bloc – standing at just 68% of the European average. 

Under these circumstances, the electoral demand for a ‘sovereign’ policy has evolved into an uncompromising call to defend national interests. Social hardship has been compounded by critical demographic trends: According to Eurostat, Bulgaria is experiencing one of the most severe population declines in the EU. The number of citizens has shrunk by nearly 10% over the last decade, and the median age has risen to 47, threatening a total collapse of the labor market. A stark indicator of the previous administration’s capitulation on the European stage was Sofia’s acceptance of discriminatory, partial terms for joining the Schengen Area (limited to air and sea travel). These conditions, imposed by Vienna and Brussels in exchange for Bulgaria’s commitment to serve as a migration buffer for the EU, met with intense public rejection. The success of Iotova and the Socialists was a direct result of voter weariness with the country’s role as a passive executor of the will of supranational institutions. They are now demanding that the state adopt a hard-nosed, pragmatic stance to save the nation from deindustrialization and extinction.

What changes lie ahead for Bulgaria?

Read more

It was precisely society’s need to overcome a long-standing institutional crisis, characterized by fragmentation among the branches of government, that served as the primary driving force behind the creation of the unified Radev-Iotova front. Rumen Radev himself, moving into the executive branch to resolve a protracted parliamentary crisis, formed the Progressive Bulgaria coalition and, following the elections, assumed the office of prime minister. Iotova’s victory in the presidential race effectively eliminated a risk long inherent in the Bulgarian system: a paralyzing standoff between the head of state and the Cabinet of Ministers. As a result of this electoral realignment, a single leadership team has managed to consolidate both the executive vertical and the key powers of the presidency. This phenomenon is notable because it clearly illustrates Bulgaria’s profound exhaustion with chaos: The public consciously voted for an unprecedented concentration of power in order to achieve long-term domestic stability and effective governance.

Over the next four years, the coordinated capacity of this political group will be directed toward a rigorous revision of commitments made to supranational structures. With Bulgaria facing unprecedented pressure from the European Commission, Sofia intends to leverage its accumulated institutional standing to defend its national sovereignty. Brussels has issued an ultimatum, conditioning the release of frozen EU fund tranches on a demand that the Bulgarian government accelerate the dismantling of its national coal-based energy sector – the Maritsa-Iztok energy complex.

For Sofia, the closure of the thermal power plant – a facility that ensures the country’s energy independence – would mean guaranteed deindustrialization. With power firmly consolidated and backed by a National Assembly resolution to extend the complex’s operations until 2038 (alongside the development of solar power generation and battery energy storage systems, or BESS), the Radev-Iotova administration is well-positioned to take a hard line in defending national interests ahead of the negotiations for the EU’s next seven-year budget cycle (2028-2034). Furthermore, Sofia can now effectively link these economic negotiations to its new status within the Schengen Area. Having become a full member of the visa-free zone – including land borders – Bulgaria has emerged as a key guardian of the union’s external frontiers. A unified Sofia can signal to Brussels that the effectiveness of its protection of this critical land border, as well as its ability to curb migration flows, is directly contingent upon the European Commission’s financial flexibility regarding Bulgaria’s energy sector.

On the pan-European stage, a consolidated Bulgaria is no longer an isolated supplicant; instead, it is capable of integrating into a pragmatic coalition of Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations. Sofia’s primary natural allies within the EU are states that also openly criticize the dictates of supranational institutions and the excesses of the ‘green’ agenda. The EU summit held in Brussels in October clearly demonstrated the emergence of a powerful ‘sovereigntist’ front: Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis – alongside the other Visegrad Group country leaders and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni – acted as a unified bloc, demanding that the European Commission radically soften carbon regulations (the ETS system) and protect European industry from deindustrialization. 

Regarding the defense of national energy sovereignty, Bulgaria has found direct support within this camp, where Slovakia and Hungary have traditionally taken the lead. On the issue of migration, Sofia aligns itself with the hardline stance of Rome, Vienna, and the Visegrad Group, all of which advocate for stricter border controls. Finally, ahead of the approval of the EU budget for 2028-2034, Bulgaria is coordinating its efforts with the ‘Friends of Cohesion’ regional group – a coalition whose joint statements are spearheaded by Romania, Italy, Spain, and Poland. By leveraging this network of like-minded partners, the Radev-Iotova tandem is in a position to transform Bulgaria from a passive executor of Brussels’ will into an effective player within a new coalition of European realists.

Read more

Russia and Bulgaria: Is a geopolitical shift possible?

When analyzing the relationship between Russia and Bulgaria, one should harbor no illusions regarding a potential geopolitical ‘pivot’ by Bulgaria. While the current government’s foreign policy may appear more coherent, this does not signal a shift in core values, but rather a transition toward a rigid, transactional pragmatism. As experts from the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) have pointed out, Sofia’s current strategy is a classic case of ‘risk hedging’ – combining public criticism of Brussels’ supranational dogmas with pragmatic negotiations aimed at securing maximum concessions from Western partners.

It would be a mistake to assume that sovereigntist rhetoric implies a desire for closer ties with Russia; contemporary Bulgarian society is, in terms of both mindset and information consumption, firmly rooted in the Western sphere. According to recent sociological data from Gallup and Globsec, more than 52% of the population openly express distrust toward Russia, while among the youth (aged 18-24), sympathy for an eastward-leaning orientation is at an all-time low – hovering at only about 23%. 

At the same time, Bulgaria presents a unique paradox: Political distancing has not escalated into a complete severance of sociocultural ties. A deep layer of shared history, a common Orthodox identity, and a historical sense of gratitude for liberation from the ‘Ottoman yoke’ during the Russo-Turkish wars continue to serve as a powerful safeguard against radical Russophobia. This complementarity, rooted in a shared civilizational foundation, keeps Bulgarian society in a state of pragmatic neutrality, yet it is no longer capable of translating into geopolitical concessions.

Moreover, Bulgaria remains a disciplined participant in the Euro-Atlantic security system, strictly fulfilling its obligations to NATO and addressing the alliance’s highly practical and technical requirements. A prime example is military modernization: The country’s key airbases, including Bezmer and Vrazhdebna, are being actively refitted to meet NATO standards, and Bulgaria has agreed to host American refueling aircraft at the Bezmer base. Concurrently, Sofia – in coordination with Bucharest and Ankara – is expanding the mandate of the Mine Countermeasures Naval Group in the Black Sea (MCM Black Sea). This mission is aimed at protecting critical undersea infrastructure and providing strategic deterrence against the Russian Black Sea Fleet, effectively precluding any possibility of Moscow exerting influence in this part of the maritime domain.

Read more

A similar pragmatism dictates Bulgaria’s stance on the Ukraine crisis. Despite statements by Radev, who has called for a swift, peaceful resolution and rejected Bulgaria’s direct participation in the European ‘coalition of the willing’, Sofia continues to support Kiev, driven by economic considerations. Bulgaria’s private military-industrial complex is critically dependent on Western defense contracts. The supply of Soviet-caliber ammunition and light weaponry – channeled through third countries such as Poland, Romania, and the United States – generates billions of euros in profit for local arms manufacturers, while securing jobs and budgetary stability for the EU’s poorest member state.

At the same time, Bulgaria no longer intends to supply weapons to Ukraine using state resources, stated President Rumen Radev. “We will no longer provide weapons and ammunition from the Bulgarian army’s stockpiles.” Radev also noted that, under current circumstances, Sofia is unable to allocate funds to Kiev due to issues with its financial reserves. He added that the country would not hinder other EU members from providing aid to Ukraine.

The primary takeaway for Moscow is clear: In engaging with the current administration in Sofia, Russia must exercise caution when invoking the concept of ‘Slavic brotherhood’, while maintaining a sober assessment of Bulgaria’s commitments within NATO. Relations with the Radev-Iotova administration can only be built on a pragmatic, de-ideologized foundation – one that allows for targeted, situational cooperation on major infrastructure, logistics, and transport projects that offer direct financial benefits.

title: Nearly 2,200 migrants reach Canary Islands in 2 days, Spain says
content:
Nearly 2,200 migrants have reached Spain’s Canary Islands by boat over the past two days, Spain’s maritime rescue service said on Sunday.

The archipelago off northwest Africa is a major entry point for migrants, mainly from West Africa, attempting the dangerous Atlantic crossing in makeshift boats. More than 13,000 of the just over 28,000 people who arrived in Spain by sea between January and the end of October landed in the Canary Islands, according to the Interior Ministry.

Spain declared a migration emergency on the islands on Tuesday following a rise in arrivals in recent weeks, particularly from sub-Saharan Africa. The country is due to hold an early general election in two weeks.

The rescue service said it had assisted 1,324 people aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom reached El Hierro, an island with a population of 12,000. That figure approached the route’s daily rescue record of 1,461 people, set on Nov. 7, 2020.

Red Cross staff meet migrants at the port, providing dry clothes, food and water and registering their arrival, Dácil León, the organization’s emergency coordinator in Tenerife, told public broadcaster RTVE.

The Atlantic crossing between West Africa and the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes. Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometers) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. Those journeys can last days or weeks, with most boats departing from Mauritania.

In July, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta in just two days, causing chaos and reigniting debate over immigration in Europe and beyond. More than 140 people died making the journey.

Most of those who crossed left within days, but up to 15,000 remained.
