title: Iran targets US military assets in Bahrain (VIDEOS)
content:
Six drones struck a US radar facility at the Al-Riffa military heliport, the IRGC claims, warning the US against further attacks on Iranian civilian areas

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it struck a US air defense radar site in Bahrain with drones, warning Washington against further attacks on Iranian civilian areas.

Six drones hit the radar installation at the Al-Riffa military heliport, southeast of the city of Riffa, early Sunday, the IRGC said in a statement carried by Fars News Agency, calling the strike a “decisive and crushing response” to US attacks against Iran.

The IRGC also claimed it shot down a number of US drones targeting Iran. It insisted that the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global oil route effectively closed since the war began in February, remains blocked despite attempts by the US to escort ships through it.

Bahrain issued two alerts overnight, urging residents to remain calm and seek shelter. The Bahrain Defense Force later confirmed Iranian drone attacks in a statement on social media, but said air defenses intercepted and destroyed the incoming aircraft before they could reach their targets.

Unverified footage circulating online purportedly shows drones flying over Riffa and striking an unidentified site.

Breaking:
🚨Iranian forces are striking U.S. bases in Bahrain, and air raid sirens are sounding.

Iran has begun targeting U.S. bases in Bahrain🔥 pic.twitter.com/YuM1ICp5FO

— Ebrahim Zolfaghari ✴️ (@IranianWarF) November 15, 2026

Another video appears to show a large fire at the heliport. Iranian military spokesman Ebrahim Zolfaghari reposted both videos on X.

🚨Iran struck the largest American base in Bahrain. pic.twitter.com/UL2zrak0bc

— Ebrahim Zolfaghari ✴️ (@IranianWarF) November 15, 2026

CENTCOM has yet to confirm any damage or casualties from the strike.

It was Iran’s second claimed attack on US military assets in Bahrain in three days. On Friday, the IRGC said it destroyed a US early-warning radar facility in retaliation for aerial provocations and oil smuggling in Hormuz. CENTCOM denied the claim, saying it intercepted two drones without injuries or damage. It was Iran’s first claimed strike on US military assets in Bahrain since early September.

Read more

The latest confrontation comes despite a scaling back of major military operations, with sporadic US strikes on Iranian targets and Iranian attacks on US facilities in the Gulf and shipping in Hormuz continuing. On Saturday, the IRGC said two tankers caught fire after striking naval mines on an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz, and two others heeded Iranian warnings and turned back.

Peace talks remain stalled, with Washington rejecting Tehran’s terms for reopening the waterway, including lifting sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets, and ending all regional hostilities. On Thursday, Trump declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Iran because “those days have long since passed.”

Read more

Iran has accused Bahrain and other Gulf states of facilitating US military operations. At a press conference on Sunday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended the strikes on US bases in the Gulf, claiming documented evidence that regional states aided US attacks against Iran. He insisted that the strikes were “purely defensive” and only targeted US military assets, without violating the sovereignty of the neighboring states.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera on Friday that Tehran is ready for either negotiations or war.

“It doesn’t matter to us at all whether America wants to negotiate or go to war,” he said, adding that an agreement is possible if the US accepts Iran’s conditions. Ghalibaf warned that continued attacks would leave Iran to determine the conflict’s geographical scope. “We will not remain in a situation of neither war nor peace.”

Following Sunday’s reports, Zolfaghari warned on behalf of Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff that continued US-Israeli attacks on Iranian civilian sites will trigger retaliatory strikes on the homes of American and Israeli officials and politicians in the region.

🚨 Breaking: The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Iran issued a strongly worded warning to Trump and Netanyahu:

"You have targeted our civilian residential areas!" "Iran will now begin bombing the homes of American and Israeli officials and politicians in the region!" 🇮🇷🚀🔥 pic.twitter.com/BJNhfmuujy

— Ebrahim Zolfaghari ✴️ (@IranianWarF) November 15, 2026

title: French TV crew mugged while covering protests (VIDEOS)
content:
A BFMTV cameraman was attacked near a burning barricade after the channel faced accusations of right-wing bias

A cameraman for French news channel BFMTV was chased and beaten by protesters in Lyon, who smashed and stole his equipment, according to local reports and footage from the scene.

The attack took place on Saturday as thousands marched through the southeastern French city for better living conditions and against a bill that would grant police the presumption of self-defense when using firearms, denounced by opponents as a ‘license to kill’.

According to Lyon Mag, the cameraman was filming near a burning barricade on Avenue Berthelot when several individuals recognized him, gave chase, and repeatedly struck him as he tried to flee toward police.

💥 | Des journalistes de @BFMTV ont été pris à partie par des manifestants à #Lyon Vue sur des angles différents https://t.co/72meLvWc19

— Gabriel BOYER (@BoyerGabriel042) November 14, 2026

The TV crew consisted of two journalists and two security guards, one of whom was seen containing some of the attackers. The incident unfolded in a particularly volatile section of the demonstration, where masked activists were throwing projectiles and fireworks at police, prompting the use of tear gas.

A freelance journalist who witnessed the attack told AFP that it was “very, very intense,” adding: “I had to remove my press badge myself, otherwise I would have been lynched too.”

BREAKING: Young people are rioting in Lyon, France, setting large barricades on fire. Some of them are carrying Algerian flags https://t.co/Dk8ZhxgdxR

— Visegrád 24 (@visegrad24) November 14, 2026

The cameraman sought medical attention. The Interior Ministry said at least one suspected attacker was arrested.

🔴LYON : une grenade assourdissante non explosée laissée au sol a semé la panique. #Lyon #manifestation #manif14novembre #france https://t.co/2934bwE9uN

— Bismuth Back (@Bismuthback) November 14, 2026

BFMTV called the attack “unacceptable” and said it would support its journalists in filing complaints. In late September, two other BFMTV journalists were assaulted while covering school blockades in Saint-Denis, a northern Paris suburb notorious for its high crime rates.

🔴LYON : manifestation ce samedi 14 novembre pour le climat, la jeunesse, et contre la loi permis de tuer ! #Lyon #manifestation #manif14novembre #france https://t.co/fIxzRrdpc9

— Bismuth Back (@Bismuthback) November 14, 2026

While there is no indication that the BFMTV crew provoked the activists in any way, the network has drawn growing hostility from left-wing protesters, who accuse it of amplifying right-wing narratives and giving disproportionate attention to immigration and security issues.

The outrage also increased after BFMTV hired presenter Sonia Mabrouk, formerly from the conservative CNews channel, who conducted interviews with right-wing politicians Eric Ciotti and Eric Zemmour. The guests respectively used the expressions “French intifada” and “Arab-Muslim scum” while discussing the unrest in France.

READ MORE: University vice president stabbed amid unrest in France

BFMTV’s new editorial policies also triggered an internal revolt, with more than 200 journalists signing an open letter to the management urging it to “cut with this image of a racist channel.” The network’s leadership rejected the accusation but announced plans to diversify its political guests.

The assault came against the backdrop of weeks of nationwide unrest over rising living costs, low wages, failing education, and police violence. The protests erupted into widespread violent clashes last month, with looting and arson reported in several major cities as police reported several thousand arrests.

Saturday’s demonstrations drew around 106,000 people nationwide, according to the French Interior Ministry, with more than 8,000 marching in Lyon alone. The city was among the worst hit at the peak of the protests on October 17, when rioters set the local tourist office on fire and ransacked dozens of shops.

title: Israel kills a top Hamas commander as Jordan sentences 3 in church attack, and other Mideast news
content:
Israeli forces killed a top commander of the militant Hamas group in an overnight airstrike on southern Gaza, Israel said Sunday.

In Jordan, three men were sentenced to death for a deadly shooting last month at a Greek Orthodox Church. In Yemen, the Houthis said they freed around 600 detainees captured in the latest escalation of fighting, even as they consolidated their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Sunday. Read our full coverage here.

Israel says it killed a top Hamas commander in Gaza

Israel said it killed a top Hamas commander in an airstrike on southern Gaza just after midnight. A Hamas statement confirmed the killing of Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis and said a funeral would be held for him later Sunday.

The Israeli military said Abu Younis had been directing plans “to advance and carry out terror attacks.” Two months earlier, an Israeli strike killed his predecessor.

The military said it targeted other Hamas militants in Sunday’s strike but provided no details.

Jordan sentences 3 men to death over deadly church attack

Jordan’s State Security Court on Sunday sentenced three men to death for a deadly shooting at a Greek Orthodox Church last month, state-run Al Mamlaka TV said. The men were charged with “carrying out terrorist acts.”

The Oct. 23 attack was one of the deadliest on Jordan’s Christian minority in decades, with nine people killed and dozens wounded. The attackers targeted mourners attending a funeral at St. George’s Church in Hamoud, a village south of the capital, Amman.

The three defendants — two brothers and their brother-in-law — were arrested three days after the attack following a shootout with security forces. Jordanian authorities described the men as followers of an extremist ideology but said they were not affiliated with an organized group.

Yemen's Houthis release hundreds of detainees

The Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday freed some 600 detainees captured in the latest escalation of fighting, the largest unilateral release of detainees in the country's 12-year civil war, said Abdul-Qader al-Murtaza, a Houthi official on prisoners' affairs.

Also Sunday, a group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government said its fighters pulled out from areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait amid relentless attacks by the Houthis.

The Southern Armed Forces said they would now focus on securing Yemen's southern city of Aden, held by the internationally recognized government, as well as trying to break the Houthi siege of the crucial city of Taiz.

The move has allowed the rebels to consolidate their grip on the strait, in a setback to the Saudi-backed efforts to dislodge them from the strategic coastal territories on the Red Sea.

In Aden, an Associated Press journalist heard sounds of explosions Sunday evening. Local media reported that the Houthis fired two ballistic missiles on the district of Buraiqeh on Aden’s western coast.

UN agency raises alarm about refugees in Yemen

Clashes were reported between the Houthis and government forces in an area in Yemen's southwestern province of Lahj, which has key supply routes close to the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

The Houthis said they fired ballistic missiles on government forces’ positions in the Kharaz area, which is home to a refugee camp sheltering thousands of African refugees.

The U.N. refugee agency warned Sunday that the clashes hindered its efforts to offer protection and aid to about 9,600 refugees.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard clashes with Kurdish group

Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard clashed with members of the Kurdish Iranian dissident group Kurdistan Free Life Party, or PJAK, near Iran’s border with Iraq, both groups said in statements Sunday.

The IRGC said it “destroyed” a group of PJAK fighters “that intended to enter the territory of the Islamic Republic of Iran and carry out terrorist actions” and seized “a quantity of weapons, equipment and explosive materials.”

The IRGC statement did not specify when the clash took place, but PJAK said that one of its members was killed Wednesday after a group of fighters were “ambushed” by IRGC forces in Sardasht, in western Iran.

PJAK and other Kurdish Iranian dissident groups have bases in northern Iraq that have been frequently targeted by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. In the early days of the war, some of the Kurdish groups said they planned to launch an incursion into Iran with U.S. support, but the plan was later abandoned.

Israel arrests freelance journalist on suspicion of terror ties

Israel’s military said it apprehended a stringer for Agence France-Presse in the occupied West Bank very early on Sunday on suspicion of “terror ties,” adding that he was transferred to the security forces for more questioning.

The French news agency called for Israel to provide evidence in the detention of Mohammad Ateeq, a video journalist who has contributed to AFP for three years.

His wife said that Israeli forces blindfolded him and took him away from his home in a town near Jenin, according to AFP.

Iran says it hit an American radar system in Bahrain

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claimed early on Sunday that it struck a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.

The U.S. military’s Central Command, which oversees American forces in the Middle East, did not immediately comment. On Friday, CENTCOM had said it intercepted two Iranian drones headed toward Bahrain and denied an Iranian claim at the time that it had struck a U.S. early-warning radar system there.

Bahrain’s military said Sunday its air defense systems intercepted a number of Iranian projectiles before they reached their targets.

___

This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

___

This story was corrected earlier to say that the shooting in Jordan took place in the village of Hamoud in the Karak governorate, not in the city of Karak.

title: Macron warns against ‘spirit of defeat’ on Ukraine
content:
The French president made the remarks amid growing debate and uncertainty over continued European support for Kiev

Cutting support for Ukraine would leave Europe vulnerable to Russia, French President Emmanuel Macron has warned, criticizing what he described as a defeatist attitude.

This comes as Ukraine’s European partners seek a greater role in negotiations with Moscow after being sidelined during US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi earlier this week.

European leaders agreed on Friday to form a negotiating team comprising EU institutions and five countries: Britain, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland.

“Let us be clear: those who want to restrict Ukraine’s resources ultimately want to force it into an unjust peace, leaving it permanently vulnerable and, by extension, Europe as well. This is the spirit of defeat. It is a recipe for the next war,” the French leader wrote on X on Saturday.

“Europe must play its full part, because the security of our continent also depends on that peace.” 

Moscow has accused European countries of seeking to undermine peace negotiations and argued that they must first demonstrate goodwill.

Macron reiterated that France and its partners are preparing “a multinational force” which could be deployed to Ukraine after a ceasefire. Moscow has stated that it would not accept Western troops on Ukrainian territory and would regard them as legitimate military targets.

Read more

Macron’s appeal comes amid divisions among EU members over further aid to Kiev. On Friday, Poland said it would not contribute additional funds to purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, citing its own military spending and budget deficit. Bulgaria also ruled out further transfers of weapons and ammunition from its stockpiles.

Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic have sought exemptions from a proposed financing scheme intended to cover Ukraine’s €70 billion funding gap for 2027. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for all EU members to contribute, threatening to block negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless the issue is resolved.

Denis Senik, Ukraine’s top diplomat in Washington, told RFE/RL on Saturday that Ukrainian forces continue to experience widespread restrictions affecting Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications service used to operate reconnaissance and interceptor drones.

Read more

Starshield first experienced speed restrictions in mid-October, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations. Service was restored on October 24, but similar problems resurfaced in November. Kiev has questioned SpaceX’s explanation that the disruptions are technical, while the company has denied imposing new restrictions.

The renewed disruptions come amid tensions between Washington and Kiev over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and US-mediated peace negotiations. No connection between these disputes and the Starshield restrictions has been established.

title: University vice president stabbed amid unrest in France
content:
Student protests continue to sweep the country, with more than 200 people detained during Saturday’s clashes with police

French police are still searching for a suspect who stabbed a university vice president near his office on Friday.

Although investigators have not established a link between the attack and the ongoing nationwide student protests, more than 80 school principals and deputy principals have been injured amid unrest surrounding the demonstrations since mid-September.

According to French media, the attack occurred at around 7:45 PM at the University of Versailles Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines (UVSQ), a public research university near Paris. The victim was working in his office when he heard a noise in the hallway. Believing it was a cleaner, he stepped outside to greet him but was confronted by a hooded man wearing a surgical mask.

The assailant attacked the vice president with a bladed weapon, leaving him with non-life-threatening injuries to his head and hand. The victim managed to escape into a nearby office and lock the door, while the attacker fled the scene.

Read more

UVSQ President Loic Josseran condemned the attack “in the strongest possible terms” and urged the public to respect his injured colleague’s privacy.

“No violence is acceptable. The state stands alongside universities, their leadership, and their staff,” Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste wrote on X. Baptiste later told TF1 that the victim had expressed concern that his assault could be “exploited by extremists.”

According to Le Parisien, UVSQ has been affected by repeated campus blockades, prompting administrators to call in police. Around 20 disgruntled students sought a meeting with the university president on November 9 but were turned away because he was absent.

Students across France have been demanding better learning conditions, including more teachers and greater funding for education. Their protests have drawn support from public-sector unions and other demonstrators protesting the rising cost of living.

Around 106,000 people protested across France on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry, while organizers claimed 200,000. Police detained at least 219 people as clashes erupted in several cities, including Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, and Montpellier. Ten officers suffered minor injuries.

title: US threatening to starve Iranians – Tehran
content:
Washington’s sanctions and naval blockade amount to war crimes, the Iranian Foreign Ministry has said

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has accused the US of threatening to starve his country’s population through sanctions and a naval blockade.

Speaking after a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris on Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the “economic pain” inflicted on Iran as “extraordinary,” warning that the impact of the sanctions will intensify over time.

He argued that mounting hardship could force the leadership to make concessions, as “eventually you have to eat.”

“This is yet another admission that Washington is pursuing war crimes, compounding the atrocities it has already committed in its wars of aggression and economic terrorism against Iran,” Baghaei wrote on X on Saturday.

“After decades of failed coercion, threats, sanctions, terrorism, and aggression, the United States continues to repeat the same mistakes, merely repackaging them under new names,” he added.

Read more

The US began blockading Iran’s southern ports in April after Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital oil and LNG shipping route, in response to the US-Israeli bombing campaign launched on February 28.

In August, the US launched Operation Economic Outcast, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatening the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran through sweeping sanctions targeting Iranian businesses and their foreign partners.

Iran has also accused the US of striking civilian water infrastructure, including desalination facilities and drinking-water reservoirs, disrupting supplies to thousands of residents. Washington denied responsibility for an attack in March on a desalination plant on Qeshm Island and said its strikes in June targeted military communications and radar facilities.

Read more

Tensions remain high despite US President Donald Trump saying that new large-scale strikes are unlikely. The US has reportedly warned Israel and Gulf states to prepare for a possible resumption of combat operations.

Washington previously rejected Iran’s terms for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which included lifting US sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian assets, and ending the hostilities on “all fronts,” including Israel’s wars in Gaza and southern Lebanon.

“The ball is now in the American court,” Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Tehran’s chief negotiator, said on Wednesday.

Rubio dismissed Iran’s conditions as “absurd.” Trump said on Thursday that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran because “those days have long since passed.”

title: Israeli settlers accused of torching Palestinian village scrapyard (VIDEOS)
content:
More than 100 vehicles were destroyed in the fire in the occupied West Bank, with no arrests reported

No arrests have been reported after Israeli settlers allegedly set fire to a vehicle scrapyard in the Palestinian village of al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday, destroying more than 100 vehicles.

According to Palestinian officials, the fire also destroyed ten cars parked outside nearby homes, a repair workshop, storage facilities, and dozens of streetlight poles and olive trees. The damage was estimated at more than 1 million shekels ($315,000), WAFA reported.

Al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya, a village south of Nablus, is surrounded by the Israeli settlements of Eli and Ma’ale Levona. The UN considers Israeli settlements illegal under international law and an obstacle to establishing an independent Palestinian state.

The Israeli military said troops were dispatched to the village following reports of arson and are searching for suspects. It added that police and forensic investigators will enter the village to collect evidence once the fire is extinguished.

title: SpaceX catches Starship spacecraft with giant mechanical arms (VIDEO)
content:
The historic maneuver marks the first successful recovery of an orbital vehicle using a launch tower’s robotic arms

SpaceX has successfully caught its Starship spacecraft returning from orbit, using giant mechanical arms to capture the vehicle in midair at its launch site in Texas.

The historic maneuver took place on Saturday afternoon, after the spacecraft completed 14 orbits of Earth during a mission lasting more than 22 hours. It’s the first time SpaceX has recovered a Starship spacecraft from orbit.

The 124-meter Starship, the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, launched from the company’s Starbase facility in southern Texas on Friday. The upper stage successfully reached orbit and deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites.

The mission suffered an early setback when the Super Heavy first-stage booster failed to return to the launch tower. SpaceX aborted the planned catch after the booster deviated from its intended trajectory, diverting it toward the Gulf of Mexico, where it exploded.

After completing the journey, the spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere and descended toward Starbase. It flipped upright and was captured by two enormous mechanical arms, known as ‘chopsticks’, mounted on the launch tower.

They did it! SpaceX has just caught their Starship rocket for the first time ever, marking the first recovery of a conventional orbital rocket upper stage in history! This is one of the greatest engineering achievements in history. Congrats to the entire @SpaceX team! 🚀 https://t.co/9KAzAcd3e8

— Sawyer Merritt (@SawyerMerritt) November 14, 2026

The recovery marks a major step toward SpaceX’s goal of making both stages of Starship fully reusable, potentially reducing launch costs and allowing more frequent flights.

The system is central to Elon Musk’s ambitions to transport humans to the Moon and Mars. NASA has also selected a modified version of Starship to land astronauts on the lunar surface as part of its Artemis program.

title: France’s Actu changed its business model and got free readers to pay
content:
In the past, Actu, owned by CIPA Ouest-France, had 400 journalists producing some 80 weekly print editions, mostly in Brittany and Normandy in northwestern France. These print titles each had their own websites. They later shifted to a single platform for digital content, which offered national reach. 

“From that, we decided to pivot to a paid model, which was quite a big challenge for us,” Amandine Briand, Deputy Director, Editorial Projects at Groupe Actu, told our Digital Media Europe participants in London.

The roots of their current efforts began in 2012, when the group decided to launch a digital-only edition, 76Actu, to see what would happen, she said.

The site quickly proved popular and gained a large audience, so the group launched Actu Toulouse, also digital only in 2015, Briand said.

WAN-IFRA Members can download Briand’s presentation slides as well as replay this session and others from Digital Media Europe on our Knowledge Hub.

A national footprint based on local news

However, the group still had many websites connected to their weekly print titles operating independently, some of which had only 2,000 or so unique visitors a month.

“We thought it would be a good idea to put everyone on the same platform and get these audiences growing, which is what we did in 2016, and got 80 titles on the same domain,” Briand said.

By doing that, she said, traffic skyrocketed. “We now reach around 115 million monthly users, and we are one of France’s most visited websites.”

This gave them a national footprint, even though they provide local news.

“But unlike traditional media, we really operate as a network,” Briand added. “We don’t have a top-down approach, more a bottom-up one.”

Everything was working quite well: “audiences exploded and the traffic was good. The advertising was fine,” Briand said.

However as market dynamics began to shift as they did for so many news publishers worldwide during the past decade, the group realised it needed to change, too.

“We decided we could no longer just count on advertising, and on revenues that are mainly dependencies, so we decided to do this shift,” she said.

‘Will this monetisation project kill the audience?’

Actu had three major goals as they started the project, Briand said.

  • Reduce dependencies
  • Transform their economic model
  • Put content at the centre

The third goal was the most ambitious of the three, she noted. 

The project itself raised many questions and some fears within Actu’s newsrooms. One major concern, Briand said, was “will this monetisation project actually kill the audience?”

They had spent years building up their audiences, and worried the move to charging readers could “just crush everything,” she said.

After all, Actu had spent years giving readers free content online, and now they were going to ask those readers to pay.

Additionally, there was a concern that maybe they were making the move too late. There were already many news sites in France charging for online content while Actu was seen as the free one in the landscape. Could they really put up a paywall now?

Trainings to boost understanding, reader value

Determined to stay the course, the group began training their journalists to help them see the reasonings behind the project and understand the way the subscription funnel works.

These trainings also highlighted the need for journalists to consider how readers determine the value of a story. This was something that Briand said was sometimes at odds with the journalists own beliefs about the value of their work.

Often, she said, the journalists believed the amount of time and effort they spent working on an article determined its value, rather than how useful the content was to readers.

As part of these trainings, Briand and her team gave the newsrooms a framework for writing articles tailored towards paywalls, in part based on the user needs model.

They also stipulated that 30 percent of all content had to be put behind the paywall. Actu decided on 30 percent because they thought it offered a good balance for maintaining advertising value. It would also help ensure that readers would encounter enough paywalled content to get frustrated, and motivate them to subscribe, she said.

However, they left the decisions about exactly what articles to put behind the paywall with the individual newsrooms and their journalists, rather than automating the process.

“We started with La Presse de la Manche, our only daily newspaper, and then after this experiment we rolled it out across all our newsrooms by waves, structured waves. We wouldn’t have all newsrooms altogether, but 10 and then 12 and then 20,” Briand said.

19,000 paying subscribers and growing by 1,500 a month

The efforts paid off: Readers were willing to pay, “and they did right from the beginning,” Briand said.

Actu now has 19,000 subscriptions on the paywall, which is 8,000 net active subscribers to their portfolio, she said.

“For the first time since Covid, our net subscribers became positive again. And also the average revenue per user (ARPU) grew. Thanks to the subscriber conversion to this new digital offer. Currently, we’re creating around 1,500 new subscribers a month.”

These paying digital subscribers have also helped with Actu’s digital revenue share in general, Briand said, adding that today, 35 percent of the group’s total revenue is digital.

They also learned that many of the people who are subscribing are super-consumers, frequently coming to the site three times per day. Furthermore, subscribers also spend much more time per visit on the website than non-subscribers: seven minutes compared with just two minutes for non-subscribers,” she said.

Also interesting for Actu is that nearly 70 percent of the content these logged-in users are consuming is actually free content.

“We were also very interested in what articles were actually going to get us subscriptions, and without many surprises, we learned that practical information, curiosity, emotion were really subscription drivers for us,” Briand said.

Every time an article inspires empathy, or touches people’s daily life, it usually helps in terms of subscriptions, she said.

Next moves: Master engagement, increase ARPU and launch services

Moving forward, Briand said they are shifting their main focus to “mastering engagement” on their website, social media and more. “We also have targets to grow audience, increase the value of each reader, the ARPU.”

More newsroom workshops are also planned. As is deploying a broader brand awareness campaign, she said. They also plan to launch new services “because we know that content is a door to subscription. But we also know that people need services, and another way of getting them engaged and staying with us,” she said.

Asked about their subscription revenue goals by moderator Nic Newman of the Reuters Institute, Briand said they are aiming to increase the current amount by four-fold next year.

The post France’s Actu changed its business model and got free readers to pay appeared first on WAN-IFRA.

title: Trump just admitted his failure in one stunning move
content:
The i Paper’s Rohit Kachroo argues that President Donald Trump’s decision to reassign Vice President JD Vance comes closer than anything else during either of his terms to admitting he was wrong. The decision came on the heels of Vance blaming the Republicans’ midterm losses on the fallout from the Iran war, much of what was revealed in voting polls. But Kachroo also says Vance’s demotion was performance-related, as he’s been unable to live up to expectations within the role.

Trump’s move involving Vance suggests he is finally acknowledging that the war with Iran has become a costly choice, with neither the U.S., Israel nor Iran achieving its ultimate goals.

But as some progress is being made with Trump trying to course correct, recent statements are contradictory to the same progress. Kachroo says even Trump’s latest declaration of him saying, “We’ve got their Strait,” is wrong. America saw another surge in oil pricing courtesy of the president suggesting a deal with Iran was no longer necessary.

What’s even worse is that Kachroo says it’s not just Trump who needs to come to the new reality that the U.S.’s involvement in this war has the possibility of becoming a semi-permanent state of affairs that will take time to undo. Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, suggested this when he said that the Strait would “never return” to its status before the war. It has been nearly a year, and it is seemingly far from over, and all sides are suffering.

On the U.S. side, Kachroo notes that it cost Republicans their control, losing by historic margins during the 2026 midterm elections. Israel’s recent elections gave the opposition bloc a potential path to ousting Benjamin Netanyahu and ending what critics call his “October 7 government.” Israel has also endured much punishment and further economic strife as a result. Kachroo writes, “Iran’s determination to retaliate has exposed both its reach and its weakness.”

Kachroo argues that in both the U.S. and Israel, military failures and economic struggles can have far-reaching political consequences, threatening the stability of democratic governments. The result, he says, is that the war may have actually made the political groups or leaders the United States wanted to weaken or eliminate more powerful. Trump is now having to come to terms with that harsh reality and work toward resolution. With Congress looking a lot different starting in the new year, he may have little choice.

title: Thousands of Travelers Still Stranded After FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop
content:
By Tom Ozimek

Thousands of travelers remained stranded on Nov. 14 as airlines worked to restore service after a nationwide ground stop halted departures for more than four hours, disrupting travel across the United States and beyond.

More than 3,600 flights within, into, or out of the United States were canceled Saturday morning, with more than 1,600 delayed, according to FlightAware data at around 8:45 a.m. ET. Those disruptions followed 9,161 cancellations and 7,292 delays on Friday. Another 56 flights were already canceled for Sunday.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the ground stop around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing departures to resume gradually. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that airlines would need time to restore normal operations.

“It’s going to be slow,” Duffy told reporters at the White House. He said tens of thousands of passengers remained stuck at airports after the restrictions were lifted, potentially facing overnight waits.

Duffy blamed an “incredibly old” air traffic control system for the outage, saying routers became overloaded with data and began to malfunction, prompting officials to order a shutdown.

“Let’s invest so we never have to come at 8:30 at night and have a press conference on why air travel was shut down, why we have tens of thousands of people in airports separated from their families without any knowledge of where they’re going to sleep tonight,” Duffy said.

He urged Congress to include $50 billion in an emergency funding bill before the end of the year to finish building a new system.

“With a brand-new state-of-the-art system, you won’t have these outages,” he said. “This is a continual problem that we have and it should be fixed.”

FAA Says Systems Tested

The FAA said in a late Friday statement that it had tested its systems before reopening the airspace for commercial flights.

“Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable,” the agency said on social media platform X, advising passengers to contact their airlines for updates.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said new equipment and technology that the FAA had been adding to the network was “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy said controllers lost consistent radar and communication with aircraft, and that the upgraded digital equipment did not fail, only the old analog equipment.

Mullin said more than 3,000 flights landed safely Friday and that no one was in danger.

He said attackers typically claim responsibility for cyberattacks and that investigators had picked up “no chatter.”

“We haven’t seen any footprints, as you would say, or identifications of people that got into the system,” Mullin told reporters at the White House. “It appears that this was mechanically driven; however, we’re still looking, so we’re not going to rule that out.”

Asked by a reporter what caused the instability, Duffy again pointed to the equipment.

“We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere,” Duffy said. “It got overloaded.”

Duffy said lawmakers had approved only part of the money needed and warned that more outages would follow unless Congress funded the rest.

“We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But you will have more of these,” he said.

The FAA has replaced thousands of copper wires with fiber-optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems under an overhaul begun last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion.

Duffy said the White House has asked lawmakers to approve another $30 billion to complete the work, adding that more is warranted.

“I want $50 billion,” he said, which, according to the secretary, would be money well spent to stand up a national air traffic control system that “actually works.”

Although the ground stop was lifted, the disruption for passengers continued. At airports across the country, travelers crowded departure halls and airline desks as delays and cancellations mounted.

Edward Kargbo, 50, from West Chester, Pennsylvania, said he planned to spend the night at the airport after his transatlantic flight to Africa was rescheduled from 9 p.m. Friday to 6 a.m. on Saturday.

“I have to squat the night here,” he said. “I’m stranded.”

Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Microsoft Says Services Restored After Global Outage
content:
By Aldgra Fredly

Microsoft said on Nov. 14 that it had restored services across all products after a global outage that affected government agencies in many countries and lasted more than 12 hours.

“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the tech giant said in an update on X.

The outage began on Nov. 12 and disrupted a wide range of Microsoft products, including Outlook, Teams, and AI assistant Copilot. The Redmond, Washington-based company said more than 430 million people worldwide use Microsoft 365 apps.

Microsoft apologized on Friday and said the incident stemmed from an earlier “network capacity upgrade” that surfaced after a network change. The company has said there was no sign of a cyberattack.

The outage had disrupted government agencies in the United States, Australia, and Japan, and delayed many companies from publishing results to stock exchanges.

A series of posts by Microsoft 365 Status, the company’s official service incident account, on X on Thursday evening indicated that its engineers encountered setbacks while working to resolve the issue.

“The servers we returned to service can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic; we’re analyzing diagnostic data to determine what’s triggering the behavior,” Microsoft posted at one point.

In an update on Nov. 13, Microsoft said services showed broader signs of improvement across North America and Europe, with recovery also progressing in the Asia–Pacific region. But it warned that some users might still experience “intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery” as the company worked to address the remaining affected infrastructure.

“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration,” Microsoft said in a subsequent post.

Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said on Friday that “technical challenges and failure modes” had made the recovery process more difficult than usual.

Lamanna said he had been working with the engineering team to complete a full post-mortem analysis.

“This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling,” he said in a post on X. “We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.”

Australia’s home affairs minister, Tony Burke, who also oversees cybersecurity, said on Friday that Microsoft likened the outage to the 2024 CrowdStrike incident, triggered by a faulty antivirus software update.

AJ Thompson, CCO at Northdoor, a cybersecurity and IT consultancy, told The Epoch Times by email that he did not believe the outage was linked to the increased demand for Copilot.

“From Microsoft’s own report, it appears that one, then other servers failed a health check,” Thompson said. “This led to these servers failing across to others, which in turn led to a cascade effect of data access requests which simply overwhelmed these failover servers.”

“It’s not a Copilot overload, but a rather more basic infrastructure issue,” he added.

Chris Summers and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Cisco Sued in California Over Alleged Link to Human Rights Abuses
content:
By Eva Fu

Tech giant Cisco is facing a continued legal challenge in California state court over allegations that it has aided human rights abuses in China.

Seventeen plaintiffs, including U.S. citizens, filed a lawsuit alleging the San Jose company helped the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) build a sophisticated surveillance system to persecute a faith group that the regime has sought to eradicate.

The plaintiffs are Falun Gong practitioners, a spiritual practice that emphasizes truthfulness, compassion, and tolerance, along with meditative exercises.

The Chinese regime began an all-out campaign targeting the group in 1999, subjecting the practitioners to slave labor, long prison sentences, and torture in a bid to make them renounce their beliefs.

Cisco’s Golden Shield was an instrumental tool in facilitating this abuse, the plaintiffs alleged.

According to the plaintiffs, it is a multi-tiered apparatus allowing the authorities to track, identify, profile, and interrogate Falun Gong practitioners, with information on each target stored in a database and constantly updated.

The lawsuit, filed in August, marks the latest effort after a long-running battle to seek corporate liability over human rights abuses. The plaintiffs filed an amended complaint on Oct. 30.

Thirteen of the plaintiffs first filed a lawsuit against Cisco in 2011 asserting multiple federal and state claims. One of the federal statutes they invoked was the Alien Tort Statute, which at the time had been interpreted to let non-U.S. citizens seek remedies in U.S. courts for international human rights violations.

In June, the Supreme Court sided with Cisco, effectively closing the door to corporate human rights accountability suits under the Alien Tort Statute in federal courts.

But while the ruling narrowed the law, attorneys on the case said victims still have ways to pursue accountability.

“The Supreme Court decision found that the Alien Tort Statute did not include human rights cases that were not about piracy, safe conducts, or ambassadors. That does not have any bearing on whether the state courts can hear cases that they have traditionally heard such as tort cases,” Catherine Sweetser, one of the plaintiffs’ attorneys, told The Epoch Times.

Of those who joined the new lawsuit, three live in California.

They include Zhang Yuhua, who, while in China, used circumvention software to access overseas websites to download Falun Gong-related materials.

In 2002, the lawsuit said, Chinese security detected her internet traffic, broke into her home, and sentenced her to four years in prison. She was arrested twice in the following years, suffering sleep deprivation, force feeding, and injection of unknown substances, according to the complaint.

The complaint alleged that Golden Shield had included her name in its database, resulting in ongoing surveillance of her activities.

It noted that in early 2013, after Zhang moved to a new place, a surveillance camera appeared near the entrance of her residential building, enabling the police to monitor her around the clock.

Similarly, the complaint said, Chinese police tracked down plaintiff Wu Jiahao. The authorities regularly cited Wu’s internet activity during interrogation, tortured him during his four-year prison sentence, forced him to watch videos vilifying his belief, and severely restricted his access to food, drink, and the restroom, according to the filing.

Surveillance and harassment continued after his release, with Party officials going to his home to make threats and directing his landlords to evict him, the filing said.

“There are a lot of people who think that the Golden Shield is just an internet censorship software. It is not,” Can Sun, another case attorney, told The Epoch Times.

The legal process is “a long and difficult road,” one of the original plaintiffs from 2011 told The Epoch Times. But given the grave allegations at the heart of this case, the plaintiff said it is important to persist.

Cisco didn’t respond to The Epoch Times’ request for comment.

title: Poland and Bulgaria put brakes on Ukraine weapons funding
content:
Warsaw has suspended further funding for US-made weapons for Kiev, and Sofia has rejected a new European aid package and ruled out more deliveries from its stockpiles

Poland has refused to bankroll further purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine, citing its own military spending and budget deficit. Fellow NATO member Bulgaria has also refused to take part in a €70 billion European aid package and says it will no longer supply weapons and ammunition from its stockpiles.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday he notified the NATO secretary-general that Poland “will not be contributing any money to the PURL [Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List] project at this time… because we spend a great deal on our own armaments.” He also cited Poland’s “high deficit.”

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev also stated on Friday that his country can no longer provide financial assistance to Ukraine, citing Bulgaria’s budget deficit.

“We will not provide any more weapons and ammunition from the Bulgarian Army’s stocks,” he added.

Radev has also ruled out Bulgarian participation in an additional €70 billion funding package requested by Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky from his EU backers. He warned that continued spending on the conflict at the expense of EU citizens is fueling social tensions and political instability across the bloc.

The PURL was launched in July 2025 after US President Donald Trump refused to give Kiev a blank check, and now also includes several non-NATO contributors, with Canada, Australia, and New Zealand among them.

According to a US government oversight report released this week, 27 NATO allies and partners pledged around $6.8 billion to the scheme by the end of September, with $4.9 billion already transferred to the US Treasury.

Poland has been among Ukraine’s staunchest supporters since the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022. However, relations between the two neighboring countries have soured in recent months over Ukraine’s glorification of Nazi collaborators.

Read more

The dispute centers on the official honoring of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and its militant wing, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which massacred Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia during World War II.

Warsaw regards the killing of an estimated 100,000 Poles in the regions – which are now largely part of modern-day Ukraine – as genocide.

The UPA and OUN collaborated with Nazi Germany during the 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union.

Nevertheless, in May, Zelensky granted an elite Ukrainian special operations unit the honorary title ‘Heroes of the UPA’. The move prompted Polish President Karol Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration.

Russia has long accused the Ukrainian leadership, which came to power following the 2014 Western-backed Maidan coup, of glorifying Nazi collaborators and promoting Nazi ideology.

Russia has also criticized Western governments for turning a blind eye to the honoring of WWII-era Ukrainian nationalist militants while continuing to support Ukraine. It has also argued that Western weapons deliveries only serve to prolong the conflict without changing the outcome, while increasing the risk of a direct military confrontation between NATO and Russia.

title: Moscow to host international human rights forum
content:
Delegates from 70 countries are expected to discuss protection of citizens abroad and human trafficking

Representatives from 70 countries will convene in Moscow for an international ombudsmen forum to discuss human rights protection, online child safety, citizens’ rights abroad, and cooperation between national institutions.

The event will run from Monday to Wednesday, drawing officials and rights advocates from countries including Brazil, Mexico, Türkiye, Indonesia, South Africa, Switzerland, and several ex-Soviet nations. The conference is being held under the auspices of Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova.

“The focus is on developing international cooperation, finding common approaches and effective mechanisms to help people in the most difficult circumstances,” she said. “It is important that a person can count on support regardless of which country they are in.”

Read more

The first day will be dedicated to discussing harmful online content and protecting children in the digital sphere. The next day will revolve around protection of citizens overseas, freedom of conscience, cultural identity, sovereign development, and support for trafficking victims.

Participants also plan to adopt the “Moscow Principles,” a declaration intended to reinforce the independence of human rights institutions and keep channels open even when governments clash.

Apart from foreign officials, the forum’s expected speakers include RT editor-in-chief Margarita Simonyan, former UN weapons inspector Scott Ritter, and former British MP George Galloway.

Lantratova recently came into the spotlight after she worked together with Ukrainian officials on a humanitarian operation in the town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region, which had been largely cut off from essential supplies for months due to a Ukrainian siege. The six-day local ceasefire brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump allowed food and medicine to enter and civilians to leave for either Russia or Ukraine.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised the operation as a success, commended cooperation between Lantratova and Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmitry Lubinets, suggesting that the arrangement “could set a precedent” for similar humanitarian pauses elsewhere.

title: OpenAI security chiefs discuss Ukraine military ties with Russian pranksters (VIDEO)
content:
Senior company officials, including two Pentagon veterans, talked about expanding cooperation with Kiev into potential military applications

Three senior OpenAI national security officials, including two former Pentagon insiders, have been duped by Russian pranksters into discussing sensitive details of the company’s AI cooperation with Ukraine, including potential military applications.

The pranksters, Vovan and Lexus, whose real names are Vladimir Kuznetsov and Alexey Stolyarov, are known for impersonating officials to draw high-profile figures into private conversations. Their previous targets include Emmanuel Macron, Angela Merkel, Giorgia Meloni, and Henry Kissinger. The duo also host a podcast about their pranks.

This time, they posed as Rustem Umerov, Ukraine’s foreign intelligence chief, securing a 17-minute video call with Sasha Baker, OpenAI’s head of global national security policy and former US deputy undersecretary of defense; Caroline Zier, a former adviser to Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin; and Ben Crampton, the company’s national security lead for Europe.

Despite their security credentials, the officials apparently failed to detect the impersonation. Baker and Zier greeted the supposed Umerov like a familiar contact, even though his camera remained off.

Read more

The discussion centered on OpenAI’s ties with Kiev. The company had publicly announced in September that it would provide Ukraine with its cybersecurity tools to protect civilian infrastructure. The prank call, however, revealed how readily its national security officials discussed expanding that cooperation to potential military use with someone whose identity they had failed to verify.

Seconds into the call, Crampton disclosed that OpenAI was already supplying Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation with a tool used to detect and fix cybersecurity weaknesses, and was preparing to offer a more advanced version capable of simulating cyberattacks. The pranksters then quickly steered the conversation toward military applications.

Crampton confirmed existing contacts with Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, while Baker expressed willingness to explore closer cooperation.

“This partnership is very, very new. I think we would certainly be open to a conversation with your Ministry of Defense about their goals and needs,” she said.

Read more

Pressed on whether OpenAI would supply Ukraine with AI models for military use in particular, Baker sidestepped the question, but left the door open to a greater role in Kiev’s war effort.

“Let’s start there and let’s grow that partnership as robustly as we can, even as we’re having conversations about where we might be able to further contribute to Ukraine’s military efforts,” she said.

Crampton admitted that senior OpenAI executives were reluctant to allow offensive military uses of its technology, but suggested those limits could be blurred.

“There’s a general reluctance on the part of many people who are senior in the company to get too involved in offensive uses of our technology in a military context,” he said. He argued, however, that “offense and defense are not necessarily distinguishable from each other under certain circumstances,” raising questions about how far the company might extend military cooperation under the banner of defensive technology.

Read more

OpenAI confirmed the hoax to The Intercept, with spokesman Nate Evans saying the company had investigated the call weeks earlier, established that it was an impersonation and taken steps to prevent similar incidents. He did not address the substance of the conversation.

The exact date of the call remains unclear, although Vovan and Lexus said in a subsequent podcast that it took place after OpenAI’s September announcement. They released the recording on Telegram on Wednesday.

Kuznetsov noted that gaining access to OpenAI’s top national security officials was surprisingly easy. Posing as Umerov, the pranksters contacted a senior Ukrainian official in San Francisco who already had ties with OpenAI. The official apparently fell for the impersonation and offered to arrange the meeting.

‘Let them play’: Fans push back against Russia’s hockey ban
content:
A court opened the door to Russia’s hockey return – politicians want it slammed shut, and some fans have had enough

When Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney decided to refuse visas to Russians to play in next month’s World Junior Ice Hockey Championships, he became the first elected leader to openly ignore a court ruling and international sports federation decision. In doing so, he unleashed dangerous and virulent anti-Russian forces in his own country, setting back sports diplomacy over 50 years.

The week before, on October 30, the Court of Arbitration of Sport (CAS) voted to allow Russian and Belarusian teams back into international play. The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) accepted the decision and a plethora of national federations in Europe reacted predictably.

Eight countries, including Latvia and France, stated that they would boycott any games with Russia. Germany, the host of the 2027 IIHF World Championships, objected but accepted Russia’s return, with only Slovakia welcoming it. Sponsors of the event in Germany have either pulled out or threatened to do so.

What seems to be missing in this entire ‘discussion’ is what hockey fans think. Not the ‘nafoids’ and bots online who rant and rage against all things Russian. Not the opinion of the handful of Canadian-Ukrainians who protested in Ottawa at the visit of Russian star Alexander Ovechkin’s Washington Capitals. And certainly not grandstanding by politicians and sports administrators beholden to them. The voices of actual hockey fans are being studiously ignored by the media – so too the inherent danger posed by Russian or Belarusian teams competing in international competitions.

Read more

‘It’s purely hate of Russians’

In October, I had a business trip with Capital Sports to EU countries. I covered a number of major sporting events, interviewed athletes and administrators, with hockey taking center stage in Germany, Italy, and Lithuania.

“I used to love watching KHL (the Russia-based Continental Hockey League) games, they [are not] as brutal as in Canada, but the skill is amazing,” Nils, an Iserlohn Roosters’ hockey fan, told me in Cologne. “You see the difference with no Russian team playing [in World or Olympic competition], it’s so hard on those guys because the career is short.”

Nils and his friend Patrick were in the city for their team’s game with the Cologne Sharks. I interviewed dozens of people attending the November 1 game, less than two days after the CAS ruling. The German Ice Hockey Federation had already voiced opposition, with social media abuzz with rumors of boycotts and worse. Patrick and I found a common thread.

“When they [speak] about security, this is correct. Because we see now, they [pro-Ukrainians] can make a lot of trouble and not only online.”

‘Security’ and ‘safety’ were words contained in the statements of most national federations, for good reason. We have seen what Kiev can do in other sovereign states when they want to make a point. From attempting to murder an exiled Ukrainian oligarch in Monaco to the case underway in Germany against a Ukrainian military officer for the Nord Stream terrorist attack, there is a basis for fear.

“These guys [politicians and sport administrators] are idiots. It’s purely hate of Russians,” Mikaela, from Dusseldorf and lifelong hockey fan, said. “We had enough war now and we have to make changes. I mean, look at the football [FIFA World Cup 2026], the Americans were allowed to host it after blowing up little girls in school [in reference to the February 28, 2026 missile strike in Minab, Iran].”

Her boyfriend did, however, mention a Nord Stream-type specter.

“Can you guarantee that they won’t blow up an arena? I can’t,” he said, before quickly adding, “but I want to see White Russia [Belarus] and Russia both playing again. Not to be bullied.”

Read more

‘Football needs to man up and bring in Russia’

Four days later in Italy, while working at the AC Milan-Ferencvaros UEFA Europa League game, the situation in hockey had become clearer. Sweden, Finland, Czechia, France, Austria, Norway, Denmark, and Latvia were all ready to sustain losses by refusing to take the ice against Russia. The Carney ban on Russian youngsters was two days old and Milanese fans and visitors from Budapest did not hold back.

“It’s bulls**t,” Nico, a 24-year-old Milan fan of football and hockey, told me at halftime of the game. “I can’t stand these people and their [two] faces. Israel, yes. Ukraine, yes. Come play, kill kids, come play, all is good. Russia, it’s not the players who are fighting. If those fat fools who want more war, go fight, let the players just play.”

Other Milan fans held the same opinion, with one drawing a parallel with football.

“I was in Russia for a game [UEFA Champions League in 2012] and me and my wife fell in love with St. Petersburg. We go back for the World Cup in 2018 and I love the culture. Football needs to man up and bring in Russia to us again. Stop this stupid hating and blocking. We’re all people. We’re all just people,” Andrea said.

He proudly showed photos of his times in Russia and said that he would go back “when all the stupid shooting stops.” Asked about the Canadian visa ban, he laughed and said, “It shows they can’t protect children from crazy psychos, that is all.”

János, one of the Ferencvaros ultra leaders who organized a protest in support of law and order in Europe outside Milan’s Duomo cathedral earlier on November 5, echoed Andrea’s sentiment.

“Hockey showed balls to allow [Russia] back in [to] play... I don’t like what they do in Ukraine, but I know what Ukraine does to my people there [ethnic Hungarians]. There’s no good side in the any war, but we have worse things to deal with in Europe than have us all fighting.”

Read more

‘Let them all refuse and lose’

Back in Vilnius, a top official from the Lithuanian Ice Hockey Federation (LIHF) told me on Wednesday about the pressure they’re under, even though they won’t play Russia anytime soon.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, they said there is tremendous political pressure to “make a statement about solidarity with our neighbor [Latvia].”

They explained that both their chief funding source, the Ministry of Education, Science, and Sport, and at least one sponsor, Ober Haus (a real estate services company in the Baltic Region) have demanded that they stand with Latvia.

“Personally speaking, I would say let them all refuse to play and lose the games. Same as Canada, let them ban Russian boys and take the tournament to a country where people have a brain.”

Carney and his government have stated that they will disobey the CAS ruling and not allow players or staff holding current visas to take part; 116 Russian-born players were given visas by the Carney government this year. There are nine Russians currently playing for NHL teams in Canada. Of the seven teams in the country, only Ottawa and Vancouver have none on their active rosters, but both have Russians under contract.

Carney is in a difficult personal and professional position. Professionally, he has relied on the large Ukrainian diaspora vote, many of whom idolize Nazi collaborator Stepan Bandera and hate Russia and Russians. Personally, he is godfather to Chrystia Freeland’s son. Freeland, whose maternal grandfather Michael Chomiak was also a Nazi collaborator, now works in Kiev as an ‘economic adviser’ to Vladimir Zelensky.

Russia’s ice hockey federation has asked the IIHF to act: force Canada to allow Russian kids play or move the tournament. According to the Lithuanian official, the latter is most likely to happen.

Read more

“Canada can’t back down and the [IIHF] are worried about terror attacks.”

This scenario, they believe, is what will force their hand.

“You need to know that many Ukrainians live out in Alberta [where the competition will take place from December 26 to January 5]. It would not be too impossible that there is attacks on Russian players, or bomb threats, this is all they need to do.”

The puck is firmly under IIHF control. They can pull the tournament out of Canada and hand it to the US. They will worry about national federations breaking away and forming a new global organization, but the chances of that are about as much as an ice cube’s chance in a volcano. What remains to be seen is if the sports administrators and politicians listen to their public and realize that they now can take a historic step to save their sport, and the world. Because sports diplomacy is needed now more than ever. The bullies cannot win, off the ice.

Ukraine aid hurts US military – Pentagon
content:
US forces have been forced to divert money intended for spare parts toward supporting Kiev under Biden-era commitments, a new report says

Ukraine support is draining resources from US troops stationed in Europe and damaging their combat readiness, according to a new Pentagon inspector general report.

In its report to Congress in November, the watchdog said the US Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF) was forced to divert resources from US forces and longstanding operations toward supporting Kiev because of the lack of dedicated Ukraine funding in fiscal years 2025 and 2026.

“These resource gaps have negatively impacted USAREUR-AF’s overall readiness, training effectiveness, and capacity to exercise operations plans,” the report states.

Read more

In particular, Ukraine-related operations were consuming funds intended for routine deployments and essential spare parts for US military equipment. On top of that, some rotating US units returned to their home bases with unpaid spare-parts bills, according to the report. An earlier report for January-March said the command redirected a total of $364.6 million from other requirements to support Ukraine.

The funding squeeze stemmed from failure to approve major emergency aid packages for Ukraine in 2025 and 2026 in Congress, where many Republican leaders vehemently opposed the “blank-check” policy for Ukraine. Since returning to office, US President Donald Trump has also opposed further large-scale US-funded aid packages for Ukraine, seeking instead to shift the financial burden onto Kiev’s European backers.

Read more

The US has committed more than $198 billion in Ukraine aid since 2022, much of it under former President Joe Biden. Of that total, around $65 billion remained available for payment as of late September. However, $60.71 billion of this is already legally committed to contracts and other obligations, leaving the Trump administration limited room to redirect or halt the spending.

The Pentagon has also struggled to replenish weapons and ammunition taken from US military stockpiles to supply Ukraine. The watchdog cited a $38.6 billion backlog of unfunded requirements to replenish US military stockpiles depleted by Ukraine aid.

In addition, last year’s Pentagon audit found that the department failed to maintain controls over the use of funds aimed to replenish aid sent to Kiev, noting that funding reallocations, worth $5.7 billion, lacked adequate documentation. Auditors also identified $920 million in missed opportunities to use replenishment funds and found that the military overstated spending commitments and payments to Congress.

Since coming into office, Trump has resisted unconditional aid to Ukraine, opting instead to sell weapons to the country as part of the NATO-coordinated PURL mechanism where most procurements are financed by Ukraine’s European backers.

While Trump’s policy does not erase Biden-era commitments, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers accused his administration this week of delaying the execution of a separate $400 million Ukraine aid package until the final weeks of the fiscal year.

Last month, Washington approved the sale of 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, funded by Kiev and its backers, but given the backlog and the Iran war, which depleted US stockpiles, the deliveries could take years.

Moscow has warned against Western military assistance to Kiev, arguing that it only prolongs the conflict without changing the outcome.
