title: Van Hollen Makes His Case to Replace Schumer as Jeffries Is Heckled at Democratic Gathering
content:
By Chase Smith

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) told a gathering of Democrats in Denver on Nov. 13 that he’s running for Senate majority leader because Americans have lost faith that Washington will improve their lives.

The speech came one day after he announced his challenge to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

Earlier in the same program, protesters repeatedly interrupted House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is expected to become speaker in January.

Van Hollen spoke on the second day of the What’s Next conference, hosted by the group Majority Democrats. He said voters in last week’s midterm elections rejected President Donald Trump’s policies without fully embracing Democrats.

“While they fired the Trump policies, they have not fully hired us,” he said.

He cited a poll, which he did not name, in which 92 percent of Americans said Washington has the power to make a real difference in their lives, and only 43 percent said it does. He called the gap a trust deficit.

“We must overcome the trust deficit,” Van Hollen said.

He said the Senate should hold floor votes on issues Americans care about regardless of whether Trump would veto the bills, confront the president over the war in Iran and health care, and put newly elected senators “on the front lines.”

He did not mention Schumer by name and said the race is not about any one person.

Schumer has expressed confidence that he will have the votes when Senate Democrats meet for a secret-ballot election in December. “The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said at a press conference.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan has endorsed Van Hollen. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who followed Van Hollen on stage, opened his speech by saying, “I’m for Chris Van Hollen.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) did not mention the leadership race in her remarks in Denver but said that on election night, “people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership.”

Earlier in the week, she joined Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) at the Capitol, where Sanders told reporters he would not vote to reelect Schumer as leader.

Slotkin said then that she would not vote for any candidate, Schumer or a challenger, who lacks a concrete plan to govern differently. “I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) said during a governors’ panel that she does not buy the idea of a fight within the party, saying a focus on lowering costs unites Democrats.

Jeffries was interviewed on stage by Fox News host Jessica Tarlov. Protesters shouted demands for a Green New Deal and asked when it would be time for Medicare for All.

“Your version of accountability is shaking hands with the Trump family,” one shouted.

Another demanded that Jeffries stop any Democrat from voting for a permitting bill now moving through the Senate.

“Remember, Jessica, I’m from Brooklyn. This is light work,” Jeffries said.

He said House Democrats are committed to passing permitting changes and will discuss the bill as a caucus once it comes over from the Senate, adding that some issues still need to be addressed.

Tarlov asked Jeffries about criticism that his leadership is too timid. He pointed to House Democrats’ fights with Republicans over Medicaid cuts, tariffs, the Iran war, and redistricting, and said the incoming majority of 260 Democrats would focus on lowering costs.

Joseph Lord contributed to this report.

title: BMW Issues ‘Park Outside’ Recall for 720,000 Vehicles Over Fire Risk
content:
By Mary Prenon

BMW of North America has issued a “park outside” recall for 720,796 vehicles because of a fire risk, even when the vehicle is parked and turned off.

According to a report posted on Nov. 13 by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), these same vehicles were recalled in 2024 due to a water pump issue and must be repaired again.

The report noted that an improperly sealed electrical connector on the water pump could be exposed to water and short-circuit, increasing the risk of a fire.

The recall involves the following models: 2012–2016 BMW 3 Series; 2012–2016 BMW 5 Series; 2012–2015 BMW X1; 2012–2016 BMW Z4; 2013–2017 BMW X3; 2014–2016 BMW 2 Series coupe; 2014–2016 BMW 3 Series sportswagon; 2014–2016 BMW 328xi Gran Turismo; 2014–2016 BMW 4 Series convertible; 2014–2016 BMW 4 Series coupe; 2015–2016 BMW 2 Series convertible; 2015–2016 BMW 4 Series gran coupe; 2015–2018 BMW X4 ; and 2016–2018 BMW X5 xDrive40e.

“If you have one of these vehicles, you should park your vehicle outside and away from buildings and other vehicles until the vehicle is repaired,” the NHTSA report stated.

Notification letters to owners of affected models are expected to be mailed starting on Dec. 25. Local BMW dealerships will offer free repairs once they are available.

To date, BMW is aware of approximately 10 incidents in the United States related or potentially related to this issue, but does not know of any accidents or injuries. The NHTSA noted that the problems were in vehicles that had been repaired under the previous recall.

In mid-October, Hyundai recalled nearly 95,000 sedans, cautioning owners to park outside and away from buildings or other vehicles due to power seat motors that could overheat and cause a fire.

BMW’s last “park outside” recall in mid-July involved more than 29,000 vehicles. In that case, the alert was attributed to a possible faulty engine starter relay that could corrode, overheat, and short-circuit, increasing the risk of fire.

Earlier in July, Kia America Inc. issued a “park outside” recall of nearly 463,000 vehicles that could suddenly catch fire due to an overheating power seat motor.

title: Record $404 Billion October Deficit Marks Start of US Fiscal 2027
content:
By Andrew Moran

The U.S. government opened fiscal year 2027 with a record-setting $404 billion budget deficit in October, according to the Treasury Department.

Last month’s fiscal shortfall was $120 billion, or 42 percent, larger than a year ago.

Spending rose 12 percent year over year to more than $773 billion.

Medicare was the top federal outlay, totaling $170 billion. This was followed by Social Security ($143 billion), national defense ($129 billion), and net interest costs ($103 billion).

The jump in federal spending was driven in part by a $14 billion increase in Agriculture Department outlays. It also reflected a $29 billion increase in national defense outlays, according to Treasury data. Within Defense Department military programs, spending on military personnel rose by about $19 billion, operation and maintenance by about $8 billion, and procurement by about $4 billion.

Receipts, meanwhile, fell almost 9 percent from a year ago to around $369 billion.

Customs duties exceeded $19 billion, down from the $31.35 billion posted a year ago. The White House’s budget, released this past spring, projected customs receipts of $464 billion this fiscal year.

Some of October’s outlays were payments due Nov. 1 that were moved because that date fell on a weekend, according to the Treasury Department. Adjusted for those timing shifts, the deficit still rose by more than $100 billion from October 2025, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate cited by Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

MacGuineas said the federal government borrowed an average of more than $13 billion per day in October.

“We’re now in the era of $2 trillion deficits—perhaps even higher, given that October’s deficit was already one-fifth of that projected total,” MacGuineas said in a Nov. 12 statement.

“Worse so, the deficit is more than 6 percent of the economy, which is about double the level that most economists think is sustainable.”

The latest numbers underscore the difficulty of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s initiative to lower the federal deficit to 3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The deficit-to-GDP ratio fell to 5.8 percent in fiscal year 2025 before rising again to around 6.2 percent in fiscal 2026 as the government posted a $2 trillion shortfall.

The United States is weeks away from reaching the $41 trillion national debt milestone.

As of Nov. 10, the Treasury’s Debt-to-the-Penny dashboard shows total public debt standing at $40.58 trillion.

Debt Ceiling Showdown on the Horizon

The federal government is close to hitting the debt ceiling, currently set at $41.1 trillion and established under last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The Bipartisan Policy Center estimated in June that the government would most likely reach the debt limit between late winter and mid-summer of 2027.

The Treasury will then employ extraordinary measures—suspending Government Securities Investment Fund reinvestments, pausing new debt issuance, and halting Exchange Stabilization Fund reinvestments—to keep paying the government’s bills. The center estimated that those measures would last another six to nine months. After this period, the X-date—the date the government defaults without congressional action—is reached.

Repeated debt-ceiling standoffs have contributed to downgrades by the leading credit agencies—Fitch, Moody’s, and S&P—over the years.

To avoid these routine standoffs, some officials, including President Donald Trump and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), have proposed repealing the debt ceiling.

“I would support that entirely,” Trump told NBC News in December 2024.

“The Democrats have said they want to get rid of it. If they want to get rid of it, I would lead the charge.”

Others have suggested letting the United States default. But this would have dramatic economic consequences, said Andrew Lautz, senior director of federal policy at the Tax Foundation.

“Default would be an even greater mistake than repealing the debt limit. A default could lead to a permanent increase in U.S. borrowing costs,” Lautz wrote in a Nov. 3 blog post.

This could raise borrowing costs and widen the gap between spending and revenues, eventually causing significant tax increases. A default could also delay Social Security and military payments and spook global financial markets.

“A middle path might be bipartisan debt limit reform that takes the worst of the brinksmanship off the table while establishing more regular intervals for Congress to debate and enact fiscal reforms,” Lautz added.

title: Nationwide Ground Stop Lifted After More Than 5 Hours
content:
By Jill McLaughlin

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted the nationwide ground stop issued for all flights in the United States on Nov. 13 for “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Officials said the reason for the ground stop was that the air traffic control system became overloaded with data and shut down, but they are not yet ruling out other possible problems.

“We have seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack or super intelligence,” Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullin told reporters at a news conference. “We’re still looking at it. We’re not ruling out anything.”

Mullin also said new technology was introduced to the older air traffic control system, which overwhelmed it.

Agents with the National Security Agency are assisting in the investigation, Mullin said.

“It’s an old system that went down. It went down everywhere,” said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. “It got overloaded.”

The emergency alert, issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, applied to all aircraft operations at all airports. Thousands of travelers were delayed, and at least 5,000 flights were canceled.

Airlines were expected to be able to catch up this weekend with many of the missed flights, Duffy said.

The system could take until Thanksgiving weekend to become fully operational again, Duffy estimated.

Medical flights and emergency ambulances were not grounded during the emergency.

The order was issued following a communication problem “impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

About 3,500 aircraft bound for U.S. airports were in the air when the nationwide ground stop was ordered, Mullin said.

Thousands of passengers were caught at airports throughout the country waiting for flights.

Gillian Hamilton, a Canadian attempting to fly from Nashville to her home in Saskatchewan, had already boarded her WestJet plane when the FAA issued the ground stop.

“We had already boarded and then had to wait an hour on the plane,” Hamilton said. “The flight attendants didn’t know what to say. They just kept apologizing and served refreshments and snacks.”

Hamilton said she and her friends did not want to wait at the airport amid the uncertainty surrounding their flights, so they decided to rent a car and drive 30 hours to Canada.

President Donald Trump has been briefed on the situation, the secretary said.

Mullin denied any connection to Microsoft’s outage the day before that took Outlook and other programs offline for most of the day.

Other agencies assisting the FAA were the State Department and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

By 6 p.m. Eastern Time, Pacific-bound flights were cleared to depart from San Francisco International Airport, including to destinations in Hawaii and Asia, the airport reported. Passengers were asked to check with their airlines for the latest information about flights.

The Air Line Pilots Association said pilots were “ready to get passengers moving again the moment it’s safe to do so.”

“Safety comes first,” the association posted on X.

Flight cancellations reached over 5,000 and continued to rise before 9 p.m. ET.

Trump told Fox News the disruption didn’t seem like a cyberattack or a problem with artificial intelligence. No groups had taken credit for the incident.

Some international flights were allowed to depart on a case-by-case basis after the ground stop was issued, Flightradar24 reported.

Congressional Democrats are calling for investigations into the situation.

“My office and I are closely monitoring the nationwide ground stop,” said New Jersey Democrat Rep. Herb Conaway. “The Trump Administration must answer for this disruption. The American people deserve a full explanation, and Congress must be immediately briefed on what went wrong and who is responsible.”

Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), a former Blackhawk pilot and Aviation Subcommittee ranking member, said she also planned to thoroughly investigate the incident, while Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) said she was “alarmed” by the news and was tracking it.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare in the United States. The last time the FAA issued one was Jan. 11, 2023. All domestic departures were halted for about 90 minutes after a contractor erased database files, crashing the Notice to Air Missions pilot safety system.

Jacki Thrapp contributed to this report.

title: US Air Force Responds to Suspected Drone Activity at UK Airbase
content:
By Aldgra Fredly

The U.S. Air Force said on Nov. 13 that its personnel had responded to suspected unauthorized drone activity over a Lakenheath military air base in Suffolk, England.

The incident did not affect any personnel, aircraft, or infrastructure at Royal Air Force Lakenheath, a U.S. Air Force spokesperson said in a statement.

“We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, U.S. and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the spokesperson said.

The British Ministry of Defence said the incident was resolved and that it was working with U.S. personnel to assess the situation. Details surrounding the suspected drone activity remain unclear.

West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said in an update that he had been in touch with authorities at RAF Lakenheath. Timothy said he was told that the incident posed no threat to public safety.

“Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities,” he said in a Facebook post.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Washington forces Gulf states to choose between cooperation and destruction, Miko Peled has argued

The US is behaving like a mafia boss in the Middle East, forcing countries to cooperate or risk being attacked, Miko Peled, founder and director of the Palestine House of Freedom, said on Friday.

He was speaking in an RT panel discussion on recent remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who blamed Iran for instability in the region.

Peled said the Gulf states fear that defying Washington could leave their countries in ruins, pointing to US military interventions in recent decades.

“The US operates like a mafia boss,” he said. “If you’re a leader in the region and you know that if you don’t comply, you’re going to end up like Iraq... and Libya and Syria and Yemen… your country is going to end up in ruins.”

He argued that cooperating with the US offers Gulf countries a chance to maintain stability. “But that’s not a question of trust. It’s a question of survival, really.”

Tehran University Professor Seyed Mohammed Marandi accused Israel of being the main source of instability in the region, citing the displacement of Palestinians and the “ongoing genocide” in Gaza.

“The US has contributed to this misery for the sake of the Israeli regime. The invasion of Iraq has brought about the destruction of that country, thanks to the US,” he said.

“They destroyed Afghanistan. They initiated a dirty war in Syria,” he added, citing a February 2012 email in which Jake Sullivan, then an adviser to Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, wrote that Al-Qaeda was “on our side” in Syria.

Naim Joseph Salem, a professor of international affairs and diplomacy at the Lebanese Army Military Academy, warned that Gulf states could come to regret hosting US military bases if the US-Israeli war with Iran escalates again.

“Gulf countries, in particular Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, and United Arab Emirates, have come to feel the heat because of the presence of American military bases on their territory,” he said. “They may regret by then their alliance with the US.”

title: Russia’s cultural diversity takes center stage in massive dance show (VIDEO)
content:
The large-scale show celebrated the country’s vast cultural diversity through the traditional Slavic folk dance

More than 600 dancers have taken part in the ‘Khorovod. The Energy of Unity’ folk dance production at the National Centre ‘Russia’ in Moscow

The large-scale dance production celebrated Russia’s vast cultural diversity, traditions and the shared identity of its many ethnic communities. At its core was the khorovod, a traditional Slavic circle dance that shares much in common with similar traditions around the world.

“What matters is that our production goes beyond classic folk dances. We have been able to present traditional art in a contemporary way. The khorovod brings people together, and virtually every people in the world has a dance like it,” ‘Russia’ National Center Deputy Director General Anastasia Zvyagina told RT.

The circle dance is especially symbolic in Russia, where so many different ethnic communities live together, she added. “No one comes first or last. It is this energy of unity that allows us to build on what we have today and, of course, look ahead to the future,” she said.

We have managed to preserve the culture and distinct identity of all our peoples, and we are proud of that.

Read more

The show combined traditional folk dances with contemporary choreography, electronic music, beatboxing and throat singing. Performers came from Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic, Karelia, Yakutia, Crimea, the North Caucasus and other regions.

The production featured original musical pieces exploring family bonds, nature, and cultural heritage.

The performances ran from Tuesday to Thursday and attracted more than 1,800 spectators. The production brought together over ten ensembles and solo artists from different regions of Russia.

title: US could spy on Germany through Tesla cars – regional intelligence chief
content:
Internet-connected vehicles could expose sensitive military and government facilities, Stephan Kramer has warned

Tesla vehicles could pose an espionage risk, Stephan Kramer, the head of Germany’s domestic intelligence agency (BfV) in the state of Thuringia, has warned. His remarks come as German officials call for restrictions on parking internet-connected cars near sensitive government and military facilities.

Tesla is an American company led by Elon Musk, an ally of US President Donald Trump. The electric carmaker operates a major factory near Berlin, making it one of the few foreign automakers with a significant manufacturing presence in Germany.

Kramer was commenting on the German Army’s decision to restrict access by internet-connected vehicles to sensitive areas of military bases. The measures apply regardless of manufacturer, including Tesla.

“We should not assume that friends do not spy on one another,” Kramer told Handelsblatt on Friday. “The same security standards should apply to Tesla and all other manufacturers.”

According to the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), Germany’s digital security watchdog, most new vehicles sold in the country have the technical capability to collect information, including location data, camera footage, and sensor readings, and transmit it to manufacturers’ back-end systems.

There is no specific evidence so far that the data has been used for espionage, Handelsblatt reported. According to the BSI, customers are often unaware of what data their vehicles generate and transmit.

“The cameras and location-tracking systems in [internet-connected] cars capture sensitive information,” Kramer warned. “At [German Army] facilities, that includes information about military installations, operational procedures and personnel,” he said, describing the restrictions as “strongly advisable and therefore proportionate.”

The intelligence chief called for similar restrictions in “particularly sensitive areas of government buildings, police facilities, intelligence agencies and other security-relevant institutions,” including designated parking zones or access limitations.

Read more

Kramer also advised civil servants and public employees against discussing confidential matters inside internet-connected vehicles.

His concerns were echoed by several MPs, including Marc Henrichmann of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Johannes Schaetzl, a digital policy spokesman for the Social Democratic Party’s parliamentary group.

“We must not be naive: Espionage today is no longer carried out solely by agents, but also through technology that we ourselves bring onto our premises,” Henrichmann told Handelsblatt.

Schaetzl expressed particular concern about vehicles produced by Chinese automaker BYD, which he described as “black boxes,” adding: “We do not know exactly what data is collected or who has access to it.”

Last month, Tesla reported that it delivered more vehicles globally than Mercedes-Benz’s passenger-car division in the third quarter of 2026. The German automaker has faced pressure from US import tariffs and growing competition in China, where domestic manufacturers such as BYD and Xiaomi are challenging established brands.

title: SpaceX launches world’s largest rocket, loses booster in fiery crash (VIDEOS)
content:
Starship reached orbit and deployed satellites, but its giant first-stage booster failed to return to the launch site

Elon Musk’s SpaceX has launched the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, attempting to recover an entire orbital launch system for the first time in history.

The 124-meter (407-foot) Starship blasted off from the company’s Starbase facility in southern Texas on Friday, carrying 26 next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit.

The mission was designed to demonstrate that both stages of the giant rocket could return to the launch site and be caught by mechanical arms attached to the launch tower, allowing them to be refurbished and reused.

Liftoff of Starship! https://t.co/lc7UtE6H7z

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 13, 2026

However, the Super Heavy booster failed to return to the tower as planned, instead making a fiery landing in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX did not immediately explain the failure, although safety systems diverted the booster offshore.

Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy Booster soft water landing. Landing looked so smooth. It hovered for a good amount of time. https://t.co/V9NW4O9Dv9

— Nic Cruz Patane (@niccruzpatane) November 14, 2026

The Starship upper stage continued into orbit and successfully deployed its satellite payload. It is expected to circle Earth 15 times before attempting to return to Texas on Saturday, where the company plans to catch it using the tower’s giant mechanical arms.

Read more

If successful, it would mark the first recovery of a Starship spacecraft from orbit.

SpaceX has caught the Super Heavy booster three times, but recovering the upper stage presents a greater challenge because it must survive atmospheric reentry after traveling at orbital speeds.

Starship is also central to NASA’s Artemis program, under which SpaceX is developing a modified version of the spacecraft to land American astronauts on the Moon. The latest test follows September’s milestone flight, when Starship reached orbit for the first time.

title: Putin, Trump, and Xi to hold rare three-way meeting in China
content:
The White House has confirmed plans for talks on nuclear arms control and international security on the sidelines of the APEC summit

The leaders of Russia, China, and the US plan to meet on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, AP reported on Saturday, citing officials.

The White House confirmed plans for the unprecedented three-way meeting on Friday, the outlet said. The talks are expected to focus on nuclear arms control and international security, including the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov subsequently confirmed the meeting.

Chinese President Xi Jinping will host his Russian and US counterparts, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, at the November 18–19 summit.

Putin aide Yury Ushakov said earlier that the Russian president discussed the upcoming meeting with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. “We hope that the first meeting in this format will have a positive impact on the overall international situation,” Ushakov said last month.

Read more

The summit will follow US-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, which marked the resumption of trilateral negotiations after a nine-month hiatus. Although the talks ended without a major breakthrough, Kushner said the sides will carry out “the largest prisoner exchange of the war.”

Ukraine’s European backers are currently discussing appointing representatives to take part in talks with Russia after being sidelined in Abu Dhabi, where European delegates met separately with Ukrainian and American teams. Moscow has insisted that the Europeans must first demonstrate goodwill, accusing them of seeking to sabotage peace efforts since 2022.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and LNG shipments, remains disrupted by the US-Israeli war with Iran, driving up energy prices. There are continued concerns in the region that Trump could resume major military operations following his Republican Party’s defeat in the midterm elections.

Washington and Beijing are still at odds over tariffs, rare-earth minerals, and restrictions on advanced technology, despite a fragile trade truce set to expire in January.

title: Tanker rams US cruise ship, capsizing it (VIDEOS)
content:
All 180 people aboard were rescued after the vessel capsized in the Mississippi River, with 32 hospitalized

An asphalt tanker rammed a docked cruise ship in New Orleans, Louisiana on Friday, causing it to capsize and sending passengers into the Mississippi River.

Videos from the scene show the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker striking the American Heritage cruise ship directly in the side.

The vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, was carrying 180 passengers and crew members at the time of the collision.

The cruise ship rolled onto its side and partially sank as tugboat operators, police, and other rescuers rushed to help.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed that everyone aboard was rescued. She added that 32 people were hospitalized, none with critical injuries.

“It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi,” Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry told reporters. “When you think about the population that was on that cruise ship, and the ability for us to get them off, get them out of the water.”

title: Gestapo 2.0? Germany grants spy agencies sweeping new powers
content:
The controversial reform allows intelligence services to carry out sabotage, secretly enter homes, and expand surveillance

The German parliament has passed sweeping legislation granting the country’s intelligence agencies unprecedented powers to conduct sabotage, secretly enter homes, and expand surveillance. The controversial law has prompted comparisons with the Gestapo and Stasi, the notorious secret police organizations of Nazi Germany and Communist East Germany.

The legislation, championed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s governing coalition, was approved on Friday by 300 votes to 190, with 71 abstentions. Only the ruling CDU/CSU bloc and Social Democrats backed the reform. The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) and The Left opposed it, while the Greens abstained.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt hailed the overhaul as a “reform of the century,” declaring a “new era” for German intelligence agencies that would put them on an “equal footing with our European partners.”

He defended the measures by citing alleged threats from espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other hostile activities aimed at destabilizing Germany.

From surveillance to sabotage

The legislation fundamentally changes the role of Germany’s two principal intelligence agencies: the foreign intelligence service (BND) and the domestic Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV).

Read more

Previously focused primarily on gathering and analyzing intelligence, both agencies will gain powers to actively intervene against perceived threats.

The BND will be authorized to penetrate foreign computer networks, disable servers used by suspected hackers, and delete data. Its new powers could extend to sabotaging foreign chemical laboratories and drone production facilities or disrupting supply chains by introducing defective components into shipments linked to potential threats.

The domestic intelligence agency will gain extensive surveillance and intervention powers, including covert access to smartphones and computers, interception of encrypted communications, and examination of stored data.

BfV operatives could also secretly enter private homes to install surveillance software and neutralize suspected weapons.

The agency will additionally be able to obtain information from payment providers, online platforms, and vehicle manufacturers, while deploying AI-assisted facial recognition and biometric searches to identify potential suspects.

Oversight of the expanded powers will be consolidated under the Independent Oversight Council, a 12-member body established in 2021 and appointed by the Bundestag’s Parliamentary Oversight Panel.

Read more

Previously focused largely on the legality of BND surveillance, the council will gain authority to approve intervention operations by both agencies, including proactive sabotage abroad.

It will also be required to report to parliamentary overseers at least annually and publish public reports excluding classified information.

Return of the secret police?

The overhaul has triggered fierce criticism from opposition lawmakers, who warn that it threatens constitutional protections and dismantles safeguards established after the fall of Nazi Germany.

AfD lawmaker Christian Wirth condemned the reform as an “attack on the rule of law with truly totalitarian characteristics.”

He criticized provisions allowing the BfV to exclude regional intelligence offices from information-sharing networks, warning that they could be used against politically “undesirable” state authorities.

In September, fellow AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio accused Merz’s government of preparing to systematically violate fundamental rights, invoking Germany’s history under the Gestapo and East Germany’s Stasi.

“Manipulating, sabotaging, deceiving – with these subversive measures, the [BfV] is being transformed into Stasi 2.0,” he warned.

Read more

The criticism has extended beyond the AfD.

Green lawmaker Konstantin von Notz supported strengthening the BND but accused the government of lacking “any sensitivity to civil rights” in its domestic intelligence overhaul. He warned that the legislation could face “serious problems” before Germany’s Constitutional Court.

The Left’s Clara Buenger went further, accusing Dobrindt of undermining democracy through nationwide AI-powered mass surveillance and laying the groundwork for a “new German secret police.”

At the heart of the controversy is Germany’s longstanding separation principle, designed to prevent intelligence agencies from acquiring police powers.

The safeguard traces its origins to the Allied powers’ 1949 ‘Police Letter’, which sought to prevent the re-emergence of an organization resembling the Gestapo. The distinction between intelligence gathering and law enforcement was subsequently incorporated into legislation governing Germany’s security services.

Critics argue that allowing intelligence operatives to secretly enter homes, interfere with property, and conduct sabotage erodes that historical barrier.

Dobrindt has dismissed accusations that the reform threatens democracy as “madness.”

Russian threat narrative

The intelligence overhaul comes as Berlin accelerates its military buildup, with Merz’s government repeatedly invoking the supposed Russian threat to justify increased defense spending and expanded security capabilities.

German officials have increasingly warned of a possible military confrontation with Russia, while accusing it of conducting espionage, sabotage, and other hostile operations across Europe.

Read more

Last month, BND chief Martin Jaeger warned that Germany could become “embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia,” accusing the country of waging a “shadow war.”

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and senior military commander General Christian Freuding have also claimed that Russia could attack NATO before the end of the decade.

Moscow has rejected claims that it intends to attack NATO members, dismissing the speculation as “nonsense” and “political schizophrenia.” Russian officials have accused Berlin of pursuing escalation.

The controversy also has a domestic political dimension.

Merz has described the AfD as Russian-backed, without substantiating the allegation, while his Social Democratic coalition partners have pushed for a ban on the opposition party.

The AfD, which calls for stricter immigration control and opposes German military assistance to Ukraine and sanctions on Russia, has become a major target of political scrutiny.

Defending the intelligence overhaul on Friday, Chancellor’s Office official Nina Warken argued that Germany faces daily threats from foreign powers that “disguise sabotage as an accident, espionage as business dealings, and propaganda as an opinion.”

title: Hope in Abu Dhabi, fighting in Europe, ‘hell’ in the Persian Gulf: RT’s reporting of the week’s top news
content:
In the past seven days we also watched Jensen Huang’s career crumble and saw how EU money finances the luxurious lives of the Ukrainian elite

Peace progress in Abu Dhabi

Read more

To follow the headlines this week, one needed simply to follow the movements of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The two American envoys arrived in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for the fourth round of trilateral talks between Washington, Moscow, and Kiev, bringing with them a plan to “create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment,” according to Kushner at least.

The mere mention of a broader European security architecture represents progress, Russian analyst Fyodor Lukyanov wrote for RT, pointing out that Moscow’s calls to rethink European security were previously dismissed by Washington. Although the idea is still in its infancy, the trilateral talks ended positively, with Russia and Ukraine agreeing to a large-scale prisoner swap

Conspicuous in their absence were the Europeans themselves, who at this point had yet to decide whether they should even speak to Russian President Vladimir Putin in the first place. At a meeting with Putin in Moscow on Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner managed to secure the EU a seat at the table in the next round of discussions. However, as RT explained, ‘Europe’ is split into squabbling camps of realists, maximalists, and fantasists, all vying for control of the peace process.

EU deadlock in Dublin

Witkoff and Kushner left Moscow for Dublin on Thursday, where Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and his European backers were meeting for the European Political Community (EPC) and EU leaders’ summits. Their arrival at Baldonnel Aerodrome in the Irish capital was a more stripped-back affair than the welcome they received at the Kremlin, but Zelensky was likely unbothered: he had already bilked tens of millions of euros worth of energy-related aid from his patrons, who used the Dublin gathering to reaffirm their unconditional loyalty to Kiev. 

None dared ask where the money would end up, but a corruption case unfolding back in Ukraine offered a potential answer: in the pockets of oligarchs happy to spend it on sports cars, marble apartments, and, bizarrely, live crocodiles.

Some locals weren’t as happy to receive Zelensky, however, and his car was pelted with eggs after he left the meeting.

Sky News correspondent Stephen Murphy shows one of Zelensky’s convoy cars beign attacked by eggs in Dublin. What a warm welcome. https://t.co/uOgjIjReNy

— Margarita Simonyan (@M_Simonyan) November 13, 2026

Witkoff, Kushner, and now Zelensky are losing their patience with the Europeans. “We need to choose who will represent Europe in the negotiations,” he said on Wednesday, before issuing his ultimatum. This decision, he demanded, must be made “no later than the end of November.”

READ MORE: Dublin summit: European leaders double down on the Zelensky disaster

In true Brussels fashion, EU leaders decided on Friday that the continent will be represented at future talks by national security advisers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, and by the European Commission and Council at leader-level discussions. With all three European factions – realists, maximalists, and fantasists – represented, and seven voices in the mix, European Council President Antonio Costa dismissed questions about potential clashes among the group.

“It is essential to have a team,” he said, yet “to speak with one voice.”

Jensen Huang gets honeypotted

Read more

Jensen Huang’s position at the helm of US chipmaking giant Nvidia made him one of the world’s most powerful billionaires. His weakness for the opposite sex, however, apparently made him a target for foreign intelligence agencies. Huang admitted on Sunday to an extramarital affair with an unnamed woman, who was quickly named in the media as Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive and no relation to Jensen. US spies reportedly believe that Ms. Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information about Nvidia and influence over its CEO.

Beijing has dismissed the allegations as “a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” and US President Donald Trump has stuck by the embattled executive, describing Huang as “an amazing guy” and “a high-quality person.”

Trump’s endorsement couldn’t stop the scandal from snowballing. As memes about the “honeypot” allegations flooded the internet, a second affair was revealed on Wednesday, and Huang resigned on Thursday, right after he was summoned to testify before Congress.

Iran threatens ‘hell’

The Republican Party’s devastating midterm election loss and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s shrinking odds of staying in power have placed the two principal antagonists of the war on Iran in limbo. If White House leaks are to be believed, Netanyahu wants Trump to restart attacks, and a conversation between the two descended into a “shouting match from hell” over the weekend.

Read more

Trump has acknowledged that the war cost his party the midterms, but the US president has rejected a deal with Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and instructed Vice President J.D. Vance – a moderate on Iran – to cease negotiations and focus on domestic issues. Whether these moves represent preparations for renewed conflict remains unclear, but Iran is taking no chances.

This week, Tehran lifted its self-imposed 2,000km limit on the range of its ballistic missiles and threatened to unveil “surprises… on the battlefield” if a new round of military confrontation erupts. Should the US and Israel “choose war,” they will “see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned in a social media post.

Iran and the US have traded tit-for-tat strikes, with Iranian forces claiming an attack on a US early-warning radar installation in Bahrain on Friday. Yemen’s Houthis have struck Saudi oil infrastructure and the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil giant Aramco in Riyadh. For all parties involved, the cost of miscalculation could be huge.

Biden gets milked

Trump’s war on Iran may have dealt a generational defeat to the Republican Party, but he is not the only American president paying a price for siding with Israel. Joe Biden’s trip to Ireland was interrupted when pro-Palestinian protesters lobbed cartons of milk at the former president outside Dublin’s Trinity College on Tuesday.

Biden, whose son Hunter had just received an honorary award from the university, was met with chants of “blood on your hands” and “Genocide Joe” as he left the campus. Irish police were seen wrestling activists to the ground, and two people were pepper-sprayed and arrested.

Biden was in office when Hamas militants attacked Israel in October 2023, prompting the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to launch a full-scale assault on Gaza. Biden vetoed multiple UN Security Council resolutions calling for a ceasefire, expedited the sale of military equipment to the IDF, and transferred just under $18 billion in military aid to Israel, on top of the $3.8 billion sent annually since 2016.

Biden’s “role in the genocide of the Palestinian people is well-documented,” Trinity College Dublin Students’ Union said in a statement after Tuesday’s protest. The union also called on Trinity to revoke the honorary doctorate awarded to Biden in 2016.

Read more

What we’re watching

Heading into the weekend, we’re preparing for further unrest across Europe, with protests planned in France, Germany, Italy and the Czech Republic, and strikes next week in France and Spain – all over the rising cost of living across a rapidly militarizing continent.

We’ll also be keeping an eye on the so-called Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U) drills in Poland, which have been running since Monday and conclude next Friday. Held by 11 nations, including France, the UK, and Poland, in preparation for a potential deployment to post-conflict Ukraine, the drills look like an exercise in wishful thinking – Putin has already warned that the presence of foreign troops on Ukrainian soil would be “a recipe for an endless war.” Moreover, they could imperil the EU’s newfound plans to take part in talks with the US, Russia, and Ukraine.

Putin will travel to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on Tuesday, where an historic trilateral meeting between him, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to take place. Ukraine will be high on the agenda when the three heavyweights meet, and we’ll be bringing you live updates and analysis as it happens.

For more on these stories, and on everything else, stick with RT.

title: US grounds departing flights nationwide
content:
A communications outage has disrupted air traffic control centers across the country

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights across the US, citing unspecified safety concerns.

The emergency directive took effect at 3:54 PM Eastern Time on Friday, with all departing aircraft instructed to remain on the ground until further notice.

According to the advisory, international flights arriving in the US were handled on a case-by-case basis. The ground stop was lifted around four and a half hours later, although flight disruptions continued.

Around 1,900 flights were canceled and 10,500 delayed as of 6:00 PM Eastern Time on Friday, ABC13 reported, citing flight-tracking service FlightAware.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the nationwide ground stop was prompted by a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them,” he wrote on X.

Preliminary reports suggest the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack, CNN reported, citing two law enforcement officials.

Read more

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the grounding was caused by a “telecommunications outage,” which the authorities do not believe was the result of foul play.

Duffy later blamed the shutdown on the “incredibly old” air traffic control system.

“Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data... and started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers,” he said at a news conference.

The National Weather Service also reported nationwide internet and communications problems, warning that some weather information on its websites could be unavailable or outdated. The agency said technicians were working to restore services.

The last nationwide ground stop was ordered in January 2023 following a failure of the system that provides safety notices to pilots. The previous shutdown occurred in the immediate aftermath of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

The outage came just days after the FAA announced the nationwide rollout of SMART, a new AI-powered system designed to optimize flight routes and reduce delays. It was deployed across all 22 regional air traffic control centers, although the authorities have not established whether it played any role in Friday’s disruption.

Similar technical failures have disrupted air travel worldwide this year. In September, a communications outage halted flights at major airports in the northeastern US, while a software malfunction caused widespread flight cancellations across Britain. Greece temporarily closed its airspace in January, and Italy halved its air traffic capacity following a technical failure in October.

title: Starshield speed limits return in Ukraine as senators demand to know who ordered them
content:
Ukraine's military is once again facing speed limits on Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that military units had detected restrictions that cut off drones moving faster than 161 kph (100 mph), along the entire front line and in Russian-occupied territory. He said a military investigation found the limits were not random errors.

On Friday, he said there are still "no clear explanations."

Trump admin offers mixed messages on limits to Ukraine's Starshield access

The cap matters most against Russia's jet-powered drones, the targets Ukraine's interceptor drones are built to chase.

"Without the speed we need, shooting down these Shaheds becomes much harder, and this means more Russian strikes get through and more of our people are killed," Zelenskyy said in a video posted Thursday.

Russia launched 117 drones at Ukraine overnight into Friday, killing at least two people, including a 17-year-old, Ukrainian authorities said. In Kyiv, a strike hit a medical facility of Ukraine's National Academy of Medical Sciences around 3 a.m., injuring one person and forcing staff to evacuate 30 patients. One person was killed in Odesa. In Zaporizhzhia, a single attack hit two apartment blocks and wounded 30 people, including six children, officials said.

Ukrainian officials are asking the U.S. State Department, the Pentagon and SpaceX to explain and fix the restrictions, Zelenskyy said. SpaceX has denied making any change. "This is false," a SpaceX official said Thursday. "There has been no change."

RELATED STORY | Ukraine disputes Elon Musk's claim that its military violated Starlink's terms of service

In Washington, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina are expressing outrage.

"Congress must determine who ordered or approved these disruptions and hold those responsible accountable," the senators said in a joint statement Thursday. "The Pentagon and SpaceX must preserve all records, turn over the contracts and communications that Congress needs to establish the facts and put safeguards in place so this never happens again."

It remains unclear who is calling the shots: the Pentagon or Elon Musk.

It has happened before. Last month, Musk acknowledged that SpaceX had throttled Starlink service in Ukraine for about a week. He had earlier written on X that limits on Starshield are "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." In late October, the Pentagon's inspector general turned down a bipartisan request from senators to investigate those disruptions.

RELATED STORY | Trump admin offers mixed messages on limits to Ukraine's Starshield access

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and with Zelenskyy in Dublin this week. More talks are planned, and the envoys say European negotiators will join the next round.

The talks have yet to stop the strikes.

title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including a doctor and a child, Health Ministry says
content:
An Israeli airstrike hit one of the main hospitals still operating in the Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, Gaza's Health Ministry said.

The Israeli military said the strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants. The commander it identified was not among the dead.

The strike hit the hospital's surgical wing, the ministry and witnesses said. Footage showed several wards and operating rooms heavily damaged or destroyed, with debris scattered across hospital beds and equipment and rebar dangling from holes in the ceiling. At least 28 people were wounded.

Israels president gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government

Among the dead were Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, a general surgeon, and at least two patients, one of them the 13-year-old, according to the ministry.

Gaza's healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war whose trajectory is not expected to be altered by the outcome of Israel's recent election. The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals across the territory, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters. Israel has also destroyed medical equipment and supplies and killed or detained hundreds of healthcare workers.

In armed conflict, hospitals and their staff are protected under international humanitarian law. A hospital can lose its protected status, however, if it is used for military purposes.

Work is halted in several areas of the hospital after the strike

British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who is volunteering at Nasser Hospital, said that the strike occurred just after midnight and shook the whole building.

"It was extremely smoky," said Rahbour, who was on the fourth floor of the surgical department at the time. The recovery area on the same floor was reduced to rubble, he said.

He said he had been operating alongside Abu Shaira just hours before the strike. "Lovely guy, happy and smiling," Rahbour said.

Ahmed al-Farra, a doctor and the general director of the hospital, said no warning came before the attack, but the Israeli army said it had warned "on several occasions, including recently, that the military activity at the hospital be halted."

Trump reverses course on Israel aid amid Tuesday's midterm election

Al-Farra said surgeries and other services had been suspended because of damage to the building where medical personnel were already struggling to provide care due to supply shortages and "miserable" conditions.

He said other nearby medical facilities were not equipped to do the type of "specialized surgeries" that Nasser Hospital had been providing, leaving patients in need of them to "face an unknown fate."

He said an attack on a hospital should be met with a forceful response from the international community. "Imagine if this event happened in another country in the world. Would the world fall silent about it? No, by God, no."

"No one's safe here," he added, switching from Arabic to English.

Israel has targeted Nasser before

A report from the United Nations, World Bank and European Union said in April that more than 1,800 medical facilities in Gaza have been partially or completely destroyed since the conflict began.

Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed 22 people when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex. Among the dead were five journalists, including Mariam Dagga, who worked for The Associated Press.

Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. In a statement on Thursday, the Israeli military said Hamas had "established a presence within the hospital complex" and that the commander had turned it "into a headquarters."

The World Health Organization said Gaza's health facilities should never be militarized or attacked. "Health needs remain immense in Gaza and will only grow as winter sets in," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.

The Trump administration-backed Board of Peace said similar attacks are inevitable unless both Israel and Hamas honor commitments made under a stalled ceasefire plan the board has struggled to move forward.

The war in Gaza started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records, and its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

The Israeli military said the strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants. The commander it identified was not among the dead.

The strike hit the hospital's surgical wing, the ministry and witnesses said. Footage showed several wards and operating rooms heavily damaged or destroyed, with debris scattered across hospital beds and equipment and rebar dangling from holes in the ceiling. At least 28 people were wounded.

Israels president gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government

Among the dead were Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, a general surgeon, and at least two patients, one of them the 13-year-old, according to the ministry.

Gaza's healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war whose trajectory is not expected to be altered by the outcome of Israel's recent election. The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals across the territory, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters. Israel has also destroyed medical equipment and supplies and killed or detained hundreds of healthcare workers.

In armed conflict, hospitals and their staff are protected under international humanitarian law. A hospital can lose its protected status, however, if it is used for military purposes.

Work is halted in several areas of the hospital after the strike

British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who is volunteering at Nasser Hospital, said that the strike occurred just after midnight and shook the whole building.

"It was extremely smoky," said Rahbour, who was on the fourth floor of the surgical department at the time. The recovery area on the same floor was reduced to rubble, he said.

He said he had been operating alongside Abu Shaira just hours before the strike. "Lovely guy, happy and smiling," Rahbour said.

Ahmed al-Farra, a doctor and the general director of the hospital, said no warning came before the attack, but the Israeli army said it had warned "on several occasions, including recently, that the military activity at the hospital be halted."

Trump reverses course on Israel aid amid Tuesday's midterm election

Al-Farra said surgeries and other services had been suspended because of damage to the building where medical personnel were already struggling to provide care due to supply shortages and "miserable" conditions.

He said other nearby medical facilities were not equipped to do the type of "specialized surgeries" that Nasser Hospital had been providing, leaving patients in need of them to "face an unknown fate."

He said an attack on a hospital should be met with a forceful response from the international community. "Imagine if this event happened in another country in the world. Would the world fall silent about it? No, by God, no."

"No one's safe here," he added, switching from Arabic to English.

Israel has targeted Nasser before

A report from the United Nations, World Bank and European Union said in April that more than 1,800 medical facilities in Gaza have been partially or completely destroyed since the conflict began.

Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed 22 people when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex. Among the dead were five journalists, including Mariam Dagga, who worked for The Associated Press.

Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. In a statement on Thursday, the Israeli military said Hamas had "established a presence within the hospital complex" and that the commander had turned it "into a headquarters."

The World Health Organization said Gaza's health facilities should never be militarized or attacked. "Health needs remain immense in Gaza and will only grow as winter sets in," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.

The Trump administration-backed Board of Peace said similar attacks are inevitable unless both Israel and Hamas honor commitments made under a stalled ceasefire plan the board has struggled to move forward.

The war in Gaza started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records, and its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

title: Who wanted Nvidia’s Huang out? ‘Honeypot’ scandal raises questions over AI power struggle
content:
Jensen Huang’s exit removes a powerful opponent of US chip restrictions, exposing divisions in Washington over how to preserve America’s technological dominance

The downfall of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang in a scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy has raised a politically explosive question: who benefits from the removal of one of Washington’s most influential critics of chip restrictions on China?

Huang resigned on Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, former head of Nvidia customer, Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Anonymous US intelligence officials reportedly suspect that she was recruited by Beijing to potentially influence the Nvidia CEO to push Washington to ease AI chip export restrictions.

Read more

The scandal came at a pivotal moment in the US-China technology war, just days before a planned summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. With congressional hawks already pushing for tougher restrictions, the timing of Huang’s downfall has fueled questions about the political interests served by his resignation.

RT examines the intrigue surrounding Huang’s exit and the struggle for control of the global AI industry.

So who benefits from Huang’s departure?

Huang’s resignation removes one of Washington’s most prominent advocates of keeping China connected to American AI technology, potentially handing China hawks a major political advantage. The Nvidia founder repeatedly warned that cutting Beijing off from American technology would accelerate China’s push for independence. In a May interview with Fox Business, he pointed to Huawei’s growing influence: “They’re flourishing in our absence.”

His exit has immediately intensified congressional demands for tighter export controls and investigations into Nvidia’s China dealings.

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

Republican Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, has seized on the scandal to question whether whether Chinese intelligence had obtained sensitive information through Huang or influenced US technology policy.

“[Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls,” Moolenaar said. “This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast has also pushed for stronger safeguards, including measures to prevent chip smuggling and restrict access to advanced semiconductor equipment.

Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk.

The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a…

— Chuck Schumer (@SenSchumer) November 12, 2026

Trump defended Huang as a “very honorable guy” and said he believed the executive’s denial that he knew Alice Huang was allegedly involved in espionage. However, the controversy appears to have given advocates of tougher restrictions on China fresh ammunition against one of their most influential opponents.

Who benefits more – China hawks or AI rivals?

Huang’s abrupt exit has also raised questions over whether rival American technology firms could benefit from his downfall.

Independent journalist Lee Fang suggested rival US AI companies could gain, pointing to Huang’s support for cheaper Chinese open-source models that threaten established American competitors. He drew parallels with earlier campaigns targeting Huawei and TikTok.

What are the odds American AI firms are playing some role in the Huang ouster? In the same way Cisco paid PR firms to spread fears about Huawei and Meta paid PR firms to stir demands for banning competitor TikTok? Huang singularly pushed cheaper Chinese open source models.

— Lee Fang (@lhfang) November 12, 2026

Venice AI founder Erik Voorhees went further, calling Huang’s removal a “coup.”

Journalist Glenn Greenwald questioned whether extramarital affairs alone explained the removal of one of America’s most powerful technology executives.

“I don’t know who wanted Jensen Huang out but I know that whoever it was wields extreme levels of power,” he wrote on X.

The resignation also provoked a backlash across Silicon Valley. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao called it “a mistake,” Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney described it as “a sad day,” and Elon Musk said hiring Huang would be “an honor.”

A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction. https://t.co/AkS5XT9HF8

— Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) November 12, 2026

“Dark, dark day. Horrible decision for the US and the western world,” wrote Andreessen Horowitz partner Martin Casado.

The media has some questions to answer

Questions have emerged over how the story reached the press. New York Times reporter Tripp Mickle, who helped break the story of Huang’s affair, revealed on The Daily podcast that he and colleague Ana Swanson began investigating Megaspeed after receiving a tip from an unnamed technology industry contact.

The disclosure reinforces suspicions that journalists may have been deliberately steered toward Megaspeed, raising questions about who supplied the tip – and why.

What did Washington know – and when?

The intrigue deepened following reports that senior US officials knew about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang months before the scandal erupted.

Read more

According to Axios, a highly classified intelligence memorandum overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated before Trump’s May visit to China. Based on surveillance of Alice Huang and an investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, the warning reportedly reached Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Rubio also reportedly briefed Trump.

Megaspeed operates AI computing infrastructure, allowing customers to rent access to powerful Nvidia processors outside China – a potential route around restrictions on shipping advanced chips directly to the country.

Washington was also approving direct sales to Chinese buyers. In May Reuters reported that around ten Chinese companies had been cleared to purchase Nvidia’s H200 processors, although deliveries had not begun. The approvals were separate from the Megaspeed investigation, and their precise timing relative to the intelligence warning remains unclear.

The dispute reportedly reached the highest levels of the Trump administration. Axios reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over his failure to blacklist Megaspeed despite repeated warnings. The Commerce Department denied the confrontation ever happened and Lutnick now faces congressional scrutiny over his department’s handling of chip exports and suspected diversion to China.

Read more

If Washington had been warned months earlier, why did the allegations become a public crisis only now?

How did Singapore become entangled in the scandal

Singaporean authorities had been investigating Alice Huang’s former company, Megaspeed International, long before her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence became central to the scandal surrounding Nvidia’s founder.

In a statement Thursday, Singapore’s Home Affairs Ministry said police began investigating Megaspeed in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving servers shipped through Singapore to Malaysia.

Alice Huang was questioned and had her passport seized in June 2025. By February 2026, however, investigators found insufficient evidence that she had committed the suspected offenses. She received a warning for knowingly providing inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed and was barred from re-entering Singapore.

Notably, Singapore stressed that she had never been investigated for espionage.

Meanwhile, the alleged Chinese spy narrative has come under growing scrutiny in Washington itself.

Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.

Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy?

- AG says no. (“no conclusions reached”).
- CIA says no. (“not yet convinced”).
- DNI says no (“not entirely accurate and over-torqued”).
- Ranking… https://t.co/9Pt1W2zjVX

— David Sacks (@DavidSacks) November 13, 2026

According to CNN, US intelligence officials remain divided over whether the evidence establishes that Alice Huang worked for Beijing. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that the Justice Department had reached “no conclusions” about her alleged intelligence ties.

The assessments leave a fundamental question unanswered: how did an unproven espionage allegation gain such traction despite the lack of conclusive evidence?

Read more

Why is Nvidia central to US technological dominance?

Founded by Huang in 1993, Nvidia has become the leading supplier of advanced processors powering the global AI boom.

Its chips and software underpin data centers and AI systems worldwide, making the company a strategic asset in Washington’s competition with Beijing.

By controlling exports of advanced processors and semiconductor technology, the US can influence which countries gain access to the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge AI.

Washington argues the restrictions are necessary to prevent China from strengthening its military and intelligence capabilities. Critics see a broader strategy of technological containment aimed at preserving American economic and geopolitical dominance.

That is what made Huang’s position so consequential: he challenged a central instrument of Washington’s effort to maintain its lead over China.

Could US chip restrictions hand China the advantage?

Washington’s campaign to contain China’s technological rise risks achieving the opposite: accelerating Beijing’s drive to build an AI industry beyond American control.

Read more

Chinese firms, including Huawei, are developing domestic alternatives to US processors, while Beijing is pushing for technological self-reliance.

In an August regulatory filing, Nvidia warned that US export controls, combined with Chinese restrictions, had effectively excluded it from China’s data-center computing market.

The company argued that its exclusion was allowing competitors to expand their developer and customer networks, potentially challenging American technology worldwide.

That was the central contradiction Huang repeatedly highlighted: cutting China off from Nvidia could weaken American influence while strengthening Chinese competitors.

Washington’s national security hawks argue the opposite – that selling powerful processors to Beijing risks advancing its military and technological capabilities.

Huang’s departure removes a prominent voice from that debate, but not the dilemma: could Washington’s efforts to preserve its technological supremacy ultimately help China escape American dominance?

Read more

Who will take control of Nvidia now?

Huang’s resignation has triggered a leadership crisis at Nvidia. According to Wired, an internal post urging the board to consider employee sentiment attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supporting Huang’s return.

Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent successor.

According to Reuters, Kress and Nvidia veteran Ian Buck, a key figure behind its CUDA computing platform, are among the possibilities. Other names floated include Arm CEO Rene Haas and AMD chief Lisa Su. On Polymarket, Buck has also emerged among the leading contenders, alongside Jensen Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, who serves at Nvidia as senior marketing director, and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, although betting odds offer no indication of the board’s intentions.

BREAKING: Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang, emerges as the leading candidate to become Nvidia's next CEO.

See all candidates: https://t.co/Ijsq636OPo pic.twitter.com/597e31lFlw

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) November 11, 2026

Trump has also weighed in, endorsing former Apple CEO Tim Cook, now executive chairman, declaring on Truth Social that “a Legend replaces a Legend.”

President Trump proposes Tim Cook to run Nvidia and says Apple would never be what it is today if Steve Jobs were still around

“Well, you know the expression, anybody can be replaced. So it’s very hard to replace him, but I had an idea this morning that I sort of just released.… https://t.co/uxJNkLoMW2 pic.twitter.com/ylwksgXenR

— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) November 13, 2026

The succession debate has extended to Israel, where media have floated Nvidia technology chief Michael Kagan, Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, and Apple‘s Srouji. All three have strong ties to the Israeli technology sector.

Whoever succeeds Huang will inherit a company caught in the escalating US-China technology confrontation, with the stakes extending far beyond the boardroom. Huang’s replacement will have to choose whether to continue advocating for keeping China within the American technology ecosystem or bring Nvidia closer to Washington’s advocates of tougher restrictions.

The broader question, meanwhile, is not simply who replaces Huang, but whether his departure will also mark a fundamental shift in America’s AI strategy.

title: Deadly floods swamp tens of thousands in Gaza (VIDEOS)
content:
The enclave’s sewage infrastructure lies in ruins after Israeli attacks, and the UN accuses the country of obstructing vital aid

At least four people have been killed after heavy rain flooded camps sheltering tens of thousands in Gaza, according to UN agencies. Much of the enclave, including its sewage system, has been reduced to rubble by Israeli bombardment.

Heavy rain and strong winds, which are unusually intense for early November, battered the coastal territory for several days, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said. Floodwaters swept through makeshift camps and tents, soaking mattresses, washing away belongings, and collapsing shelters.

At Al Berka Reservoir, west of Deir al-Balah, a rain-soaked sandy embankment collapsed onto tents, reportedly killing five people, including three children and two women, with an infant feared drowned, according to local rescuers cited by OCHA. UNICEF, however, reported four deaths in the collapse.

At least 5 people are dead and thousands more without shelter after heavy rains hit Gaza. While Israeli authorities are not responsible for the rain, they are responsible for the displacement of 1.9 million Palestinians and obstructing entry of humanitarian aid. https://t.co/sVTTpc5g7n

— Human Rights Watch (@hrw) November 12, 2026

According to Gaza’s Government Media Office, around 70,000 tents were flooded within 12 hours. The UN separately recorded more than 6,000 family shelters destroyed and 17,400 damaged. UNICEF reported that around 950,000 displaced Palestinians live in flood-exposed areas, including 400,000 at extremely high risk.

The scale of the devastation is exacerbated by the aftermath of more than three years of Israeli bombardment, which destroyed or damaged 82% of structures, forcing vast numbers of Palestinians into flimsy tents, according to the UN.

Israeli attacks also ruined drainage and sanitation infrastructure, which was neglected before the conflict. According to UNICEF, not a single wastewater treatment plant in Gaza is operational, and just two out of six pumps at the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin still function, raising the risk of sewage-contaminated floodwater overflowing into nearby neighborhoods.

The agency also stressed that it sought Israeli approval to bring in repair equipment for more than a year.

💔 HEARTBREAKING Scenes From GAZA Heavy rainfall floods displacement camps, soaking the few belongings Palestinian families have left. They are exposed to freezing wet conditions. Israeli restrictions on aid must be condemned. The world cannot look away https://t.co/xjs3bh1ztr

— Dr Ahmad Rehan Khan (@AhmadRehanKhan) November 13, 2026

The UN humanitarian team suggested that Israel is responsible for the fallout, saying the damage was mainly caused “not by the storm alone, but by policy decisions.” It accused Israel of obstructing essential supplies and access to safer ground, noting that more than 150,000 tents were waiting outside Gaza for delivery.

Even the US-backed Board of Peace, established under President Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan, criticized Israel’s handling of the crisis, warning that delays in approving shelter, sanitation, and drainage equipment “exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge.”

An extremist Israeli settler says the deadly floods in Gaza are a "baptism" to prepare the land for Jewish settlement. They are literally cheering for children to drown because it makes the real estate easier to steal. Pure evil https://t.co/cDodLKFBRt

— Ounka (@OunkaOnX) November 13, 2026

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the accusations, claiming that “Hamas alone is responsible for the suffering of the people of Gaza,” while urging the militant group to disarm. He also stressed that Israel facilitated the entry of more than 91,000 tents and thousands of truckloads of winter supplies.

READ MORE: Israel bars French presidential hopeful over Gaza flotilla pledge

Some Israelis publicly celebrated the flooding. According to Middle East Eye, Israeli weather forecaster Tzachi Peleg expressed “happiness” over images of submerged tents and said he wouldn’t mind if people do not survive. Social media user Elad Huminer also mocked the disaster, writing that Palestinians who wanted the ‘Al-Aqsa Flood’ received the “Gaza Flood,” referring to Hamas’ name for its October 2023 attack.
