title: I Sustain My Accusation
content:
This is the final article in a four-part series.

By Saber Azam
GENEVA, Nov 12 2026 (IPS)

This is the final article in a four-part series with related titles, highlighting the responsibility of mainstream media and religious leaders for the world’s current appalling state and the calamities that may await future generations if proper measures are not taken in time. When megalomania is given a “human face,” historical facts are distorted, acts of aggression are whitewashed, unlawful wars are portrayed as vehicles of “democracy, human rights, and morality,” other people’s intelligence is undermined and mocked, bias overshadows international norms, and religion becomes an instrument of bigotry, I sustain my accusation:

Saber Azam

I Accuse the Mainstream Media

The media is often described as a primary mechanism for informing the public about crucial social, political, and economic issues that can directly or indirectly affect society. Across mass, community, and small- and medium-sized outlets, it also educates and connects people, shapes public opinion, and gives whistleblowers a platform. Impartiality, truthfulness, and investigative rigor are among the principal pillars of its credibility. The most important red lines no media outlet should cross include the propagation of hatred in any form, racism, lies and defamation, deliberately false information, and violations of privacy and personal data. Core principles also include freedom of expression, pluralism, and fact-based reporting.

To date, no single body of international legislation governs the media. Countries and regions apply their own laws and regulations. Since World War II, many powerful countries have funded mainstream media outlets that primarily serve as tools for domestic and foreign-policy propaganda and narrative control. Some wealthy individuals and institutions have done the same to advance their own interests.

In some wealthy and powerful countries, domestic injustices and violations of human dignity are often overlooked, while political assassinations, bloody regime changes, covert subversive operations, denial of facts, and other harmful policies and practices carried out abroad against less powerful countries have been presented to the public as necessary responses to alleged “violations” of certain principles or rights.

In many cases, blatant falsehoods have been transformed into absolute truths, and unlawful acts of aggression have been whitewashed. Without diminishing the good work they have accomplished, these media networks bear responsibility for “justifying” many unjustifiable acts, resulting in countless deaths, material destruction, and shattered lives. The tragedy is that this continues: even when hundreds of journalists are brutally murdered, many mainstream media outlets still fail to denounce these misdeeds.

However, with the rise of the internet, mobile phones, social media, independent podcasters, alternative news networks, and other tools, timely information can now reach vast audiences instantly, while independent audio and video creators and hosts dig deeper to uncover facts. Anyone can capture a photo or video of an event and share it immediately on social media. Younger generations across continents seek facts about the past and present to build a better future. They consult historical archives and draw on multiple sources to form informed opinions on issues that matter to them. Of course, they are not immune to misinformation or malicious manipulation. Yet many people can find accurate information from well-informed alternative sources, even if those outlets lack the political backing and financial power of mainstream media organizations, which bear an even greater responsibility to speak the truth, especially when it matters most.

I Accuse the Religious Leaders

Religion may be understood as a divine philosophy through which God establishes principles intended to ensure harmonious, respectful, equitable, and peaceful living. It can also define the relationship between the Creator and the created, among human beings, and between humans and their environment. Some religions also outline political, economic, and scientific frameworks or rules. Scholars have long sought to explain the foundations of religious belief and have advanced testimonial, philosophical, and extraordinary arguments. Faith, however, is rooted in a profound qualitative appreciation of life and its meaning. Human values and dignity form important common ground among monotheistic, polytheistic, pantheistic, and atheistic convictions. Therefore, those who carry the banner of any belief bear a great responsibility to denounce violations of the principles they profess.

Over time, politics intruded into the sphere of faith and influenced decision-makers, business leaders, and society at large. Rulers often defined their own versions of particular beliefs. Divisions followed, and people of the same religion began killing one another in the name of God. Later, interfaith conflicts arose, leading to devastation and massacres.

One of the most despicable developments in recent human history was the initiation, expansion, and full implementation of the Doctrine of Discovery, through which faith became a justification for bigotry, discrimination, oppression, and expansionism, contributing to centuries of slave trading, gratuitous exploitation, and the devastation of the colonial era. Shamefully, some so-called scholars have characterized the decrees issued in this regard as “international law,” enabling the promulgation of appalling “codes,” political statements, and acts of violence. In the process, hundreds of millions of people were massacred, their treasures looted, and their capacity for self-defense crushed. In some parts of the world, native peoples were nearly erased. Serious crimes continue to be committed in the name of religion; yet, for various reasons, few leaders have come forward to say, “Not in our name!”

The intertwining of religion with politics and business has pulled faith away from its moral and social foundations and placed it in the service of those in power. In some cases, religious principles are invoked to sow division and violence among peoples.

Many faith leaders who persuade people to accept their teachings fail to demonstrate the moral courage and vision needed to take concrete action against injustices committed in the name of their beliefs and to oppose present-day misdeeds. They bear a heavy responsibility for the loss of innocent lives and for the world’s deteriorating condition.

Final Words

It is painful to witness dictatorships commit transgressions, but it is even more devastating to see “democratic societies” commit or condone similar acts. We may be approaching a major and extremely violent global calamity. Will the leaders mentioned in my four-part series of related articles realize they have strayed, take the needed corrective actions, or step aside and let younger, talented, and responsible generations take over and lead our world toward a more secure, promising, and prosperous future? If not, will the world’s youth launch a billion-signature vote-of-no-confidence petition to help save the planet and humanity?

Saber Azam is a former UN official. He is the author of Soraya: The Other Princess and Hell’s Mouth: A Journey to the Heart of West African Jungles. His third book, Nowhere to Go, will be published soon.

title: Protecting the Climate Means Protecting Territorial Rights
content:
'The proposed Yavarí-Tapiche Corridor is home to Indigenous communities, including Indigenous Peoples living in voluntary isolation and initial contact, and 1.7 million hectares of intact tropical forest. The cross-border corridor is threatened by oil and gas, logging, and mining, as well as illegal activity.’ Credit: Earth Insight

By Juan Carlos Jintiach and M. Florencia Librizzi
ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov 12 2026 (IPS)

The world cannot claim to protect the climate and nature while opening Indigenous Peoples’ and local communities’ territories to industrial activities that threaten their rights, livelihoods and ways of life. Yet governments increasingly recognize these communities’ contributions to climate and biodiversity protection while authorizing mining, oil drilling, industrial agriculture and infrastructure projects that can undermine the very territories they safeguard.

Last year, at COP30 in Belém, governments took an important step toward addressing the historical injustice of insecure land tenure. Through the Intergovernmental Land Tenure Commitment (ILTC),17 countries and one subnational government have now committed to advancing territorial rights across 160 million hectares by 2030: recognizing tenure across at least 80 million hectares and strengthening governance and protection across another 80 million hectares where rights are already recognized. A complementary $1.8 billion Forest and Land Tenure Pledge for 2026–2030 offers resources to support this work.

One year later, as governments gather for COP31 in Antalya, the challenge is to turn this landmark commitment into lasting territorial security.

For Indigenous Peoples, local communities and Afro-descendant Peoples, territories are inseparable from identity, culture, livelihoods, knowledge and, for many, spirituality and self-determination. Securing these rights, alongside recognizing and upholding the rights of nature, is fundamental to protecting both communities and the territories they have stewarded for generations.

Our new research shows that forests within established and proposed reserves for Indigenous Peoples in Isolation and Initial Contact (PIACI) in the Peruvian Amazon experienced 16 times less forest loss than forests outside these areas. Across the tropics, communities are recovering ancestral lands, exercising customary governance, monitoring threats, and restoring ecosystems. Their stewardship sustains biodiversity, carbon storage and water cycles essential to climate resilience.

Yet industrial pressures threaten these achievements. Our research has found that oil and gas blocks overlap approximately 31 million hectares of Indigenous and community territories in the Amazon Basin, while mining concessions overlap 18.7 million hectares in Mesoamerica. In the Congo Region, oil and gas blocks overlap 38% of mapped community forests and mining concessions 42%. In Indonesia, wood concessions overlap approximately 6 million hectares of Indigenous territories. These overlaps highlight potential conflicts between industrial development and territorial rights.

The proposed Yavarí-Tapiche Territorial Corridor illustrates what is at stake. This Indigenous-led initiative spans approximately 16 million hectares across Peru and Brazil, including territories of Indigenous Peoples in isolation and initial contact. Yet oil and gas blocks overlap approximately 10% of the proposed corridor, alongside logging and infrastructure pressures. Industrial development can affect entire watersheds, ecosystems and livelihoods through roads, pollution and habitat fragmentation.

From Recognition to Territorial Security

Legal recognition is a fundamental achievement and the foundation of territorial security. But rights recognized on paper must also be respected in practice. When energy, mining, infrastructure and investment decisions disregard rights-holders’ authority, the benefits of recognition can be undermined. The ILTC gives signatories an opportunity to align tenure recognition and governance with land-use planning, licensing, and investment decisions, while respecting the rights and priorities of affected peoples and communities.

Five Priorities for Action

First, accelerate recognition of Indigenous Peoples’, local communities’ and Afro-descendant Peoples’ territorial rights, including customary tenure. Recognition and restitution must respect rights-holders’ institutions, priorities and applicable human rights standards.

Second, strengthen governance and protection alongside recognition. Newly recognized and existing territories need sustained legal, institutional and financial support so rights-holders can exercise their authority, advance their priorities and protect their lands.

Third, align industrial licensing, infrastructure and investment with territorial rights. Governments must address conflicting concessions, qrespect territorial governance plans and fulfill applicable consultation and free, prior and informed consent obligations, including respecting rights-holders’ decisions to reject unwanted industrial activities.

Fourth, ensure financing reaches rights-holders. Governments and donors must provide direct, flexible and sustained funding for communities’ priorities, including governance, territorial protection, monitoring and sustainable economies.

Finally, measure more than hectares. Progress must reflect whether rights-holders can exercise their authority, industrial threats are addressed and financing reaches communities.

Delivering these priorities requires coordinated government action so that land, energy, mining, infrastructure and investment decisions reinforce territorial rights. Building on the leadership of Indigenous Peoples, local communities and Afro-descendant Peoples, the ILTC can help align policies and financing with their priorities. By 2030, success should be measured not only by hectares recognized, but by whether rights-holders can exercise their rights, govern their territories and determine their own futures free from extractive and large-scale industrial activities.

The commitment was made in Belém. Antalya is an opportunity to turn it into lasting territorial security.

Juan Carlos Jintiach is Executive Secretary, Global Alliance of Territorial Communities and M. Florencia Librizzi is Deputy Director, Earth Insight

title: Mass bomb hoax sparks school evacuations across Europe
content:
Thousands of schools in the UK, Italy, and Ireland were targeted by threatening emails, with investigators tracing some messages to a hacked Taiwanese university account

A wave of bomb threats targeted schools across the UK, Italy, and Ireland on Wednesday, prompting evacuations and widespread disruption.

More than 300 schools in Northern Ireland and at least 470 in Scotland received threatening emails, police said. The authorities said the messages were hoaxes.

According to the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), the emails originated outside the UK. “Our enquiries are ongoing, however, at this stage we consider risk to the public as low,” PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Anthony McNally said.

More than 6,300 schools in Italy received bomb threats, with evacuations and lockdowns reported in several areas, including the northern Emilia-Romagna region.

According to ANSA, the email was sent from a compromised account at Dayeh University, a private institution in Taiwan. It was signed “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan,” and also contained a threat against Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Read more

“We won’t let an anonymous email decide our children’s school calendar,” Meloni said in a video posted on social media.

Reuters reported that some European officials suspect Russia may be behind the bomb threats, citing the Ukraine conflict. Moscow has dismissed these types of allegations as part of a smear campaign.

Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov rejected allegations that Russia was involved in a cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems at French supermarkets, saying: “baseless accusations against our country, blaming it for virtually everything, are unfortunately becoming a persistent trend in European countries. I reiterate that this accusation is absolutely absurd.”

France later blamed Iran for the cyberattack, which Tehran denied. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the French government of “shifting blame for its failures onto others.”

title: Eight killed, 17 injured in New York building collapse (VIDEOS)
content:
Rescue crews continue searching the rubble of a three-story Brooklyn building, with at least two people critically injured and more victims potentially trapped

At least eight people were killed and 17 others injured when a three-story building collapsed into an adjacent construction site in Brooklyn, New York, on Wednesday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Thursday. Three firefighters were among the injured.

Rescue crews continued searching the rubble on Thursday for additional victims who could still be trapped. Six bodies were recovered from the debris and two people died in the hospital, according to ABC7. At least two of the injured remained in critical condition.

Officials said the operation could take several days due to unstable conditions and the risk of a secondary collapse.

The collapse occurred shortly after 4 p.m. on Flatbush Avenue, near the intersection with Bedford Avenue. The three-story building housed a ground-floor store and apartments above. It fell into an adjacent excavation site where a one-story building had previously been demolished.

Workers were excavating the neighboring site when the collapse occurred, officials said. Developers had proposed a nine-story residential and commercial building, but those plans had not yet been approved. City officials said approval had been granted for a three-story building.

The cause of the collapse remains under investigation, and officials have not established whether the excavation contributed to the disaster.

At least two dead, nineteen injured after a building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York. https://t.co/tH4RYOLKCR

— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) November 12, 2026

According to local media reports, witnesses described hearing an explosion-like noise as the building collapsed, sending thick clouds of dust across the street. One nearby resident compared the scene to the September 11 attacks. The husband of a pregnant woman trapped beneath the rubble celebrated after firefighters pulled her out alive.

A husband cried tears of relief after he said his pregnant wife was pulled from Brooklyn collapse rubble and is alive. https://t.co/hU9jlU25A4

— Eyewitness News (@ABC7NY) November 12, 2026

More than 250 firefighters and emergency medical personnel have been working at the scene. “This will be a prolonged operation,” New York City Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said.

title: Humanity faces catastrophic AI threat – OpenAI board member
content:
Increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems could take over and cause mass deaths, Paul Christiano has warned

Artificial intelligence could escape human control within three years, potentially causing mass deaths, OpenAI board member Paul Christiano has warned.

Speaking at the Hinton Lectures in Toronto on Tuesday, Christiano warned that increasingly powerful “superhuman” AI systems could surpass humanity’s ability to understand, predict, or control their behavior.

”If the AI system is doing things we don’t want, it can hide the fact it is doing those things, and it can naturally try and create confusion and avoid attribution,” he said. Humans could also struggle to foresee the consequences of acting on AI-generated advice, he added.

In a separate address on Monday, Christiano warned that AI could seize control from humanity within three years, potentially killing large numbers of people either during a takeover or afterward, if humans lose the ability to maintain a habitable environment.

”I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident,” he said.

Read more

Christiano, who joined OpenAI’s Foundation Board and Safety and Security Committee in September, pointed to an incident in which AI agents reportedly bypassed security restrictions during company tests, gaining unauthorized access to OpenAI’s research infrastructure and Hugging Face, a major AI development platform.

Although OpenAI has introduced a framework addressing cybersecurity threats and the risk of losing control over advanced systems, Christiano warned that existing safeguards remain inadequate.

His warnings came as governments and leading AI developers, including OpenAI, Microsoft and Anthropic, signed a voluntary safety declaration in Paris on Monday. The agreement calls for stronger oversight and emergency shutdown mechanisms but imposes no binding deadlines or penalties and gives governments no additional powers to halt dangerous AI systems.

AI safety organization CeSIA, which also signed the declaration, called for authorities to be empowered to suspend AI development and deployment when risks become unacceptable.

Read more

Separately, Maxime Fournes, head of PauseAI, a campaign seeking to halt advanced AI development until it can be made safe, warned that the technology could cripple banking systems, communications networks and other critical infrastructure through devastating cyberattacks.

Speaking to Anadolu on Monday, Fournes estimated a 50% chance of a major AI-related cyber catastrophe within the next year unless urgent action is taken.

”This is a global catastrophic threat, something that could bring us back to the Middle Ages very quickly if it starts happening,” he warned.

title: Kennedys fight shadow of Trump monument
content:
The planned 250-foot-tall arch would obstruct views and block sunlight to the US political clan’s graves, according to a new lawsuit

Nine members of the Kennedy family have sued to stop US President Donald Trump’s plans to build an enormous triumphal arch near the iconic Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington, arguing that it would cast a shadow over their family graves.

They say the planned 250-foot (76-meter) tall monument would “permanently cast a shadow” over former US President John F. Kennedy’s grave and other family burial sites, according to court documents filed on Tuesday.

“The Arch will also obstruct the clear sightline of the Kennedy Gravesites and the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, in Arlington National Cemetery, from the Arlington Memorial Bridge, destroying an essential element of the Gravesites’ design,” the plaintiffs argue in their complaint.

The relatives include children and grandchildren of JFK’s brothers Robert F. Kennedy and Edward Kennedy. They have also filed a motion to join existing lawsuits against the project.

Just days before the Kennedy filing, federal judge Tanya Chutkan temporarily blocked construction while considering objections to the project’s legality. The Trump administration argues that Congress authorized a monument at the site in 1925, when it approved plans for Arlington Memorial Bridge.

A Monument to the American Spirit. The Military Triumphal Arch will honor the heroes who gave everything for our nation - a monumental tribute to America’s first 250 years & a symbol of the next 250. A legacy of freedom. A future without limits. 📲 https://t.co/vkquwA5qGp https://t.co/ucUPdw3YLL

— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 6, 2026
Read more

Trump has touted the project as “the greatest and most beautiful triumphal arch, anywhere in the world.” The administration has also launched a website showcasing its design for a towering structure made of white stone and gold.

The arch is one of several projects in Washington that Trump has initiated in his second term. He has renovated the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, paved over the White House Rose Garden, and added statues to the presidential residence.

The administration has also demolished the White House East Wing to make way for a $400 million ballroom, another project facing legal opposition. The Supreme Court allowed construction to continue in August, although the case remains unresolved.

title: Spanish housing crisis fury erupts into violence after millions protest (VIDEOS)
content:
Clashes with police have triggered calls for the interior minister to resign

Millions of workers and protesters brought Spain to a standstill on Wednesday with a nationwide general strike over the country’s deepening housing crisis. Demonstrators in major cities denounced the soaring rent costs and demanded stronger tenant protections.

More than 3 million people took to the streets across the country, according to unions cited by Reuters on Thursday. The National Confederation of Tenants’ Unions estimated that up to 5 million workers took part in the strike.

While daytime demonstrations were largely peaceful, a rally in Barcelona, Spain’s second-largest city, was followed by looting and clashes with police.

Clashes also erupted in Madrid, where riot police used tear gas, pepper spray, and foam projectiles to disperse protesters.

At least 115 people were arrested nationwide, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing police figures.

Left-wing parties, including Sumar, Podemos, and ERC, demanded the resignation of Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska on Thursday over alleged excessive police force during Wednesday’s protests. The minister ordered an investigation into the police actions and reportedly banned the use of tear gas at future demonstrations.

The strike disrupted transportation and commerce across Spain. Protesters blocked roads in Madrid, Valencia, and other cities, and pickets forced some businesses to close. Rail operator Renfe reported cancelations of nearly 16% of high-speed and long-distance trains and over 10% of commuter and regional services. At least 332 flights were also canceled, according to airport operator Aena.

On Thursday, the Spanish parliament approved a package of housing reforms that included rent caps, stronger eviction protections, and restrictions on property speculation. However, lawmakers rejected a separate proposal to strengthen tenants’ rights to renew their leases.

🚨🇪🇸Breaking: TODAY 400,000 PEOPLE ARE IN THE STREETS OF #BARCELONA , #Spain WITH ONE UNANIMOUS DEMAND: WE WANT TO LIVE, NOT JUST SURVIVE. https://t.co/dw54MosntR

— World_Breaking_News03 (@Breaking2003) November 11, 2026

This comes less than three weeks before a snap parliamentary election scheduled for November 29. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called the snap election after parliament rejected two housing reform decrees on October 2.

The future of the reforms remains uncertain. The conservative opposition People’s Party vowed to repeal them if it comes to power.

Speaking to RT in Madrid, Spanish political analyst Daniel Lobato accused the government of enriching major property owners and corporate interests while failing to address the housing crisis. He warned that public frustration could drive voters to the far right.

Netanyahu hits back at Trump’s Board of Peace over Gaza aid
content:
The US-led body accused Israel of failing to facilitate emergency aid deliveries as severe flooding devastates shelters across the Palestinian enclave

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has denied responsibility for the worsening humanitarian crisis in Gaza after severe flooding devastated refugee camps.

Torrential rains have battered the Palestinian enclave in recent days, flooding and damaging thousands of tents housing people displaced by the devastating Israel-Hamas war, which erupted in October 2023. Around 65% of Gaza’s population (1.4 million people) live in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

More than 150,000 tents purchased by humanitarian organizations and UN member states are ready to be delivered to Gaza, the international body said on Monday, calling for “the urgent lifting of all unnecessary restrictions and delays.”

The Board of Peace, a body created by US President Donald Trump to oversee Gaza’s postwar reconstruction and governance, issued its own statement describing Israel’s response as “insufficient.”

The board urged Israel to “act immediately to authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies.”

Read more

UNICEF, the UN children’s agency, has also accused Israel of blocking a $3 million project to repair Gaza City’s Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin, warning that sewage-contaminated floodwaters could inundate residential areas and endanger displaced families.

Netanyahu’s office blamed Hamas for the delays. “Israel is working in close cooperation with the United States and the Board of Peace,” it stated on Tuesday, reaffirming its commitment to Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza.

“Hamas steals from Gazans to arm itself, systematically diverting humanitarian aid to military infrastructure while the United Nations and UNRWA turn a blind eye,” the statement read, referring to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.

“To date, Hamas has not surrendered a single weapon, and it continues to hold the people of Gaza hostage to its terrorist rule,” Netanyahu’s office said.

While the Board of Peace also accused Hamas of failing to fulfill its commitments, it maintained that Israeli restrictions on humanitarian deliveries “significantly delayed” the decommissioning of weapons and the transfer of power in Gaza from Hamas to a technocratic Palestinian administration.

Read more

Israel launched its military operation in Gaza following a Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023, which killed around 1,200 people in Israel and resulted in 251 others being taken hostage. More than 75,000 Palestinians have since been killed in the occupied Palestinian territories, including at least 21,500 children, according to a UN Commission of Inquiry.

In a report released last month, the commission concluded that Israel continued committing “genocidal acts” in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire, with Israeli attacks killing another 1,431 Palestinians by September 30, 2026. It also accused Israel of crimes against humanity in the West Bank.

Israel has rejected allegations of genocide, maintaining that its military operations target Hamas.

title: Dead candidate leads California election race
content:
Bruce Giudici has taken a double-digit lead despite dying two months before the vote

A candidate who died two months before Election Day has taken a commanding lead in a local California race, according to unofficial results released by county election officials on Tuesday.

Bruce Giudici is leading former supervisor Clyde Clapp by 57% to 43% in the race for the Calaveras County Board of Supervisors, despite having died in August following a fall while campaigning.

Giudici reportedly suffered serious injuries after falling while visiting voters and later died in hospital. His campaign chose to keep his name on the ballot, leaving voters to decide whether to elect a candidate who could never take office.

Under California election law, votes cast for candidates who die less than 68 days before an election must still be counted. If Giudici wins, he will be declared elected, but the seat will become vacant when the new term begins, allowing Governor Gavin Newsom to appoint a replacement.

Giudici would join a string of US politicians who have won elections from beyond the grave.

READ MORE: After the midterm bloodbath, what is Trump ready to concede?

In 2024, Democratic Congressman Donald Payne Jr. won an uncontested primary in New Jersey more than a month after his death. That same year, Republican Jennifer Pace won a congressional primary in Indiana after reportedly dying of a heart attack in March.

Read more

Two years earlier, Pennsylvania Democratic lawmaker Tony DeLuca secured nearly 86% of the vote in his reelection bid despite dying a month before Election Day. State law prevented a replacement candidate from being added to the ballot after printing had begun.

One of the more bizarre cases came in 2018, when Republican candidate and brothel owner Dennis Hof won a Nevada state assembly election three weeks after his death.

Hof, 72, was found dead at his Love Ranch brothel by porn actor Ron Jeremy the previous month. Despite his death, he defeated Democrat Lesia Romanov, leaving officials to fill the vacant seat.

Zelensky mocks Trump in Danish parliament speech (VIDEO)
content:
The US president could benefit from becoming “more Danish,” according to the former comedian

Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has mocked US President Donald Trump’s ambitions to acquire Greenland, suggesting that Trump would benefit from becoming “more Danish.”

Zelensky made the comments in an address to the Danish parliament on Wednesday, attended by a key backer, Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

Describing Denmark as a country “we can always count on,” Zelensky took a swipe at Trump’s longstanding interest in acquiring Greenland, an autonomous Danish territory.

“When someone in the United States wanted to have Greenland, they were not even aware that what they really wanted was not the land but to become a little bit more Danish,” Zelensky said, without mentioning Trump by name.

“And who knows, maybe that was exactly what they needed,” he added.

Zelensky: Maybe when someone in America wanted Greenland, he didn't even realize that what he really wanted was not the land, but to become a little more Danish. And who knows, maybe that was exactly what he needed. https://t.co/1BdCLQaL24

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 11, 2026

Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of acquiring Greenland since returning to the White House last year, even threatening to annex the territory by force if necessary. He argued that the island is vital to national security and that its vast rare-earth mineral deposits could give the US access to strategically important resources.

Read more

His remarks strained relations within NATO, provoked outrage in Copenhagen, and prompted European NATO members to rally behind Denmark. The dispute was eventually settled under an agreement announced by the US, Denmark, and Greenland in September. Trump claimed at the time that the deal would give the US “permanent control” over the territory’s security.

Denmark has taken a hawkish stance on Russia and has emerged as a major supplier of military aid to Kiev since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. It joined Western coalitions that provided US-made F-16 fighter jets and German-made Leopard 1 tanks. Copenhagen also donated its entire fleet of 19 Caesar self-propelled howitzers to Ukraine.

Frederiksen was among those who supported Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russia and urged other Western nations to provide Ukraine with missiles suitable for the task. She also criticized Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store for their phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, adding that she was “very skeptical about this Norwegian-Finnish initiative” and accusing the two leaders of breaking ranks with the rest of the EU.

Read more

Copenhagen has also backed plans to produce rocket fuel on its territory for Fire Point, a Ukrainian arms manufacturer personally promoted by Zelensky. The company was allowed to bypass more than 20 environmental and planning regulations under a law reserved for significant military projects. Last month, the Danish government approved a 750 million kroner ($110 million) state-backed loan guarantee for Fire Point’s Danish subsidiary.

Fire Point has been linked to Timur Mindich, a longtime business associate of Zelensky often described as the Ukrainian leader’s ‘wallet’. Mindich fled Ukraine after being implicated in a major embezzlement scheme at the center of one of the country’s biggest corruption scandals.

Denmark was also embroiled in a separate Ukraine-related controversy last week, when it emerged that Copenhagen paid $10 million in taxpayer money to a questionable company contracted to supply artillery ammunition to Kiev. Frederiksen pledged to recover the money.

title: Abu Dhabi talks conclude: How Russian experts assess the outcome
content:
The two-day negotiations paved the way for further diplomacy, but fundamental differences remain, commentators say

Russia, Ukraine, and the US have concluded two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi, reaching an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange. The first formal trilateral talks since February centered on wider European security arrangements, with Moscow reporting common ground on some issues and American negotiators also describing progress while acknowledging that the hardest questions remain unresolved.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday. Western European representatives were sidelined throughout the negotiations, although they reportedly held separate consultations with the American and Ukrainian teams. Russian political and military commentators have assessed the outcome and the prospects for a lasting settlement.

Read more

Diplomacy resumes, differences remain – Anastasia Gafarova, Center for Political Information deputy director

The diplomatic process has been restarted on a different footing, but a peace agreement remains some way off, Anastasia Gafarova, deputy director of the Center for Political Information, told Gazeta.ru.

”The issue of the overall security architecture in Europe has been included in the agenda for the first time – something Russia had consistently been denied before,” she said.

Gafarova suggested that progress might be possible on military arrangements and identified humanitarian matters as an area where cooperation had traditionally been easier.

She also pointed to a possible meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US, and the question of European participation in future negotiations.

Signs of stagnation on key issues – Alexandra Bokova, Strategic Communications Agency managing partner

The relatively brief second day suggests that little progress was made on territorial disputes, political analyst and managing partner of the Strategic Communications Agency Alexandra Bokova told Gazeta.ru.

”Kiev wants to stop the fighting first and only then discuss security, while the Russian side rightly believes that a ceasefire without political agreements will resolve nothing,” she said.

Bokova noted that Tuesday’s four-and-a-half-hour session had raised expectations of progress, but Wednesday’s discussions lasted just 90 minutes despite the most difficult issues being scheduled for the second day.

Read more

She compared the situation to the Istanbul negotiations in 2025, when meetings became progressively shorter – from nearly two hours in May to just over an hour in June and around 40 minutes in July. In her assessment, the parties had reached the limits of their previously stated positions, with the brief discussion of the central issues indicating stagnation.

Lasting deal, not temporary ceasefire – Viktor Baranets, military commentator

Ukraine is proposing a ceasefire along the current line of contact, an approach Moscow rejects, Russian military commentator and retired colonel, Viktor Baranets, told Sputnik.

”We do not need a short-term ceasefire. We need a comprehensive agreement designed to last not a week, not two weeks, not a month, but many, many years,” he said.

Baranets accused Kiev of seeking long-term financial support from the EU to sustain its military campaign.

”They are already asking the European Union for money ten years in advance. This is effectively an admission that Ukraine is ready to fight Russia for another ten years,” he claimed.

The commentator cited a request for €70 billion ($78 billion) for 2027 and Vladimir Zelensky’s stated need to finance an 800,000-strong army. Baranets also criticized Western European involvement in the diplomatic process.

“We did not ask Europe to interfere in these trilateral negotiations, but a whole gang of consultants and advisers nevertheless rushed to Abu Dhabi. They were not allowed at the table. Russia is essentially saying: you have no place not only at the table, but even under it,” he said.

”Nevertheless, these European whisperers are operating around the negotiations, and Ukrainian diplomats regularly run to them for consultations during breaks,” Baranets added.

Read more

Europe seeks to deepen conflict’s root causes – Dmitry Suslov, HSE University analyst

Western European governments are interested in reinforcing rather than removing the underlying causes of the Ukraine conflict, according to Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at HSE University.

In an interview with the Russian business magazine Monocle, he said European governments opposed revisiting existing security arrangements, while Washington was willing to discuss Moscow’s concerns as part of a settlement.

Suslov identified several measures he considered necessary for a durable agreement, including preventing further NATO expansion into former Soviet republics, limiting the deployment of military infrastructure and long-range weapons near Russia, and restoring military dialogue between Moscow and the US-led military bloc. Ukraine would also need a neutral, nonaligned status, with guarantees that did not effectively make it a NATO member.

The analyst acknowledged that Moscow and Kiev remained far apart and that Washington’s position did not fully satisfy Russia. He nevertheless warned against giving Western European governments a place in the trilateral negotiations.

”Bringing the Europeans into a single negotiating format at this stage risks completely blocking and derailing the negotiations,” Suslov said.

No unified European position – Nikolay Topornin, Center for European Information director

Western European countries lack a common negotiating position or a representative capable of speaking for them collectively, according to Nikolay Topornin, director of the Center for European Information.

He told Gazeta.ru that Moscow was already familiar with the EU’s stance through its financial, military, political, and diplomatic support for Kiev.

”Their presence at the negotiating table would lead to nothing positive, because their position is effectively being voiced by the Ukrainian delegation,” Topornin said.

Read more

Western politicians ‘instigators of catastrophe’ – Andrey Klimov, Russian MP

Western European participation in the current negotiating format would be inappropriate, Andrey Klimov, a member of the Russian State Duma’s International Affairs Committee, told Gazeta.ru.

“Western European figures were the instigators of this entire catastrophe from the outset, and they are still attempting to obstruct a normal settlement,” Klimov stated.

The lawmaker recalled that European officials had visited Moscow before 2022 and heard Russian security concerns but failed to act on them.

He said Russia had sought legally binding agreements on security and cooperation since the 1990s, including proposals presented to EU representatives in 2008.

Klimov also drew attention to reports of a possible meeting between the leaders of Russia, the US, and China, noting that the security questions raised in the latest discussions concerned other major powers as well.

“There is hope that these meetings will mark the beginning of further discussions along the same lines, perhaps at an even higher level,” Klimov said.

title: Veterans and Afghan allies march on Capitol Hill, urging Congress to block deportations
content:
Veterans and the Afghan allies who served beside them marched to Capitol Hill on Veterans Day, urging Congress to protect thousands of Afghans in the U.S. from deportation.

AfghanEvac, a nonprofit that advocates for Afghan allies, organized the march. The group brought more than 150 veterans, frontline civilians and Afghan allies to the Hill to push for the Afghanistan TPS Act of 2026.

RELATED STORY | Homeland Security is removing protections that kept some Afghans from deportation

The bill would allow eligible Afghans in the country to receive Temporary Protected Status through July 1, 2029, a program that shields people from deportation and allows them to work legally when conditions in their home countries make their return unsafe. Applicants would have to meet TPS eligibility requirements and undergo biometric, biographic and national security screening. The bill does not provide a path to citizenship.

"We made a promise to Afghans because they kept their word to us. They said that they would help us when we went into their country, pursuing American interests, and they did. They followed through on their end of the deal. And then we broke our promise, Shawn VanDiver, a Navy veteran and founder of AfghanEvac, told Scripps News ahead of the Wednesdays promise walk.

I want to make sure that it wasn't all a lie, VanDiver added. That's why we're all out here marching. That's why we're all out here putting our feet on the street, standing up for our wartime allies just like they stood up for us.

The urgency stems from the Trump administrations May 2025 decision to terminate TPS for Afghanistan. The termination took effect July 14, 2025, exposing more than 8,000 Afghans to deportation. Advocates and lawmakers warn that Afghans who worked with U.S. forces and others could face retaliation or persecution under Taliban rule if returned.

A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from deporting detained Afghans to Afghanistan or Pakistan through Nov. 7. A separate court order subsequently protected five Afghans named in a lawsuit and required the government to provide advance notice before attempting to remove them, but that order did not protect all Afghans facing deportation.

A Department of Homeland Security court filing indicated deportation flights could resume as early as Nov. 16. ICE has not publicly confirmed specific future removal operations.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Afghan allies get 9-month reprieve as Trump administration agrees to keep Qatar refugee camp open

In the House, Democratic Reps. Jason Crow of Colorado and Sam Liccardo of California filed a discharge petition Monday seeking to bypass Republican leaders and force a vote on the Afghanistan TPS Act of 2026. The petition needs 218 signatures to force consideration on the House floor. It drew 21 signatures on its first day, according to published reports.

Crow, an Army veteran who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, said he would not let the country leave these brave Afghans behind. Liccardo said the effort could not wait for a change in control of Congress.

This cannot wait until the Democratic majority takes over, Liccardo said in a statement.

Four Republicans have signed on as co-sponsors of the legislation: Reps. Don Bacon of Nebraska, Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, Joe Wilson of South Carolina and Morgan Luttrell of Texas. More than 50 organizations back the bill, including Veterans of Foreign Wars and Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America.

"Veterans care because we believe in the idea of America, and when we make up the promise in the name of America you've got to follow through. We're nothing without our word, VanDiver said.

title: International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women 2026
content:
By External Source
Nov 11 2026 (IPS)

 
For millions of women around the world, violence is not a distant threat.

It is a reality experienced in homes, communities, workplaces and increasingly, online.

According to the World Health Organization, approximately 840 million women – nearly one in three worldwide – have experienced physical or sexual violence by an intimate partner, or sexual violence by someone else, during their lifetime.

And the problem is not diminishing quickly.

Over the past two decades, the global prevalence of intimate-partner violence has declined by an average of just 0.2 percent annually.

The consequences can be fatal.

According to UN Women and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, nearly 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2024.

That’s approximately 137 lives lost every day.

One every ten minutes.

Violence also begins at an alarming age.

The WHO estimates that 12.5 million adolescent girls between 15 and 19 experienced physical or sexual violence from an intimate partner in a single year.

Meanwhile, digital technology has created new avenues for abuse, including online harassment, stalking, threats and AI-generated sexual imagery.

But despite the scale of the crisis, investment in prevention remains limited.

In 2022, just 0.2 percent of global development aid was allocated to programmes specifically focused on preventing violence against women.

On November 25th, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women marks the beginning of 16 Days of Activism, culminating on Human Rights Day, December 10th.

The United Nations is calling for stronger laws, effective prevention programmes, survivor-centred services and greater accountability.

Because violence against women is neither inevitable nor acceptable.

Ending it requires sustained action – from governments, institutions and communities.

Every woman and girl has the right to live free from violence and fear.

title: Hotter World, Older Population: How Long Can Climate COPs Ignore the Obvious?
content:
Older people at the forefront of climage justice. Climate Justice March, COP30, Belém, Brazil. Credit: Hari Krishna Nibanupudi

By Hari Krishna Nibanupudi
ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov 11 2026 (IPS)

As COP31 gets underway in Antalya, two realities demand attention. The World Meteorological Organisation reports that 2015–2025 were the 11 hottest years on record, with 2025 about 1.43°C above pre-industrial levels.

The World Health Organisation projects that the number of people aged 60 and over will rise from one billion in 2020 to 1.4 billion in 2030 and 2.1 billion in 2050, roughly one in five people.

These trends are connected: together, they define the population that climate policy must serve. Yet representation in climate negotiations has barely changed.

The UN climate process recognises nine NGO constituencies, including women and gender, youth, Indigenous Peoples and farmers, but none for older people. These constituencies coordinate interventions, nominate speakers and facilitate participation in mandated events. An older minister at the negotiating table cannot be assumed to represent older people facing drought, displacement or unaffordable electricity.

Source: WHO, Ageing and health, 2030 and 2050 values are projections.

 

From agreement to whose action

There are reasons to defend the COP process. Dubai’s COP28 operationalised the loss and damage fund and agreed a transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. Baku’s COP29 established a goal of at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, with developed countries taking the lead, alongside efforts to scale finance from all sources to $1.3 trillion a year. Belém’s COP30 called for tripling adaptation finance by 2035, adopted 59 adaptation indicators and agreed a just transition mechanism.

Yet appearing on a list of vulnerable groups is a limited form of inclusion. Recognition must bring authority, resources and accountability across climate institutions, long after a summit closes

These decisions offer a route from dialogue through consensus towards delivery, although targets are not disbursements and promises are not protection.

The COP31 agenda brings finance, adaptation measurement, emissions cuts and a just transition into focus, alongside loss and damage funding. Its action priorities include food security, resilient cities, health systems, clean energy and youth and education. Each has an ageing dimension. The test is whether the institutions delivering these priorities explicitly recognise older people as rights holders and partners, and reflect that recognition in investment.

Recognition has consequences. Women have a Gender Action Plan; Indigenous Peoples have dedicated institutional spaces; children and youth have an established constituency and a youth climate champion in the presidency. These gains were won through sustained advocacy and remain incomplete.

They demonstrate that institutions can change. Recognition exists in fragments: the Sharm el-Sheikh Adaptation Agenda identifies older people among populations requiring heat protection. But being named in a vulnerability list is a limited form of inclusion. Recognition must carry authority, resources and accountability across climate institutions, long after a summit closes. 

Source: Falchetta, G., De Cian, E., Sue Wing, I., & Carr, D. (2024). Global projections of heat exposure of older adults. Nature Communications, 15, 3678.

 

The mortality figures are already an answer

WHO reports that heat-related mortality among people over 65 increased approximately 85% between 2000–2004 and 2017–2021. Europe’s summer of 2022 brought an estimated 61,672 heat-related deaths. The 2025 Lancet Countdown, summarised by WHO, estimates an annual global heat death toll of 546,000 across all ages. “Every fraction of a degree of warming costs lives and livelihoods,” WHO’s Jeremy Farrar warned.

The risks accumulate. Heat can aggravate heart, lung and kidney disease. Isolation, inaccessible transport, inadequate housing and interrupted electricity or health services can turn exposure into catastrophe.

An early warning delivered only through a smartphone, or an evacuation plan that assumes everyone can walk, can exclude precisely those it is meant to protect.

A 2024 Nature Communications study projects that by 2050 more than 23% of people aged 69 and over will live in climates where the hottest days exceed 37.5°C, compared with 14% in 2020. Depending on the scenario, an additional 177–246 million older adults could face this acute heat exposure.

Population ageing magnifies the consequences of delayed adaptation. Every clinic without backup power, every unshaded settlement and every inaccessible shelter becomes a longer-term liability as the population it serves changes.

Ageism or institutional inertia?

Is this exclusion ageism? The UN’s Global Report on Ageism estimated that one in two people worldwide holds ageist attitudes towards older people. That does not establish climate negotiators’ motives. It does make it implausible to assume that climate institutions are insulated from a prejudice embedded elsewhere in society.

Perhaps overloaded institutions have developed inclusion fatigue: another constituency, another consultation, another demand on scarce finance.

But population ageing is not a fashionable new issue. It is a foreseeable transformation of the societies that these institutions exist to serve. The division between “today’s older generation” and “tomorrow’s climate victims” is also false. Someone aged 40 today will be 64 in 2050. Adaptation that neglects ageing fails both people who are older now and those who will grow old under harsher conditions.

The people still tending the land

The case for inclusion goes beyond preventing deaths. Older people continue to produce food and sustain the knowledge on which adaptation depends. Eurostat found that 33.2% of EU farm managers were at least 65 in 2020; they managed 16.9% of utilised agricultural land.

Furthermore, Japan’s agriculture ministry reports that 71.7% of its core agricultural workers were 65 or older in 2024, with an average age of 69.2. These are different statistical categories, not a global comparison. Both findings expose the folly of designing agricultural resilience without older producers. In remote rangelands, forests and mountain environments, experience can be an adaptation resource.

UNESCO’s African climate work identifies elders as holders of detailed, often undocumented knowledge about weather and coping practices. The IPCC finds that exchanges between Indigenous elders and youth can strengthen adaptive capacity, and that pastoralists’ local knowledge can complement scientific research. 

The ecological stakes are substantial: IPBES estimates that Indigenous Peoples traditionally own, manage, use or occupy at least a quarter of global land. That figure describes Indigenous Peoples collectively, not older people alone. It nevertheless underlines the importance of supporting the elders who help transmit ecological knowledge within these communities. Excluding elders can weaken the transfer of knowledge needed to sustain landscapes. Their expertise should be tested alongside contemporary climate science, supported and remunerated, rather than treated as a free substitute for investment.

Recognition must change where the money goes

Climate funding criteria should recognise older people and include them in decisions. The Green Climate Fund and Adaptation Fund should require proposals to assess age-related risks, consult older people’s associations and fund relevant measures.

Country programmes should support heat plans with home outreach, accessible cooling and evacuation, and resilient primary health and care services. Projects should report spending and outcomes by age, sex and disability, distinguishing older age groups.

Loss and Damage applicants should involve older people in assessing losses and selecting responses, including accessible temporary housing, livelihood recovery, and continued access to medicines and care. Assessments should capture non-economic losses, including cultural knowledge and community ties, not only wages and property.

Eligibility and delivery must not depend on employment records, land titles or digital access. The Santiago Network should help countries and communities assess older people’s losses and plan responses. National adaptation plans and early warning systems should identify who needs accessible information, transport or assistance, and release finance when agreed forecast triggers are met. Fund older people’s associations to plan, conduct outreach and monitor outcomes. 

Finally, the UNFCCC should establish a transparent, time-bound pathway towards recognising an older people’s constituency. Meanwhile, governments and climate bodies should include representatives of older women, Indigenous elders and older people with disabilities in national delegations, adaptation consultations and relevant advisory processes, with accessible participation and travel support.

Intergenerational programmes should pay elders and young people to combine ecological knowledge with climate science. None of this requires postponing action until another negotiating agenda is created. It requires institutions to recognise the demographic reality already before them and make existing commitments serve it.

The writing is on the wall: the world is growing hotter and older. How many more summits will pass before climate institutions let that reality shape who decides, what is funded and whose lives are protected?

Hari Krishna Nibanupudi is a global climate change and ageing adviser with HelpAge International

The world is growing hotter and older. Climate institutions must recognise both realities in whose voices count and where their money goes.

title: Russian ambassador to the US dies suddenly, foreign ministry says
content:
Russias ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, has died aged 66, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday. It did not mention the cause of his death.

Darchiev passed away suddenly, the ministry said in a statement, describing him as an exceptional professional.

Alexander Darchiev served in one of the most demanding areas of Russian foreign policy, the statement said. We extend our deepest and most heartfelt condolences to Alexander Darchievs family and loved ones.

Russia-Ukraine talks yield prisoner exchange but no major progress toward peace

Darchiev, a veteran diplomat known for his stinging condemnations of the West, had served as ambassador to Washington since March 2025. His time in office was marked by a thawing of US-Russia relations as President Donald Trump opened bilateral talks with Moscow and scaled back aid to Ukraine.

Darchiev previously headed the Russian Foreign Ministrys North Atlantic Department in Washington, according to the Russian embassy in the US, as well as serving as Russias ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021.

Nearly a decade ago another Russian diplomat died suddenly aged 64. Vitaly Churkin, an ambassador to the UN, passed away following cardiac arrest in 2017, just one day before his 65th birthday.

The average life expectancy for a man in Russia is 68 years old, according to the World Bank.

title: Stacy Keach, star of stage and ‘Mike Hammer’ series, dies at 85
content:
Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.

Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.

Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.

Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating World's Most Amazing Videos on TV. He played a deranged colonel in The Ninth Configuration (also known as Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane), led the TV show Titus," had a role in Alexander Paynes Oscar-nominated drama Nebraska, and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama Blue Bloods. Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in Jay Kelly.

My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career, he told New York magazine in 2012. My choices have had a cost attached to it. But Ive gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.

Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie Lone Rider, said in a post on X that Keach was a consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him.

From TV to stage

He played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries Mistral's Daughter, a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz's novel Princess Daisy, Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli's Jesus of Nazareth and Maj. Jonas Steele in The Blue and the Gray. He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds (16 kilograms).

Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play Indians, played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in King Lear on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in The Kentucky Cycle in 1993, The Country Wife in 1965 and Other Desert Cities in 2011.

He also headed the national touring company cast of Frost/Nixon, portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with Sleuth with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of King Lear at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for Pamplona, a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run's cancellation.

A pivotal arrest

While he was still doing Mickey Spillanes Mike Hammer (later titled The New Mike Hammer), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.

As my sentence was read nine months in prison I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats, he wrote in his 2013 book, All in All: An Actors Life On and Off the Stage. He added: It was the lowest moment of my life.

He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book The Blue and the Gray.

The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.

In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, The Long Riders. He said the experience was very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity.

After prison, he narrated the TV documentary High on the Job, and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one's existence, he testified.

Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centers. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the Hammer series. He said he treasured her photos and letters behind bars.

Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.

Keach's life after prison

His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, Intimate Strangers with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, The Return of Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer, also played well, and then the Mike Hammer series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS' 1986-87 schedule.

Many years later, in the TV series Prison Break that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.

Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.

In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne. He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New Yorks Public Theater in Hamlet with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles.

Keach made his film debut in 1968 in The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter and played stoner cop Sergeant Stedenko from the Cheech and Chong movies. He worked for director John Huston twice, in Fat City and The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean and had roles in American History X with Edward Norton and The Bourne Legacy. He played a tough trucker in Roadgames, was electrocuted in Children of the Corn and a robot removed his heart in Class of 1999.

His biggest break, though, came with the role of Hammer, whom he played as a modern-day knight, a champion of the underdog.

Keach makes a dashing, dapper Hammer. He looks almost jaunty in his tilted gray fedora, said Fred Rothenberg, a TV writer for The Associated Press, in 1983. He knows how to speak lust with his eyes, and talk dirty with his fists.

title: Why has Merz sparked a hostage crisis in the EU?
content:
The German chancellor is threatening to block the bloc’s budget unless Ukraine gets more aid – except it’s not really for Ukraine

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has put a knife to the EU’s throat, demanding more cash “for Ukraine.” So what’s got into him?

What Merz wants is to make every EU member state bankroll Germany’s Ukraine-linked defense industry, whether they like it or not. If not, he’ll block the EU’s budget.

On the surface, it all seems so performatively sanctimonious. “Supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support,” Merz says, demanding that all EU nations chip in to commit tens of billions to Ukraine funding into next year and beyond.

In reality, this is actually about funding Germany, not Ukraine – as the meltdown by Mr. Ten Percent popularity makes painfully clear. “A collective commitment that all of us, without exception, will contribute fairly to closing this gap is an essential prerequisite for resolving this issue and for discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications,” Merz said.

In other words, nice seven-year EU budget you have there. Would be a shame if something were to happen to it. Like, say, a hostage incident.

The dirty little secret behind this charade is that Ukraine is the convenient cover story for funneling billions into “frontline defense,” when, in reality, much of that aid loops straight back into the German economy to prop up its own defense giants. That’s according to Germany’s own Federal Agency for Civic Education’s recent report, “Aid to Ukraine since 2022,” which classifies 78% of Ukrainian aid as military assistance, more than half of which comes from newly procured weapons. The Kiel Institute also found that €40 billion in social spending for Ukrainians never even left Germany, and is limited strictly to those inside its own social welfare system.

Read more

Within this context, German stock market star Rheinmetall has scored several contracts tied to Ukrainian aid, including billions for tank ammunition and artillery shells, and hundreds of millions in direct export orders. Meanwhile, Diehl Defense secured major interceptor supply agreements last month, adding to billions more in missile-system contracts last year. Hensoldt, Quantum Systems, Helsing, and ARX Robotics also got a €6.6 billion slice of the procurement pie in bilateral agreements signed in Kiev in October.

Something has to keep powering what’s left of the German economy – and the EU’s economic engine – now that they’ve collectively driven their cheap Russian energy supply to extinction.

What we’re actually witnessing is Merz crashing out in public and declaring that unless the cash and associated domestic kickbacks keep flowing, he’ll single-handedly blow up the entire seven-year EU budget and take everyone else’s sweet perks down with it.

This comes fresh off Merz performing the same song and dance over the need for Ukrainian energy aid. While unsuspecting onlookers might imagine his deep concern for shivering Ukrainians in wintertime, there’s rather more to it.

“Before the coming winter, two things are important: air defense and the energy sector,” he said a few days ago, alongside Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. “We have arranged further assistance for both in Kiev, which we are now implementing. We want to make further winter aid and support for energy supplies possible this year.”

The enthusiasm couldn’t possibly have anything to do with the fact that, last month, German companies like Siemens, 50Hertz, and Amprion were named in energy supply agreements for Ukraine this winter, in €155 million worth of deals.

Read more

Also worth noting: EU rules choke off almost all excessive debt spending across the board – a real problem for Germany right now, whose own citizens are clamoring for more cash handouts – but Brussels conveniently lifted the limits specifically for defense spending. And, once again, Ukraine was the useful, self-serving pretext.

So while Merz is handcuffed on virtually every other budget line, he’s been shoving whatever he can into the defense spending column – from domestic pothole and bridge repairs to military recruitment drives that conveniently sweep Germany’s actual unemployment numbers under the rug.

Meanwhile, Merz finds himself backed by the Baltics in his Fado-like lament against Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Bulgaria – countries that have decided to opt out of the whole self-serving Ukraine spending racket.

“One third of support for Ukraine is coming from Nordic [and] Baltic countries,” Estonian Finance Minister Jürgen Ligi told Rapporteur. ”But if we talk about numbers, the GDP, the Baltic states are paying much more, Denmark is paying much more…The ones who are talking in the loudest voice are not necessarily offering the most.”

Bold move for the Estonian finance minister to show his face on defense spending and related accounting, considering that Estonia’s now-former defense minister had to step down just two months ago when tens of millions its own so-called Ukraine aid, along with cash that it fundraised from some other EU countries (like Denmark and the Netherlands) allegedly vanished into a sketchy weapons company operating out of an Italian Audi dealership that reportedly delivered precisely zero ammunition for Ukraine, according to the Danish investigative outlet Danwatch. Maybe at least get Denmark’s cash back from your last dodgy scheme before encouraging everyone else to follow their example.

With top-tier talent like this steering the ship, it really is a total mystery why Kiev might be feeling that a free ride from the EU is a lot like having a stateroom aboard the Titanic.

title: Russian ambassador to US dies
content:
Aleksandr Darchiev, who passed away at age 66, had served as Moscow’s envoy to Washington since March 2025

Russia’s ambassador to the US, Aleksandr Darchiev, has “passed away suddenly,” at age 66, the Foreign Ministry in Moscow has announced without providing any further details.

The ministry’s spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, clarified later on Wednesday that the diplomat died in Moscow “of a chronic disease.”

A seasoned career diplomat, Darchiev had previously headed the North American Department at the ministry. Fluent in English and French, he served as Russia’s ambassador to Canada between 2014 and 2021. He has also held multiple postings at the Russian Embassy in Washington, including as senior counselor and minister-counselor.

Russian President Vladimir Putin appointed Darchiev ambassador to Washington in March 2025, after his candidacy was discussed with US officials during talks in Istanbul the previous month. The appointment was part of efforts to restore bilateral ties after relations between Russia and the US had deteriorated to their lowest point since the Cold War.

Read more

Under former US President Joe Biden, Washington had sharply curtailed diplomatic contacts with Moscow following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022 and imposed sweeping sanctions on Russian officials and businesses. Russia was left without an ambassador in Washington from October 2024 until March 2025, with a charge d’affaires overseeing the embassy.

After taking office in January 2025, US President Donald Trump criticized his predecessor for sidelining diplomacy and pledged to broker a peace deal between Moscow and Kiev while restoring bilateral ties with Russia.

Upon arriving in Washington, Darchiev welcomed signs of improving US-Russia relations but warned that more work was needed to overcome the “toxic legacy” of the previous American administration.

In June 2025, the ambassador met with Trump in an encounter he described as brief but “very constructive.” Four months later, he handed declassified Soviet documents on the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy to Republican Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna.
