title: Russia-Ukraine talks yield prisoner exchange but no major progress toward peace
content:
Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, both sides said Wednesday as two days of U.S. mediated talks concluded, but they announced no major breakthrough on ending the conflict that began after Moscows full-scale invasion nearly five years ago.

RELATED STORY | Melania Trump hosts Russian, Ukrainian officials to mark ceasefire she brokered

Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement.

U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washingtons peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.

As well as postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles for negotiators are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement.

US envoys to meet with Putin and Zelenskyy

The session was the first such meeting since February on Russias invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

The talks lasted just under two hours Wednesday, after a four-hour session the previous day.

One of the positives is we agreed that were going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which were going to finalize the numbers tomorrow, said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trumps son-in-law, after the talks in Abu Dhabi ended.

Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyivs contingent, confirmed the planned POW exchange, although Medinsky noted that the agreement was in principle.

Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staffs information department who attended the talks, told Russian state TV that it would be one of the biggest such swaps following the 1,000 soldiers returned home last year.

The latest exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks, he said.

Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

European officials were excluded by Moscow from the talks

Umerov said Kyivs delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks.

Moscow doesnt want European countries, which are concerned about Russias conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks.

Ukraines priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace, Zelenskyy said on X. We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war that is Russia.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks, but he said their current statements "dont indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace. Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine.

Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps.

RELATED STORY | Trilateral talks between US, Ukraine and Russia to resume this week

Ukraine wants to make sure Moscow doesn't invade again, and EU officials have declared that any discussions on Europes security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire. Many in Europe see the inclusion of Russia in those plans as a concession to Putin, who has described NATOs eastward expansion as a top threat to its security. Russia has demanded that the alliance pull back its troops from its borders.

Russia's security concerns were discussed at the talks, Kushner said, adding that Moscow was told it needs to provide different de-escalation and proposals for them to be acceptable to Europe.

The reality is, is theres no trust right now between the sides. And thats to be expected after a conflict like this, he said.

The talks were held in a new political atmosphere

The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration now has to reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections, and they could demand more support for Ukraine.

Also, Russias wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.

The talks came against the backdrop of continued fighting on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year. Both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones.

Three people died and 11 were injured after Russia launched a daytime attack on a market in the southern Odesa region, local authorities said. Residential buildings were damaged and emergency crews responded, said Oleh Kiper, head of the regional military administration.

Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, Ukrainian officials said.

Russias Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight,. 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko. The drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers, he added.

An Indonesian man is reportedly captured on the battlefield

Meanwhile, a 49-year-old Indonesian man reportedly was captured on the battlefield in southern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region after he claimed he was unknowingly recruited to fight for the Russian military.

RELATED STORY | High-stakes Ukraine talks resume as Europe pushes to be included

The Indonesian Embassy in Kyiv was seeking access to the man, who was in Ukrainian custody, according to Yvonne Mewengkang, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to Ukraines I Want to Leave project that offers Russian troops the opportunity to surrender, the man was taken to occupied Donetsk with no military training and then to the Zaporizhzhia region, where his unit was attacked and he was captured, according to the group's post on Telegram.

The man said he signed what he believed to be a contract to work in construction for one year in Moscow, the group said.

Ukrainian and Russian officials made no immediate comment.

Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, Ukrainian officials said.

Russias Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight,. 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko. The drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers, he added.

An Indonesian man is reportedly captured on the battlefield

Meanwhile, a 49-year-old Indonesian man reportedly was captured on the battlefield in southern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region after he claimed he was unknowingly recruited to fight for the Russian military.

The Indonesian Embassy in Kyiv was seeking access to the man, who was in Ukrainian custody, according to Yvonne Mewengkang, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to Ukraines I Want to Leave project that offers Russian troops the opportunity to surrender, the man was taken to occupied Donetsk with no military training and then to the Zaporizhzhia region, where his unit was attacked and he was captured, according to the group's post on Telegram.

The man said he signed what he believed to be a contract to work in construction for one year in Moscow, the group said.

Ukrainian and Russian officials made no immediate comment.

Witkoff and Kushner arrive in Moscow for Ukraine talks with Putin (VIDEO)
content:
The US envoys are expected to brief the Russian president on the outcome of two days of trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow for talks on resolving the Ukraine conflict, following two days of trilateral negotiations between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi, UAE.

Representatives of the three countries concluded two days of discussions in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, marking their first formal three-way meeting since February. Following the talks, Kushner said he believes there is room for progress on some of the issues.

Kushner and Witkoff landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport on Thursday morning, where they were greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev. Footage of the arrival shows Dmitriev embracing Witkoff while Kushner smiles beneath an umbrella. In a post on X, Dmitriev described the mood of the American negotiators as positive ahead of their talks in Moscow.

Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told Kommersant that Kushner and Witkoff will meet Putin before noon.

“We do not yet know the outcome of the Abu Dhabi negotiations,” he said.

BREAKING: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrive in Moscow for a meeting with President Putin. pic.twitter.com/dp4mtgWaZi

— Kirill Dmitriev (@kadmitriev) November 12, 2026

Kushner previously described the negotiations in Abu Dhabi as “very substantive,” saying the delegations covered all major issues. He added that a final agreement would not be possible without resolving territorial disputes. Moscow has long insisted that a lasting agreement must address the root causes of the crisis.

Read more

The negotiations also produced an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine, according to Russian presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, who headed Moscow’s delegation. The number of prisoners involved has yet to be finalized.

Kushner said the upcoming meeting with Putin would also address the possibility of involving European countries in future negotiations.

European representatives remain outside the trilateral talks, although they met separately with US and Ukrainian officials on Tuesday.  Moscow has questioned their contribution and has accused European governments of undermining previous peace agreements and prolonging the fighting through continued weapons supplies.

Following their visit to Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff plan to travel to Dublin to meet Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky.

title: France fears Germany could trigger nuclear war – FT
content:
Moscow has said that it harbors no aggressive designs against Europe, but promised a harsh response if attacked by NATO first

France is pushing Germany to define how it would use its long-range missiles in the event of a possible conflict with Russia due to concerns that it could trigger a nuclear war, the Financial Times has reported, citing officials from the two European nations.

Moscow has said repeatedly that it harbors no aggressive designs against Western Europe, adding that a conflict with NATO is only possible if the bloc attacks Russia first or if its members deploy their forces to Ukraine.

FT said in an article on Wednesday that Paris is in talks with Berlin in order to align the German doctrine on the use of its deep strike capabilities with France’s nuclear strategy.

The discussions with Germany and several other EU nations started after French President Emmanuel Macron said in March that he was open to expanding his country’s nuclear umbrella to protect them as well, it said.
France is the only country to have developed its own nuclear arsenal in Europe aside from the UK and Russia, although several other countries, notably Germany and Turkey, host American nuclear weapons and Belarus hosts Russian nuclear weapons.

Read more

An unnamed French official told the outlet that there’s a possibility that the Europeans would “get a nuclear response” after solely deploying conventional weapons to attack Russia. “If the Russians don’t get the signal right you could get to the nuclear threshold without realizing,” he warned.

Paris is also worried that Macron’s concept of “forward deterrence” would result in Moscow holding France accountable for any strikes conducted by its allies, according to FT.

Germany pledged to spend €780 billion ($868,5 billion) on defense between 2026 of 2030, citing concerns over the Ukraine conflict and plans by US President Donald Trump to reduce American military presence in Europe. It’s currently obtaining and developing several types of missiles with ranges from 500 km to over 2,000 km. The distance between Moscow and Berlin is about 1,600km.

A senior German official, who talked to FT, said that Berlin is in full agreement with Paris on the need for “a joint doctrine and a joint understanding about the escalation ladder.”

Read more

The development of deep strike capabilities “necessarily had to be accompanied by a joint understanding of how to deploy them. It was clear from the outset,” he stressed.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said in late October that the European leaders are wrong when they speak about preparing for a conflict with Moscow in the next four years.

“We are ready for it, but we do not want any war with Europe,” Putin stressed. Ukraine’s Western backers “have failed to achieve their goal of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia, and it is highly unlikely that it’ll be possible by 2030,” he said.

“And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget about that,” Putin warned.

title: Zelensky issues ultimatum to Western Europe
content:
Confusion over who could speak at peace talks must be clarified by the end of November, the former actor has demanded

Vladimir Zelensky has demanded that a Western European representative be approved to join the peace talks initiated by the US, Russia and Ukraine by the end of November.

Speaking in Copenhagen as trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi closed with a confirmation that Western Europe has effectively been sidelined from the discussions, Zelensky insisted that “we need to choose who will represent Europe in the negotiations. This would be better, as they would receive a mandate for the talks – a mandate from all of Europe.”

The decision must be made “no later than the end of November” or during the meeting of Kiev’s Western European backers in Berlin on the 19th of the month.

Speaking following the Abu Dhabi trilaterals, US envoy Jared Kushner pointed out that “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

Read more

The Western European countries have refused to negotiate with Moscow practically since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Recent attempts to reopen a dialogue with them have only exposed divisions.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni complained last week that the EU was “all over the place” on the issue, undermining its own credibility.

Last month, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store came under fire from fellow EU leaders for breaking ranks and unilaterally contacting Russian President Vladimir Putin. Moscow welcomed the engagement, despite it not leading to any breakthroughs.

Moscow has said repeatedly that Europe has lost its credibility because it continues to supply weapons and funds to Ukraine and discusses the need to deliver a strategic defeat to Russia. It also rejected calls for an unconditional ceasefire coming from Brussels, arguing that they are only set up to win time for Kiev to reconstitute its forces.

Stubb, Store, Meloni as well as Czech President Petr Pavel and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who has already rejected the job, have all been mentioned by the media as possible candidates to become the sole European representatives in the negotiations.

READ MORE: EU to deploy military advisers to Ukraine

When asked by journalists after the discussions in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday about when the Europeans could become full-fledged participants of the peace talks, Russia’s top negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, replied that it will only happen “when they grow a conscience.”

title: US Treasury chief hides at military base following Iran ‘threats’ – media
content:
Scott Bessent, who vowed “financial violence” against Tehran, is the latest Trump official to leave his home over security concerns

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has reportedly taken refuge at a military base after receiving alleged death threats from Iran.

Bessent has led Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Tehran since August, threatening to impose “economic asphyxiation” and unleash “financial violence” through sweeping sanctions targeting Iranian businesses and their foreign partners. Dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, the campaign is part of Washington’s broader confrontation with Tehran, which erupted into war following US-Israeli strikes in late February.

The New York Times first reported Bessent’s relocation on Tuesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Reuters subsequently corroborated the report through two sources. The credibility and severity of the alleged Iranian threats remain unclear.

Washington has also warned of heightened security risks for senior American figures. Last month, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton claimed that Tehran had “substantially increased” its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond, with some plots allegedly reaching “advanced stages.”

Read more

On Tuesday, FBI Director Kash Patel announced charges against three alleged Iranian-backed operatives accused of carrying out or plotting nearly 20 attacks across the US and Europe. The Justice Department said the suspects had targeted Jewish communities and plotted to strike RAF Fairford, a British airbase used by American military forces.

Tehran has dismissed previous US assassination plot allegations, accusing Washington of portraying itself as a victim while waging war against Iran. Responding to similar claims in June, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said that “playing the victim cannot whitewash” what he described as American war crimes against the Iranian people.

Bessent joins several senior Trump administration officials who are said to have sought refuge on military installations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly moved onto the same base in Washington. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem also lived at a military facility near the capital, while new White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller relocated to military housing in September 2025 after reporting harassment at his Virginia home.

Read more

Security concerns have extended to US military installations overseas. In early October, American bombers were hastily withdrawn from Britain following reports of a suspected terrorist plot against RAF Fairford, which had been used to launch strikes on Iran. On Monday, US refueling tankers and Osprey aircraft were also moved from RAF Mildenhall to other bases in Britain and continental Europe.

The Pentagon also revealed in late October that it was preparing major US bases to operate independently for at least 90 days, allowing them to withstand prolonged power outages, supply disruptions, and infrastructure damage during a major conflict.

Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts to end the war have continued. Rubio said Tuesday that Washington saw no need to resume major military operations against Iran, claiming that economic pressure is proving effective. Tehran has insisted that any settlement must address its demands for ending hostilities before it reopens the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Sharia-compliant student loans spark row in UK – Telegraph
content:
British universities have begun promoting government-backed “interest-free” student loans scheme

Six UK universities have begun advertising “interest-free” student loans designed to comply with Islamic law. The government-backed scheme is drawing sharp criticism over fears it could create a “two-tier” system, the Telegraph has reported.

The planned scheme, known as Alternative Student Finance, is set to comply with sharia law, which prohibits the payment or receipt of interest. Based on the Islamic finance principle of Takaful, it would require students to pay an equivalent “contribution” instead of interest on top of their principal, with the funds ring-fenced to finance future participants.

Takaful, an Islamic system of mutual financial assistance and risk-sharing, is widely used in Muslim-majority countries, primarily in insurance rather than higher education financing.

The Telegraph noted on Tuesday that the British authorities paid Islamic Finance Council UK more than £365,000 ($486,000) of public money to devise the new loan scheme.

Read more

The loans are expected to be introduced as part of wider changes to student finance due to begin this year, although the Department for Education (DfE) has yet to announce a launch date.

According to the newspaper, the institutions include the University of Bristol, the University of Leeds, University College London (UCL), City St. George’s, Newcastle University, and De Montfort University.

Muslims number just under four million people in the UK, accounting for around 6% of the population, according to census analysis by the Muslim Council of Britain.

Critics have questioned whether the government should create a separate student finance system to accommodate the religious beliefs of one group, arguing that this could undermine equal treatment within higher education.

Suella Braverman, Reform UK’s education spokeswoman, called the scheme “outrageous,” “anti-British” and “exclusionary,” and told The Telegraph that it would create a “two-tier education system.” She also argued that taxpayers would have to cover any shortfall if borrowers failed to repay their loans in full.

Read more

A DfE spokesperson was cited by the newspaper as calling it “completely false to assert that Alternative Student Finance arrangements would give favorable treatment to Muslim students.” He stressed all graduates would repay their loans in full regardless of which system they used, including an equivalent alternative to interest, adding that student loans differ from commercial lending, with the repayment burden managed and the system already heavily subsidized by the government.

Official forecasts show that 45% of undergraduates in England taking out their first loans in the 2025–26 academic year are expected not to repay them in full, a risk that also applies to the conventional student loan system.

A report by research center Equi, cited by Times Higher Education last month, argued that introducing the alternative financing scheme could generate an additional £450 million for the UK economy by enabling around 6,000 students who annually turn down university places because of the existing loan system to pursue higher education. The report also said the alternative funding mechanism should be available to all students, regardless of their faith.

title: From Nuclear Weapons to Artificial Intelligence, a New Test of Humanity’s Restraint
content:
Hiroshima atomic-bomb survivor Katsuko Tanaka, center-left, joins nuclear-disarmament advocates and experts at the “Nuclear Between Disarmament and Proliferation” forum during Sant’Egidio’s International Meeting for Peace in Assisi, Italy, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Community of Sant’Egidio

By Katsuhiro Asagiri
ASSISI, Italy, Nov 11 2026 (IPS)

Eight decades after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the world is confronting a new and potentially dangerous question: What happens when decisions involving human life increasingly pass from people to machines?

Community of Sant’Edigio

That concern ran through discussions at an international peace gathering in Assisi, where religious leaders, nuclear disarmament campaigners and technology specialists examined the risks of nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence — two very different technologies united by the possibility of catastrophic harm.

The meeting, organized by the Community of Sant’Egidio from Oct. 25 to 27, marked 40 years since Pope John Paul II brought representatives of the world’s major religions to Assisi to pray for peace.

This year’s theme, “Unarmed and Disarming Peace,” carried particular urgency. Nuclear arms control has weakened, military spending has reached record levels, and artificial intelligence is rapidly entering defense systems whose consequences remain difficult to predict.

The question was no longer simply whether humanity possessed the means to destroy itself. It was whether governments and societies retained the judgment to prevent those means from being used.

Katsuko Tanaka, Hibakusha from Hiroshima (Left). Credit: Beppe Raso/ Soka Gakkai

The Warning From Hiroshima

The human consequences of nuclear warfare formed the moral foundation of a forum devoted to disarmament and proliferation.

Katsuko Tanaka, also known as Toshiko Tanaka, a Hiroshima atomic bomb survivor, recalled the bombing of Aug. 6, 1945, when she was six years old.

Her account recalled a catastrophe that killed indiscriminately and left survivors carrying physical and psychological wounds for decades.

Archbishop Peter Michiaki Nakamura of Nagasaki, in his published remarks, drew on the legacy of Takashi Nagai, the physician and atomic bomb survivor who devoted his later life to peace.

Together, their perspectives challenged the language of nuclear deterrence, which measures security in terms of military capabilities rather than the lives potentially lost.

Susi Snyder, the Director of Programmes at ICAN. Credit: Community of Sant’Egidio / Assisi 2026

Susi Snyder of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, or ICAN, addressed the growing danger posed by the modernization of nuclear arsenals and the erosion of arms control.

The expiration of the New START treaty between the United States and Russia in February, followed by the failure of the 2026 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference to reach consensus, has reinforced concerns about the future of nuclear restraint.

Attention is now turning to the first Review Conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, scheduled to begin in late November.

But disarmament advocates face a persistent obstacle: The governments possessing nuclear weapons largely remain outside the treaty.

Teaching a Generation Without Memories of War

Credit: Simone Giara per Senzatomica

For the Italian Soka Gakkai, a Buddhist organization engaged in nuclear abolition campaigns, education has become an essential part of the response.

Alessja Trama, representing the Be The Hope Foundation, an organization affiliated with the Italian Soka Gakkai, described in her prepared remarks the work of Senzatomica, an initiative that has organized exhibitions and educational activities on nuclear weapons in communities across Italy.

The campaign traces its inspiration to a 1957 declaration by Josei Toda, the second president of the Soka Gakkai, calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons.

Its premise is that remembering Hiroshima and Nagasaki must lead to public responsibility, particularly among younger generations who have no personal connection to the war.

Yet even as campaigners seek to reduce the threat from existing weapons, advances in artificial intelligence are transforming the nature of military power.

When Human Judgment Becomes Optional

At a separate forum titled “Humanity in the Age of Technology,” Archbishop Vincenzo Paglia warned that technological capabilities were advancing faster than the institutions meant to govern them.

Tiziana Catarci, an Italian artificial intelligence researcher, raised a critical distinction: placing a human in a decision-making process does not necessarily mean that person exercises meaningful control.

An operator may formally approve a machine-generated recommendation without fully understanding how it was produced or being able to challenge it.

Embedded gallery image from the Soka Gakkai Italy article ‘Ad Assisi la speranza come scelta di pace: la Soka Gakkai ai forum sul nucleare e sulla tecnologia’. Credit: Beppe Raso

In military operations, that gap could become deadly.

Catarci called for stronger oversight of AI systems and the prohibition of autonomous weapons capable of making lethal decisions without meaningful human control.

Embedded gallery image from the Soka Gakkai Italy article ‘Ad Assisi la speranza come scelta di pace: la Soka Gakkai ai forum sul nucleare e sulla tecnologia’. Credit: Beppe Raso

Yoshiyuki Nagaoka, executive director of the Office of Public Affairs of Soka Gakkai, approached the problem through Buddhist teachings on the dignity of life.

Nagaoka noted that AI is increasingly being embraced as a source of advice in everyday life in Japan, with some people turning to it for guidance when making deeply personal decisions about their lives.

One example he cited was the case of an elderly woman who turned to generative AI for advice about the medical treatment of her terminally ill husband.

For Nagaoka, the issue was not whether AI could provide useful information. It was whether reliance on such systems might gradually weaken the human willingness to make difficult moral judgments.

He warned particularly against delegating decisions about killing to autonomous weapons, advocating international rules to prohibit systems that independently select and attack human targets.

His argument extended beyond warfare to healthcare, where statistical predictions cannot replace compassion, personal choice and professional responsibility.

A Technology That Can Also Help

Other participants cautioned against viewing artificial intelligence solely as a threat.

Matt Vasey of the Gates Foundation argued that AI could improve access to healthcare, education and agricultural knowledge, especially in communities historically neglected by technological development.

But he also warned that people could voluntarily surrender moral responsibility to systems designed to make decisions easier.

Cisco executive Gianpaolo Barozzi emphasized the need to redesign work around human capabilities, while Rabbi Noam Marans of the American Jewish Committee distinguished the accumulation of information from the exercise of wisdom.

The speakers offered no single regulatory blueprint. They nevertheless returned repeatedly to the need for accountability, transparency and human judgment.

The gathering’s closing Peace Appeal connected these concerns to a broader agenda, urging that resources devoted to weapons be redirected toward food, water, education, healthcare and decent work.

It also identified nuclear threats, rearmament and artificial intelligence as challenges requiring international cooperation.

Closing ceremony. Credit: Community of Sant’Egidio / Assisi 2026

The message underscored a growing dilemma.

Humanity has developed technologies of extraordinary power. Yet the institutions and moral commitments needed to restrain their destructive uses have not necessarily kept pace.

From Hiroshima’s surviving witnesses to researchers confronting autonomous weapons, the warning emerging from Assisi was that security cannot be measured simply by what humanity is capable of building.

It must also be measured by what humanity is prepared to refuse.　

This article is brought to you by INPS Japan in collaboration with Soka Gakkai International in consultative status with UN ECOSOC.

IPS UN Bureau

At an interfaith gathering in Assisi, nuclear survivors, scientists and religious leaders confronted a troubling question: Can humanity control the destructive powers it continues to create?

title: House Republicans block Hegseth impeachment bid
content:
US Congressman Thomas Massie has accused the War Secretary of conducting illegal military operations without lawmakers’ approval

The Republican-controlled US House of Representatives has blocked an attempt to impeach US War Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the conflict with Iran and other military operations, effectively shelving the initiative until the next Congress takes office.

Outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie reintroduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth earlier this week, following the Democrats’ victory in the November 3 midterm elections, which gave them control of both chambers of Congress beginning in January.

The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, where Republicans hold a majority. The party will retain control of both chambers until the end of the year, making it highly unlikely that the impeachment measure will advance before the current congressional term expires.

Read more

Massie has accused Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and failing to minimize civilian casualties during US strikes. The conflict, triggered by a joint US-Israeli attack on Iran on February 28, has been “unlawful from its inception,” the congressman said.

He also denounced the 2025 US strikes on Yemen and the January abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro as illegal, while accusing Hegseth of ordering extrajudicial killings of suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific. The Pentagon chief’s military operations have drawn fierce criticism from Democrats and some Republicans.

Hegseth dismissed the impeachment effort as a “farce” and a “political spectacle” during a Pentagon press conference on Tuesday. He rejected the accusations and defended the military operations, saying: “I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.”

Read more

Massie first introduced the impeachment articles in September, but the initiative stalled after Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson canceled the chamber’s remaining votes ahead of the midterms. The congressman warned on Monday that his renewed impeachment effort was a “much gentler version” of what could follow when Democrats take control of Congress.

The Democrats’ victory in the November 3 midterms has been widely seen as a rebuke of US President Donald Trump’s policies, particularly the unpopular Iran war, which has sent energy prices soaring by disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key global oil and LNG route. The party will gain the power to investigate Hegseth when it takes control of Congress in January.

Trump has fiercely defended Hegseth, branding Massie a “total loser” and praising the Pentagon chief as “perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the country.” On Monday, he reaffirmed his support, telling reporters: “I’ll stand by him.” Following Hegseth’s press conference on Tuesday, Trump gave his performance an “A PLUS, PLUS, PLUS.”

title: ‘Data-informed, mission-driven’: Kyiv Independent combats war fatigue – while monetising editorial integrity
content:
Five years ago today, the editorial team that was fired from the Kyiv Post announced it was launching a new news outlet. “We hadn’t even chosen a name,” recalls Olga Rudenko, founding chief editor of the Kyiv Independent, “but we went public on 11 November 2021, and that’s our official birthday.”

They moved fast: the announcement came three days after the Post temporarily shut down. Within a week, they sent out their first newsletter and in less than two weeks, on 22 November, the first edition was launched.

When full-scale war arrived three months later, the English-language startup was propelled into the global spotlight as news from and on Ukraine became paramount.

“What matters to us is that we’ve grown slowly and consistently since then: in team, in subscribers, in platforms, and in the output, the offering. We’ve worked hard to turn that boost of attention into what the Kyiv Independent is now,” asserts Rudenko.

Today, the Kyiv Independent is the largest English language news outlet in Ukraine, with a 36,000 subscriber base that is a mere fraction of its more than 2 million monthly readers.

The outlet has been consistent in its editorial, advocacy and promotional efforts to retain and grow that base.

This includes award-winning investigative reporting and, since 2023, a documentary division developed to combat war fatigue among readers, notes Rudenko. “It’s a format with a much longer shelf life, and it’s used a lot in advocacy as well. That’s our way of trying to do something with a longer and more profound impact than regular stories.”

“We have to be smart about war fatigue, and we need to be reminded all the time of our mission, because the stories that matter are sometimes the ones that don’t get many clicks and aren’t popular with the audience,” explains Rudenko, referring to the outlet’s daily roundup of Russian strikes on Ukraine. This takes real reporting effort to assemble, but is least likely to be read.

”If we were driven by fatigue and the audience’s needs as we deduce them from data, we would probably slash them. We continue because they need to be there, even though fewer and fewer people want to click on them. So we need to be data-informed, but mission-driven.”

Mutually beneficial membership

This editorial resolve is equally evident in the Independent’s approach to its subscribers, and the role that news media can play within its communities, notes Rudenko. “We need to think of ourselves as gravity centres for our communities, not just providers of a product, which is news. That’s too narrow a way for a media outlet to define itself.”

She’s a big believer in membership funding for journalism, with good reason: About 70 percent of the outlet’s 2025 revenue comes from members – and the paying base grew from 22,200 to 35,400 between September 2025 and August 2026, even as global interest in the war fell.

Rudenko attributes it to two winning decisions: “Our first great decision was to start the Kyiv Independent. Our second was to go for a community-funded outlet. Instead of a paywall, we built a community of people supporting us.”

‘We use the word community not as a marketing trick – it really feels like one; they matter to us, and to each other, and they interact with each other. We get much more than funding from them: ideas, inspiration, support.’

They are also readily mobilised: when the US administration abruptly ended USAID early last year, leaving many independent Ukrainian media financially bereft, the Kyiv Independent raised $60,000 for three small regional newsrooms near the front line, from its community.

”We’ve done similar things several times since, for local media and for charities in Ukraine. To be honest, it’s probably my favourite thing we do. Having worked in Ukrainian media for some time, it’s a privileged position to be able not just to sustain yourself but to help others. It makes me so proud.”

Turning readers into members: A case study

The funnel starts with free reporting. People find Kyiv Independent through social media, search, YouTube, partner media and ads, then return through newsletters, videos and familiar reporters.

Trust is built through transparency, and behind-the-scenes access. Then comes the ask – and the outlet stresses that this journey is not linear: readers enter at any point, and often need several touchpoints.

Here’s how they navigate it:

  • Public campaigns: Campaigns name a number of members the outlet needs, and why, and show a live progress bar so readers can see their sign-up move it. A spring 2026 drive to add 4,000 members reached its target. For this fifth birthday, it is appealing for 5,000 new members. 

  • Localised hooks. The same mission is repackaged for each country, using its own goal, its per-capita ranking or a local news moment. Dutch readers were asked to help expose Russian war crimes while the Hague waited; Germans were invited to grow their community from 800 to 1,000; Americans were told the outlet was looking for 10,000 who care.
  • Iterative testing. On paid channels, the outlet separates cold audiences, who have never read it and meet free reporting first, from warm ones who need a well-timed reminder. Every two weeks it launches new assets, tests messages and formats, then scales the winners and cuts the rest.
  • Platform-native strategy. The outlet’s YouTube channel has more than 450,000 subscribers, fewer than 1 percent of whom support it financially. It has a dedicated landing page, a channel banner, pinned comments and short pieces to camera from reporters, around one line: “Fund the reporting you just watched.”

Personalisation is key: personal storytelling email from a reporter produced three times the conversions of a polished, designed promotional email, with higher open and click rates.

Five years after first signing up to what would become a war newsroom with global reach, Rudenko affirms: “I can’t imagine doing anything else now. It’s been difficult, but it’s also been a privilege to have this outlet during the war, to do something we really think makes a difference. We feel we’re on the right side of history, and at a time like this it matters to have something that gives you a sense of purpose. Best decision ever.”

The post ‘Data-informed, mission-driven’: Kyiv Independent combats war fatigue – while monetising editorial integrity appeared first on WAN-IFRA.

title: ‘Independence isn’t declared, it’s built’: How Mediapart turned reader trust into a business model
content:
By Maria Lisicka

“Exclusive and verified information has value, and people are okay to pay for it.” This principle has shaped Mediapart since 2008, the company’s CEO, Cécile Sourd, told participants of WAN-IFRA’s Asian Media Leaders Summit.

For Mediapart, independence has become not just an editorial value, but a legal and financial structure.

In 2008, “everything was for free on the internet, including news,” Sourd recalled. Mediapart’s founders made “this crazy bet that people would actually be willing to pay for exclusive and verified information.”

At first, the bet was costly: Mediapart lost money for two years, financing long investigations without enough subscribers.

“It all changed when we started revealing facts that no one would have revealed if we hadn’t been there,” she explained. From then on, “people knew they could find something at Mediapart they wouldn’t read anywhere else.”

“Eighteen years later, this bet paid off,” she said.

Mediapart has more than 280,000 individual subscribers, who account for 99% of its annual revenue. “This is the foundation for everything else,” she said. “If your only boss is the reader, your accountability is to them only.”

After reader funding, the second pillar is legal: in 2019, Mediapart created the Fonds pour une Presse Libre (Fund for a Free Press), an endowment fund that supports independent French media.

Crucially, it permanently holds Mediapart’s capital, “which makes it impossible for an outside shareholder to take control of the newsroom.”

The third pillar is financial sustainability. Mediapart has been profitable for 15 years, carries no loans and self-finances its investments. Together, these pillars mean “independence isn’t just a slogan, it’s a financial and legal architecture.”

‘Not above, but within society’

“Being financially independent isn’t enough,” Sourd stressed. “You also have to build a direct relationship of trust with your audience.”

That starts with participation. Subscribers publish their own posts in Le Club, and Mediapart co-produced a reader-funded cinema documentary on the Sarkozy-Gaddafi affair, Personne n’y comprend rien. “The core idea is that journalism shouldn’t be above, but within, society, in a direct interaction with it.”

It continues with transparency. Mediapart publishes its full annual accounts, explains its investigative methods in a section called La Boîte Noire (“The Black Box”), and asks journalists to declare their interests.

“You can’t demand transparency from the powerful people you scrutinise if you don’t hold yourself to the same standards,” Sourd noted.

Finally, Mediapart meets readers at free events and answers them through customer service run by real people rather than AI. Such closeness is no extra, she said: “It’s what turns a reader into a long-term supporter.”

“Independence isn’t declared, it’s built: legally, financially and every day in [our] relationship with the readers.”
– Cécile Sourd, CEO, Mediapart

Journalism that shifts the debate

“Our job is to look for the truth of facts, not to defend opinions,” Sourd said. Mediapart’s investigations have opened public debates and at times led to legal or political consequences, from police violence to corruption. “This isn’t journalism reporting into a void.”

Beyond good timing and some luck, Sourd said, it takes a clear value proposition centred on real journalism, and a “journalistic promise” that “doesn’t change over the years.”

See more: No ads. No investors. No compromise: How Mediapart makes independence pay
and also: Mediapart transforms B2B from revenue niche to growth lever

Why no advertising? Because Mediapart investigates companies, “having advertisements is a weakness for real, real independence,” Sourd said, while acknowledging that “it’s a luxury for us not to need them.”

Long reads come at a cost: “the first reason why people unsubscribe” is “the lack of time,” Sourd conceded. Mediapart has responded with free newsletters, summaries, audio versions and video shows. Still, half its subscribers have stayed over three to four years.

 Mediapart’s bet is that “keeping a real, vivid relationship to the readers” will help it withstand AI. “Maybe that’s too optimistic,” she said, “but that’s how we are trying to fight it.”

About the author: Maria Lisicka is a young professional in PR and strategic communication, currently pursuing her studies at the University of Amsterdam and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.

title: Second day of Russia-Ukraine-US talks concludes in Abu Dhabi
content:
Negotiations in the UAE could reshape European security as Kiev’s backers seek a seat at the table

Russia, Ukraine, and the US have concluded the second day of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. Wednesday’s meeting lasted just under two hours, compared to the nearly five hours of closed-door negotiations on Tuesday.

The Abu Dhabi November round marks the first formal trilateral negotiations since February, and were made possible only by Washington’s mediation efforts, which involved talks between US envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin last month.

Presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky is leading the Russian delegation. Also present were US envoy Steve Witkoff, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The Ukrainian team is headed by Foreign Intelligence Service chief Rustem Umerov, who has said Vladimir Zelensky has authorized the delegation to discuss all issues related to ending the conflict.

Read more

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov explained on Tuesday that the first priority for negotiators is establishing the parameters of security for Russia, Ukraine and the wider region before moving on to a settlement of the conflict.

Moscow has long insisted that a lasting agreement must address the root causes of the crisis.

Kushner has outlined Washington’s priorities as ending hostilities, establishing postwar security guarantees, supporting Ukraine’s economic recovery and addressing humanitarian issues.

Territory remains a major obstacle as Zelensky has once again ruled out Ukraine withdrawing its forces from Russia’s Donbass. Speaking at a press conference in Dublin on Tuesday, he argued that Washington should find “another way” to reach a deal with Moscow. 

Read more

The Telegraph also reported that Kiev has rejected a US proposal to redraw administrative boundaries as part of a territorial compromise. Russia has consistently demanded recognition of the territorial realities on the ground, including an end to Ukrainian control over the remaining parts of Donbass.

European representatives remain outside the trilateral talks, although they met separately with US and Ukrainian officials on Tuesday. Umerov said Wednesday’s trilateral session would also be followed by another separate meeting with Ukraine’s European backers.

Moscow has questioned their contribution and has accused European governments of undermining previous peace agreements and prolonging the fighting through continued weapons supplies.

title: Before We Declare Gender Bias Dead, Read the Footnotes
content:
By Stephanie Hodge
NEW YORK, Nov 11 2026 (IPS)

The United Nations knows how to announce a milestone. What interests me, after a career that has included working inside UNICEF and UNDP and evaluating institutions from outside them, is what happens between the announcement and the working day.

Thalif Deen’s IPS article of 3 November 2026 asks whether gender bias at the UN is approaching an “inglorious end.” It is a question, not a declaration, and the reporting gives considerable space to continuing inequalities. Alongside achievements in representation, staff representatives describe barriers to advancement, weaknesses in accountability and fears about reporting discrimination. The article itself supplies reasons to resist a premature obituary for institutional bias.[1]

I bring a perspective to this question, certainly. But the discipline of evaluation requires me to challenge my own expectations as carefully as an institution’s claims. If the evidence demonstrates progress, acknowledge it. If it supports a narrower conclusion than the public celebration, say so.

The UN’s published figures demonstrate substantial progress towards numerical gender parity. They do not, on their own, establish whether discrimination in recruitment, advancement, treatment or access to authority has diminished.

UN Women reports that women’s share of Professional and higher categories across the UN system rose from 47 per cent in 2021 to 48.8 per cent in 2023, reaching 50.4 per cent in 2025. It also reports that parity among the Senior Management Group and resident coordinators has been maintained since 2018. These are meaningful achievements, and dismissing them would weaken any serious critique.[2]

The dates matter. The Secretary-General’s 2025 report principally covers January 2022 to December 2023, with developments through mid-2025. Its figures should not be presented as a fresh assessment of the workforce in November 2026.[2]

But an institutional average is an exceptionally comfortable place to hide an uncomfortable distribution.

UN Women’s accompanying infographic presents the following figures for 2025, citing the system-wide dashboard in June of that year:[3]

These figures appear in the same published presentation. They show how an overall majority can coexist with women’s underrepresentation at director levels. Under the UN’s operational definition, parity falls within a range of 47 to 53 per cent; the D-1 and D-2 figures above remain below that range.[3] [5]

That distribution does not, by itself, prove discrimination in individual appointments. Nor does a snapshot establish that women progress more slowly than men. It establishes why an aggregate percentage cannot answer the question of equal advancement. For that, we need to follow careers: who applies, who is shortlisted, who is selected, who progresses, how long progression takes, and who leaves.

There is another question beneath the celebration: which UN are we measuring?

The Secretariat dashboard cited in the article explicitly covers a defined population of international staff. Its explanatory notes say General Service and national staff are not shown and are intended for a subsequent phase. It also specifies appointment types and excludes entities with ten or fewer people. These are legitimate statistical boundaries, but they are boundaries all the same.[4]

This does not mean the UN collects no information about those groups elsewhere. It means this particular dashboard cannot establish what is happening across the whole workforce.

The Secretariat and the wider UN system are not interchangeable reporting populations. Neither are international professionals, national personnel and consultants. Every claim should tell the reader whose working lives it describes.

The Secretariat’s own human resources strategy also identifies a measure that reaches beyond headcounts. In A/80/550, the gap between women and men in the employee-empowerment dimension of the staff engagement survey is recorded as eight percentage points in 2021 and nine in 2024. Closing that gap is an explicit objective.[5]

The table does not explain the causes, establish whether the change is statistically significant, or identify which group scored higher. It should not be used as proof that discrimination worsened. It does, however, identify a workplace-experience gap that representation figures alone cannot resolve.

Nor should scepticism escape scrutiny. Shihana Mohamed, quoted in the IPS article, argues that reductions in male-dominated parts of the workforce helped produce the improved percentages. That is an explanation requiring examination, rather than a demonstrated finding we can simply adopt. The article does not provide the underlying analysis needed to establish how much of the change resulted from workforce reductions.[1]

An illustrative example shows why the question matters. An organisation employing 400 women and 600 men has 40 per cent female representation. Remove 200 men, recruit nobody, and it reaches 50 per cent. The calculation is correct; the explanation determines what achievement can reasonably be claimed. This is a hypothetical example, not a description of what happened at the UN.

Conversely, that possibility cannot justify assuming that the UN’s gains are merely arithmetic. We need comparable data on recruitment, promotion, retirement, separation and post abolition, using consistent dates and staff populations. Scrutiny must work in both directions.

What would persuade me that institutional bias was diminishing? Evidence of fairer career progression across grades, nationalities and contract types; greater confidence in raising concerns; credible protection against retaliation; and demonstrable consequences for discriminatory management. These are proposed tests of institutional change, not findings that the representation statistics have already established.

I would also ask whose experience disappears inside the category “women.” An international director, a national officer and a consultant awaiting renewal may share a gender while having profoundly different access to security and influence. An assessment of equality should examine those differences, rather than assume that one aggregate can represent them all.

The UN deserves credit for its documented gains in women’s representation. It should welcome equally rigorous examination of what those gains mean for working lives.

Count the women, certainly. Then examine who advances, who has authority, who can challenge a decision safely, and whose expertise changes the decision. Numerical parity is a meaningful achievement. Establishing that institutional bias is diminishing requires further evidence.

References

1. Deen, Thalif. “Is Gender Bias at the UN Coming to an Inglorious End?” Inter Press Service, 3 November 2026. Syndicated version.
2. UN Women. “Improvement in the status of women in the United Nations system: Report of the Secretary-General (2025).” Publication summary accompanying report A/80/260, 25 July 2025.
3. UN Women. “Representation of Women in the UN System.” Infographic accompanying the 2025 Secretary-General’s report, p. 1; 2025 figures attributed to the UN System-wide Dashboard on Gender Parity, June 2025.
4. United Nations. “UN Secretariat Gender Parity Dashboard.” Coverage and methodological notes. Accessed 3 November 2026.
5. United Nations, Secretary-General. “Implementation of human resources management reforms: outlook for 2026–2029.” A/80/550, 28 November 2025, p. 13: gender-parity definition, employee-empowerment indicators and targets.

Stephanie Hodge, MPA Harvard (2006), is an international evaluator and former UN advisor who has worked across 140 countries. She is a former staffer of UNDP (1994-1996 & 1999- 2004) and UNICEF (2008-2014). She writes on governance, multilateral reform, and climate equity.

IPS UN Bureau

title: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt Biden with milk in Ireland (VIDEOS)
content:
Demonstrators at Trinity College Dublin accused the former US president of complicity in Israel’s military campaign in Gaza

Pro-Palestinian protesters threw cartons of milk at former US President Joe Biden during his visit to Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday.

According to the University Times (UT), a student newspaper, the protest broke out after Biden arrived at the university to watch his son, Hunter, receive the Gold Medal for Outstanding Contribution to Public Discourse from the College Historical Society.

Demonstrators chanted “shame on you” and “genocide Joe,” accusing Biden of complicity in Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, which has left more than 74,600 Palestinians dead since October 2023 and displaced much of the enclave’s population.

Protesters threw milk cartons as US Secret Service agents escorted the former president and his family from the venue. Security personnel used umbrellas to shield them, while other demonstrators were filmed scuffling with Irish police.

Objects were thrown as former US President Joe Biden and Jill Biden left Trinity College Dublin today. Pro-Palestinian protesters had gathered outside, and Gardaí arrested at least two people. https://t.co/GxS2NuHUlj

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 10, 2026

At least two people were arrested. UT reported that officers used batons and pepper spray against protesters.

NOW: Irish pro-Pals just tried to get at President Joe Biden as he arrived at a Trinity College in Dublin. The crowd is chanting “blood on your hands”. These ghouls will never be appeased. https://t.co/oCluflYoWo

— Heidi Bachram (@HeidiBachram) November 10, 2026

Trinity College Dublin Students’ Union (TCDSU/AMLCT) and Aontas na Mac Léinn in Éirinn (AMLÉ), Ireland’s national students’ union, condemned the police response. In a joint statement, they said Biden’s “role in the genocide of the Palestinian people is well-documented” and called on the university to revoke the honorary doctorate awarded to him in 2016.

Read more

Biden, who has Irish ancestry, faced widespread criticism during his presidency for continuing to provide military and diplomatic support to Israel. Some commentators have argued that his handling of the Gaza war contributed to Democratic candidate Kamala Harris’s defeat by Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

Ireland, one of Israel’s most outspoken critics within the EU, formally recognized Palestinian statehood in 2024. West Jerusalem has rejected accusations that its military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide.

title: El Salvador calls in ‘X killstreak’ on Haitian gang HQ (VIDEO)
content:
The platform’s users flagged the house of criminal warlord Wilson Joseph for destruction by Nayib Buklele’s forces

Salvadoran forces have destroyed the alleged headquarters of Haiti’s largest criminal gang, after a social media user shared its location with Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele. He has vowed to eradicate the gangs if they refuse to return four hostages.

In a post on Friday, a Haitian X user shared a picture of a palatial compound, which she alleged that the notorious ‘400 Mawozo’ (‘400 Simpletons’) gang had built on the eastern outskirts of Port-au-Prince. Led by Wilson ‘Lanmo San Jou’ Joseph, 400 Mawozo is the largest of Haiti’s criminal gangs.

“Give us the exact address, and we’ll destroy it,” Bukele responded in Haitian Creole. Multiple users shared GPS coordinates with Bukele, but the original post was deleted over the weekend. 

However, Bukele kept his word. A fleet of Salvadoran light attack helicopters blitzed the compound, firing rockets and partially destroying its main structure and outbuildings as its occupants fled the scene. Bukele posted a video of the attack on X on Tuesday, calling the gang members “cowards” for running away “without even trying to fight.”

“Some guy on X called in a killstreak on a gang’s HQ and Bukele went through with it. Insane timeline,” one X user responded, summing up the online reaction to the strike.

Haitian police and private security contractors stormed the compound after the rocket barrage, the Miami Herald reported. 

What is El Salvador doing in Haiti?

Read more

Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti late last month, after four Salvadoran military aircraft technicians were kidnapped while assisting the UN-authorized Gang Suppression Force (GSF) mission. The technicians were reportedly kidnapped by Chen Mechan, a smaller member of the broad confederation of gangs that has de facto ruled Haiti since 2021.

The hostages have not yet been returned, despite an attempt by a Chen Mechan-linked NGO to pass four unrelated corpses to Salvadoran forces last week. Bukele has claimed that El Salvador has “no interest in coming to dominate the Haitian people, nor in laying hands on Haiti’s wealth,” but has promised to wage war against the “Satanic” gangs until the captives are handed over. Bukele has also suggested that Salvadoran forces could remain longer in Haiti to assist the anti-gang mission.

Joseph initially vowed to drive the Salvadoran troops out of Haiti, but has since requested mediation from UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, according to AP. Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime will reportedly travel to El Salvador next week to meet with Bukele’s government, the news agency reported on Tuesday.

Crowdsourced airstrikes 

Bukele may be the first national leader to solicit targeting data from social media, but the concept of crowdsourced airstrikes is not a new one. During the height of the Syrian Civil War in 2016, a group of 4chan users geolocated videos posted by Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS) and other jihadist fighters and fed their locations to a Russian military blogger who went by the alias ‘Ivan Sidorenko’. 

4chan users find coordinates of terrorists in Syria and call in Russian airstrikes. 5-30-2016 https://t.co/wsfomyxONT

— Middle East Observer (@ME_Observer_) November 29, 2020

At least one jihadist training camp was subsequently destroyed by Russian airstrikes, although it remains unclear whether ‘Ivan Sidorenko’ supplied the coordinates to the Russian Defense Ministry, as he claimed.

Throughout the Russia-Ukraine conflict, both sides have used information gleaned from social media videos to locate and strike military deployment points, arms factories, and critical infrastructure.

title: Trump and Netanyahu in ‘shouting match from hell’ during Iran call – media
content:
The Israeli PM has reportedly been pressing Washington to resume strikes on Tehran despite the US president’s reluctance to escalate

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a heated phone call with US President Donald Trump over the possibility of renewed military strikes against Iran, Ynet reported on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the conversation.

Several media outlets, including Axios, the Associated Press and the Financial Times, previously reported that Netanyahu had been urging Trump to resume military operations against Iran shortly after the US midterm elections. Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in the November 3 vote, widely seen as a rebuke to Trump’s policies, including the unpopular war with Iran, which has driven up energy prices.

Ynet described the weekend conversation as unusually tense, with one source calling it a “shouting match from hell.” Netanyahu’s office dismissed the report as “fake news, absolute nonsense,” while a senior Israeli official confirmed that the call took place but denied that it had been confrontational.

Read more

Trump said on Sunday that he saw no reason to escalate the conflict with Iran, amid opposition to renewed strikes from Washington’s Arab allies in the region. He and US Vice President J.D. Vance have acknowledged that the Iran war contributed to the Republicans’ election defeat.

Nevertheless, Trump stood by his decision to launch the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran on February 28. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told the Wall Street Journal after the vote.

Netanyahu’s political future is also uncertain after his coalition failed to secure a parliamentary majority in Israel’s October 27 elections.

On Sunday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Netanyahu’s main rival, former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, with forming a new government after parties representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended him for the premiership, compared with 46 who backed Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days to assemble a governing coalition, with a possible two-week extension. 

The war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies that normally carries around a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil and liquefied natural gas trade. Trump has vowed to maintain the naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Iran has been attacking tankers using US-designated shipping routes, which Tehran considers illegal.

title: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies as the new parliament was sworn in.

The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israels longest-serving prime minister.

While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu's opponents now control a solid majority in parliament.

Eisenkot's bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies. They include launching an official government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead.

Israels president gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government

Competing calls for unity

The former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated on Tuesday that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions.

We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment, Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony.

Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties stole the elections.

In a speech following Tuesdays ceremony, Netanyahu reiterated his claim that Arab politicians, who represent a minority comprising 20% of Israels population, cannot be trusted. He attacked Jewish opposition leaders who have signaled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israels identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group.

I ask you: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state? Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot said Netanyahu's speech was divisive and hate-filled, adding: I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute. He later said he had canceled a meeting with Netanyahu's Likud party planned for Wednesday because of the speech.

RELATED STORY | Arab bloc signals willingness to back coalition seeking to oust Netanyahu

Netanyahu's opponents already have a legislative agenda

Eisenkot's bloc also triggered a process on Tuesday to install a new parliamentary speaker as they kicked off work on their legislative agenda.

A majority of members submitted signatures calling for the ousting of the current Netanyahu-backed speaker, Amir Ohana, the first step toward a vote on his replacement. The vote can take place even before a coalition government is in place.

The Knesset speaker is a powerful position. The speaker determines what bills the Knesset will take up, meaning one picked from among the Eisenkot-led opposition parties could propel their legislative agenda forward.

The opposition nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Eisenkots Yashar party, for the job. A vote to appoint him speaker could come as early as this week.

Netanyahu as caretaker

The swearing-in of the new Knesset ushered in an unusual transitional period in Israeli politics Netanyahu and his Cabinet remain in power, while the new lawmakers can introduce legislation.

Meanwhile, Eisenkot will meet with party leaders as he works to build a coalition that would likely make him prime minister. If he fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu the next opportunity to form a government.

As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu faces court-imposed limits on his powers. But he can still pursue appointments and could try to block new legislation. He retains full authority over national security, including the military.

Netanyahu has argued that Jewish-led parties should form a unity government to counter the threat of an Iranian attack. He renewed that call Tuesday, urging them to set aside all other considerations, and said Israel should work to topple the Iranian government.

A governing coalition without Netanyahu could leave him politically vulnerable as he faces an ongoing corruption trial and possible findings of security failures in the lead-up to the Oct. 7 attacks.

title: Eisenkot unveils agenda to reverse Netanyahu’s policies as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
content:
Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies as the new parliament was sworn in.

The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israels longest-serving prime minister.

While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu's opponents now control a solid majority in parliament.

Eisenkot's bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies. They include launching an official government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead.

Israels president gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government

Competing calls for unity

The former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated on Tuesday that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions.

We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment, Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony.

Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties stole the elections.

In a speech following Tuesdays ceremony, Netanyahu reiterated his claim that Arab politicians, who represent a minority comprising 20% of Israels population, cannot be trusted. He attacked Jewish opposition leaders who have signaled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israels identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group.

I ask you: Are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state? Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot said Netanyahu's speech was divisive and hate-filled, adding: I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute. He later said he had canceled a meeting with Netanyahu's Likud party planned for Wednesday because of the speech.

Spanish neo-Nazis trained in Ukraine for ‘armed uprising’ – media
content:
Members of the Nucleo Nacional group reportedly received weapons training from the Azov brigade to prepare militants back home

Members of a Spanish neo-Nazi organization have received military training from Ukraine’s notorious Azov brigade to prepare for an “armed uprising” back home, according to police findings reported by El Pais on Tuesday.

Militants from Nucleo Nacional (National Nucleus) traveled to Ukraine in August, where they established contact with the neo-Nazi-linked Azov unit, now part of Ukraine’s National Guard, the newspaper reported, citing investigative documents.

The Spaniards reportedly trained with AK-47 assault rifles and body armor, seeking to acquire combat skills they could pass on to recruits across Spain. In an intercepted conversation, one member warned that “without training, no uprising will work.”

Investigators traced the extremists to Kiev, a military training camp and an unidentified town roughly 20 kilometers from the Russian border. Photographs showed members wearing Nucleo Nacional clothing, including one carrying a rifle and displaying a Nazi flag patch. Others wore sweatshirts bearing the logo of Stormfront, a prominent white supremacist online forum.

Spanish police launched a crackdown on Nucleo Nacional last week over fears of violence at a planned November 7 march in Madrid. The authorities cited the group’s military training, international extremist connections and potential access to military-grade weapons.

Read more

Fourteen suspects were arrested across seven provinces. Ten were subsequently released under restrictions, including passport confiscation, travel bans, and mandatory weekly court appearances. The investigation involves suspected incitement to hatred, unlawful association, and possession of prohibited weapons.

Police also uncovered links between the group and extremist organizations in Germany, France, Hungary, Romania, and Croatia.

Moscow has repeatedly accused Western governments of turning a blind eye to Ukrainian neo-Nazi networks while continuing to arm and finance Kiev. Russia maintains that denazification remains a key condition for a lasting settlement of the Ukraine conflict.

Russian officials have also warned that Western support for Ukrainian neo-Nazi formations could backfire, allowing extremist networks, weapons, and violence to spread across Europe.

European law enforcement agencies have previously raised concerns about weapons supplied to Ukraine entering criminal markets. Ukrainian investigators have also uncovered arms trafficking from the front line.

In May, the Ukrainian authorities intercepted a shipment of grenades, anti-tank weapons, mines and ammunition allegedly destined for the black market. The seized weapons were subsequently handed over to the Azov unit.
