But that cooperation is fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israels wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Eisenkot and other opposition parties, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israels policies but reject its identity as a Jewish state.

One of Eisenkots partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beytenu party, already has said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot has laid out four conditions for parties that want to join him. They must recognize Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept its declaration of independence, support military, national or civil service for all citizens, and declare the Hamas militant group a terrorist group. It remains unclear whether his would-be Arab partners are ready to accept these conditions.

Furthermore, Netanyahu has repeatedly asserted unsubstantiated claims that the election was stolen by Arab parties. In a pressure tactic on Eisenkot, he says any alliance with these parties would be an act of betrayal.

Israels Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the countrys Central Elections Committee and Herzog say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing is found, it did not have a significant impact on the electoral results.

Eisenkot faces significant challenges on the road to becoming prime minister

Eisenkot has vowed to form a government as quickly as possible. But each likely scenario appears to entail compromises or broken promises.

Aside from seeking the support of the Arab-led parties, Eisenkot has two options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.

Eisenkot and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the long-standing draft exemptions.

The religious parties, which were part of Netanyahus outgoing coalition, want to preserve them, calling them essential to their devout lifestyle. But the exemptions have grown especially controversial among the broader public during the past three years of war.

Anticipating its position as a swing vote, the ultra-Orthodox party United Torah Judaism has left the door open to cooperating with Eisenkot.

Eisenkot has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two-week extension from the president. If he is unable to form a government, Netanyahu could then be given a chance to put together a coalition. If Netanyahu is also unable to do so, the country would return to elections early next spring.

Israels new members of Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday evening. Netanyahu and his cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity, with limited powers, until a coalition is formed.

Wars, international support remain big challenges for next government

Despite tenuous ceasefires, Israel's military remains engaged in fighting Hamas militants in Gaza and Iran-backed Hezbollah militants in Lebanon and the war the country launched jointly with the United States against Iran remains unresolved as well.

Both Eisenkot and Herzog mentioned these challenges on Sunday, as well as what Herzog called the new political situation in the United States," where the midterm elections suggested weakening support for Israel on both sides of the aisle.

He called on Eisenkot to use his military leadership skills as well as his experience of loss, since Eisenkot lost a son in combat in Gaza to unite the country.

You have commanded soldiers from every part of the Israeli people and Israeli society. Your face bears the scars of bullets from decades of command and combat, Herzog said. In the coming days, Gadi, as you and your counterparts enter the negotiating rooms, I ask that you remember that the eyes of the entire nation, with all its pain, hopes, prayers, and fears, are upon you.

title: Gunman who killed at least 6 in Kraków mass shooting has died in hospital
content:
A gunman who killed at least six people during a deadly rampage in the Polish city of Krakw on Saturday has died in hospital, Reuters news agency reported on Monday, citing police.

The country was horrified by the rare mass shooting in the historic main square of the city in the countrys south, which prompted national mourning and heightened security, as authorities said the attack was likely driven by far-right ideology.

The Polish citizen, in his 20s, was shot and injured by police during the attack before being transported to hospital. There, he underwent multiple surgeries and had been in a critical condition prior to his death.

The mass shooting which authorities said they are investigating as a possible terror attack has generated a wave of fear in a European nation with exceptionally tight gun laws.

Krakw police said the gunman drove into the citys main market square, typically popular with tourists and locals, and started firing randomly at people, initially from his car, killing four women and two men, on Saturday afternoon. Sixteen others were injured, including two police officers.

The alleged attacker was wearing military-style clothing and used military weapons, Police Deputy Inspector Katarzyna Ciso told Polish news outlet TVN24. Weapons and ammunition were also found in his vehicle.

The bodies of his sister, mother and father were later found at the suspects home in the town of Ostrowiec witokrzyski, about 120 miles northeast of Krakw. Polands prosecutors office said Sunday that it is highly likely the killings were carried out by the same person, but investigations were ongoing.

Eleven firearms were recovered from both sites, the prosecutors office spokesperson said.

Gunmans clothing examined

Little is known about the gunman, who has not been identified by police, and his motive was not immediately clear. But Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiski said that the shooter was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held very radical views.

Emblems on his clothing were being examined by experts, an interior ministry spokesperson said on Monday.

These patches were associated with various motifs that are currently being analyzed by specialists, Karolina Galecka told radio TOK FM, Reuters reported.

The suspect was a member of a shooting club and appeared to be highly skilled marksman, the club spokesperson Adam Chyb told Reuters on Sunday.

Poland, like other European Union countries, has strict rules about acquiring guns and very few people are allowed to own military-style weapons or carry guns in public. About 411,000 people have gun permits in the country, which has a population of more than 37 million, according to the Associated Press.

Off-duty surgeons saved lives

An off-duty surgeon who rushed to the scene of the shooting to treat victims of the attack, including a police officer, said he had just finished eating lunch with his family when he heard what sounded like gunshots.

Michal Pedziwiatr described being in the eye of the storm as he and a friend also a surgeon began providing care to the wounded.

Pedziwiatr told a press conference on Sunday that his friend, Mateusz Wierdak, was a hero for saving the life of a police officer who subdued the attacker, after he applied pressure to the bleeding wound without any protective gear or gloves and stuffed gauze pads into the chest cavity, Reuters reported.

The two wounded police officers, who Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk praised for also saving many lives, underwent surgery and remain in hospital, police said.

title: COP31 Litmus Test for International Cooperation
content:
Around the venue of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. Credit: Kiara Worth/UN Climate Change

By Yamide Dagnet
ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov 8 2026 (IPS)

As the world heads toward COP31 Türkiye starting this week, I’ve been reflecting on how I think COP31 could prove to be a more revealing “Transition COP”. Let us remember that the Paris Agreement came from a series of “institutional heartbeat” COPs – NOT from annual blockbuster headlines.

Yamide Dagnet, Senior Vice President, International at the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC). Credit: COP30

Every five years, countries face a “moment of truth”, as they are legally required to submit updated, increasingly ambitious national plans and measurable commitments on paper. To inform these submissions and make them more ambitious, countries agreed on some sort of “mid-term stocktaking exercise to audit collective progress” (the so-called Global Stocktake).

This design divides COPs into high-stakes political moments (like the one last year) and rigorous, technical “working” sessions in between, like COP31. This means that mid-cycle COPs are not failures if they lack a historic declaration. Instead, they serve as the vital connective tissue to fuel implementation on the ground.

Yet, I do believe COP31 will be an interesting litmus test for international cooperation in the midst of a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape in front of us, shifting alliances, growing competition over energy, technology, and critical minerals, and an impending transition in global leadership at the UN.

I believe three questions will define its identity and success:

1. Who is shaping the next chapter of climate leadership?
2. Can COP31 strengthen accountability ahead of the next Global Stocktake?
3. Can the transition be both fast and fair? 

The climate landscape is evolving. The question is not just who is at the table but whose priorities ultimately drive outcomes. Countries across the Global South are increasingly shaping the agenda and advancing solutions grounded in development realities.

In the end, COP31’s story will not be written only inside negotiating halls. The conversations, partnerships, and momentum generated outside the formal process may ultimately be just as important as the negotiated outcomes themselves.

What is exciting is that we will not be alone. My Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) team and I look forward to seeing our partners, friends, and many of you on the ground in Antalya!

IPS UN Bureau Report

title: Pope wraps up Uruguay visit and heads to most fraught stop of his tour in Milei's Argentina
content:
Pope Leo XIV wrapped up his visit to Uruguay on Sunday by marking an important Catholic feast day that is tied to the countrys independence, capping his effort to draw attention to the role the church played in the founding of Latin Americas most secular country.

Leo traveled to the city of Florida, north of Montevideo, before heading to Argentina for the second leg of his three-nation tour of South America. It's expected to be the most politically delicate, given the Catholic Church's sharp criticisms of the austerity program of libertarian President Javier Milei.

For his final event in Uruguay, Leo was commemorating the feast of the Virgin of the Thirty-three. Every year, thousands of pilgrims flock to Florida on the second Sunday of every November to pray before the small wooden icon of the Virgin Mary housed there.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Pope Leo XIV casts mail-in ballot, becoming first pope to vote in US election

According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaran statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.

Leo became the first pope in nearly four decades to visit Uruguay, in hopes of reminding its people that the Catholic Church is part of their very identity as a nation even if in subsequent decades the country went on a deeply secular, and at times anticlerical, route.

Thousands of people poured into Florida's main square on Sunday ahead of the Mass under brilliant blue skies, some walking for several kilometers (miles) to reach the site.

An assessment after the first leg of the trip

Leo was hoping to leave a parting message before opening the second leg of his South American trip, which he went ahead with despite having undergone surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung. The final stop is in Peru, his second homeland.

Leo, 71, has appeared in fine form at his events, singing loudly, bounding up stairs and gamely greeting the crowds in his popemobile. He has not cut any events short, including those that have kept him out until past midnight Rome time.

This visit will also serve to reinforce the image of Leo as a leader, not merely in a spiritual sense, but in a much broader capacity as a political leader and a widely recognized figure who, far from shying away from conflict or tension, offers a powerful perspective and commands a highly respected voice, said Luis Bahamondes, a professor at the Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Chile.

A potentially delicate meeting with Milei

In Buenos Aires, Milei is due to greet Leo at the airport and then the two will appear together for the traditional welcome ceremony and exchange of speeches. The encounter could be tense, given the Catholic Church's criticism of Mileis austerity measures that have slashed social spending, and his embrace of artificial intelligence.

Milei has staked his presidency on cutting social spending to overhaul Argentinas troubled economy and deliver a long-elusive budget surplus. He has called social justice an aberration that amounts to stealing, and mocked as huge stupidity the increasingly common complaint in Argentina that families squeezed by his austerity program cant make it to the end of the month.

Leo, who took his name from the 19th-century pope whose encyclical on labor laid the foundation of Catholic social teaching, has made the poor and vulnerable a focus of his papacy, carrying on the legacy of his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis.

Posters reading At last, a Lion who unites appeared across Buenos Aires this weekend, a jab playing on the popes name in Spanish Len, or lion and the lion imagery Milei often uses to portray himself on social media.

Argentina is a society currently experiencing significant upheaval, deep polarization, and an economic crisis, along with a president who defies conventional protocol a leader who, at one point, even challenged Pope Francis, Bahamondes said.

The Argentine church is a sharp Milei critic

Since taking office in December 2023, Milei has slashed Argentinas health care budget by 48% in real terms. Planned cuts to the public university system, which represents a near-universal point of pride in the crisis-prone country, sent students into the streets.

According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people.

Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts as part of a necessary reform process to remake Argentinas troubled economy and eliminate fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy.

Like Trump, Milei has also courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation. Leo has warned that the AI race poses threats to humanity and the environment and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development.

Mileis government insists the papal trip is purely religious. The pope belongs to all Argentines. He doesnt belong to a political party or a political camp, Karina Milei, the presidents sister and secretary general of the presidency, told reporters after a recent planning meeting for Leos visit with church leaders.

A trip to complete Francis unfinished business

In Argentina, Leo is completing unfinished business left by his predecessor, Francis. The Argentine Jesuit, the former archbishop of Buenos Aires, never returned home during his 12-year pontificate, confounding friends and foes alike.

Theres a lot of disagreement over Francis and his legacy in Argentina, said David Lantigua, a theology professor and faculty fellow at the University of Notre Dames Kellogg Institute, which focuses especially on Latin American affairs.

Much of the polemics stems from his tenure in Buenos Aires, when the former Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio was a sometimes divisive partisan figure in a politically polarized country. Bergoglio was a slum priest, who advocated for the poorest and most marginalized the sector of Argentines feeling Mileis social spending cuts the most.

I think well see that kind of tension with Leo thats the ministry Francis left behind, Lantigua said.

Leo, who spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru ministering to poor people, is very much a pastor in Francis' image and owes his pontificate to the late pope.

Argentinas state intelligence agency said Saturday that a person had been arrested over death threats against Leo ahead of his visit to the country. A federal court in Campana, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) northwest of Buenos Aires, ordered the arrest less than 24 hours after the agency was tipped off, it said, without elaborating on the suspect or the nature of the threat.

title: US offers millions for information on Iran’s nuclear program despite Trump’s claims of obliteration
content:
The United States is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Irans nuclear program, despite US President Donald Trumps repeated claims to have obliterated Tehrans capabilities.

Rewards for Justice (RFJ), a State Department program, is seeking tips on Irans nuclear facilities, equipment and associated personnel, the program said in a Friday social media post, which stated that relocation may be offered to informants.

During the 12-day conflict last year, Trump was quick to declare that Irans key nuclear enrichment facilities had been completely and totally obliterated. He kept up this assessment on several occasions after and attacked media organizations including CNN for challenging the claim.

Democratic leaders lay out plans for Congress after blue wave

This years conflict saw the US and Israel again attack Iranian nuclear sites, and Trump has made fresh claims to have tackled Irans threat, telling reporters on Friday that if we didnt hit Iran, you wouldnt have Israel today.

But the State Departments move and independent assessments suggest that concerns remain over Irans program, which Tehran has always insisted is peaceful.

Last year, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported that Iran was enriching uranium to 60% purity which is a short technical step from the 90% required for a nuclear weapon, according to an RFJ statement.

RELATED STORY | Vance blames Iran war for sweeping Republican midterm losses

Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce uranium at such a high enrichment level. Experts estimate this quantity, if enriched further, could be enough for several nuclear weapons, it said.

It also referred to a loss of continuity of knowledge regarding Irans production and inventory of key components like centrifuges due to the regimes lack of compliance with the IAEA.

Preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon has been stated as a key objective for Washingtons war with Iran. This week, President Donald Trump repeated claims that the US might have to go after Irans Pickaxe Mountain, the suspected underground nuclear site where Israel believes Tehran has stored part of its enriched uranium stockpile and advanced enrichment centrifuges.

In response, Iran warned that any US attack on Iranian nuclear facilities would be treated as an expansion of the war in the region. Tehran maintains that it has the right to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, including enrichment.

RFJ has also offered rewards for information on senior Iranian regime figures since the war began in February.

Mediators are continuing to try to broker an agreement between Iran and the US, but both sides appear unwilling to shift on key red lines, with Tehran seeing the ability to enrich uranium as a matter of national sovereignty.

Trump ordered new strikes on Iran overnight, describing them as minor.

Cost of war with Iran now at $47.1 billion

Explosions were heard on Irans Qeshm Island and in the southern Iranian port of Jask, Reuters reported on Saturday, citing Iranian media.

Iran has not officially confirmed the source of the reported explosions, according to Reuters.

Earlier on Saturday, Irans semi-official Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on potential damage. But later that evening Tasnim cited an Iranian source as saying that the explosions heard on the Island were not related to missile strikes.

In a separate development, CENTCOM has launched a task force with the intention of preventing Iran from accessing land routes that might facilitate the transportation of advanced weapons and other materials.

A naval blockade is already in place as part of US efforts to choke off Irans vital oil industry.

title: Gunman opens fire in Polish city of Krakow, killing at least 6 people and injuring over a dozen
content:
Six people were killed and 15 wounded after a gunman opened fire Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Krakow, Poland, authorities said.

The gunman, a 24-year-old Polish citizen, aimed at random people as he drove into the Main Square, a major tourist destination in the center of the city, Krakow police said. Four women and two men were killed. Two police officers were wounded, one seriously, Poland's interior minister said on X.

The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a gunfight with officers a short distance away from the initial violence, police said, and was taken to the hospital for surgery. The death toll earlier stood at five, but police updated it to six in a post on X.

Bomb threats hit more than a dozen European flights, forcing diversions and emergency landings

Katarzyna Ciso, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, said the perpetrator was wearing military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest and used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.

Ciso added that the gunman acted alone and that the public is safe.

It was not immediately clear whether the firearm used in Saturday's attack, or the guns found in the perpetrator's car, were legal. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in a post on X, praised the police officers who responded to Saturday's tragedy. Polish President Karol Nawrocki said his thoughts were with the victims, the wounded and their families.

More than 600,000 rally across France to demand higher wages and school funding

"America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow," Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X.

Images from the scene showed police officers and ambulances covering the area, and a Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter also landed in the square.

A tram driver reported around 3 p.m. that his vehicle was shot at from a man in a moving car while passing nearby the main square, the Krakow municipal transport company said. The window to the tram driver's cabin was shattered.

Around 15 million tourists a year visit Krakow, Poland's second-largest city, the majority passing through the Main Square.

Around 15 million tourists a year visit Krakow, Poland's second-largest city, the majority passing through the Main Square.

title: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
content:
Drone and missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.

Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.

The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.

Melania Trump hosts Russian, Ukrainian officials to mark ceasefire she brokered

Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.

"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace nothing. The children aren't sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. "I'm old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?"

Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 816-meter-long (892-yard-long) Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."

Zelenskyy slams Russian attacks ahead of trilateral negotiations

In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by "launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine's critical infrastructure."

Later, he said that Moscow was stepping up strikes to build pressure on Ukraine ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. "Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way as a form of aggression," he wrote in an online post.

The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, of which only four were shot down due to a lack of Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy also said that Russia had used North Korean-made ballistic missiles to strike energy facilities, citing preliminary findings from investigations at impact sites.

The barrage involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said.

"When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv a city of millions and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone," Zelenskyy said. He urged greater U.S. support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia.

Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.

The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.

Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.

It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.

Kyiv's power now travels 200 miles, and Russia knows the weak point

Death toll rises to 55 after the strike on aid center in Komyshuvakha

Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.

Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.

Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.

"She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" he said. "She didn't come home, and they didn't find her body there. She isn't in the morgue, and she isn't here alive."

The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Ukrainian attack on Russia's Belgorod region kills 1 person

A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.

The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.

Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

title: Crisis deepens in Ukraine as Russian official's White House visit draws scrutiny
content:
Russia is escalating its assault on the infrastructure that keeps Ukraines capital functioning, leaving residents facing repeated disruptions to electricity and water as temperatures fall.

Repeated Russian strikes have damaged the power network serving Kyiv and surrounding areas. Outages are stretching for hours, water service has been interrupted and parts of the citys electric transit system have also been affected. Ukrainian officials say the capital region is facing some of the countrys most severe energy disruptions.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko has warned that continued Russian attacks could push the capital toward a far more serious blackout, saying repeated strikes are putting critical energy facilities at risk.

The infrastructure campaign comes as Ukraine is also reeling from a mass-casualty Russian attack in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Ukrainian authorities now say at least 53 people were killed when Russian bombs struck a school compound being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha. Search crews are still working through the wreckage, meaning the death toll could rise further.

The Nov. 2 attack has become the deadliest Russian strike in the Zaporizhzhia region since the full-scale invasion began. Authorities say roughly 50 people remain missing.

Another development, this one thousands of miles from the battlefield, is drawing anger from advocates for Ukrainian children taken by Russia.

First lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House Thursday, highlighting a humanitarian operation in Russian-occupied Oleshky that allowed civilians to leave the area and humanitarian assistance to reach them.

But one member of the Russian delegation has a controversial history.

Yana Lantratova is Russias human rights commissioner. She is also under U.S. sanctions, and Ukraine accuses her of helping remove children from occupied Ukrainian territory and transfer them to Russia.

It is a story Scripps News has followed for nearly four years.

READ MORE | Scripps News Investigates: Ukraine's stolen orphans

One of the children tied to those allegations is Margarita Prokopenko, who was just 10 months old when she was taken from the Kherson Childrens Home in 2022. Ukrainian authorities accuse Lantratova of involvement in removing Margarita and another child from the region.

Margarita was later given a new Russian identity and adopted into the family of prominent Russian politician Sergey Mironov, according to Ukrainian authorities and records uncovered by subsequent investigations. Her Ukrainian family has spent years trying to bring her home.

For advocates trying to recover Ukraines stolen children, Lantratovas appearance at a White House event devoted to humanitarian cooperation presents a stark contradiction: The woman Russia now calls its human rights commissioner is someone Ukraine accuses of helping take its children.

title: Melania Trump accused of delivering Putin the victory he craved
content:
A Ukrainian researcher has said Melania Trump may have walked straight into the Kremlin’s trap.

Petro Andrushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, was livid following a Russian drone strike at a train station in Dnipro, about 160 miles from Oleshky, on October 29. The attack killed 14 civilians and injured at least 14 more as they were waiting on the platform

“While screaming to the world how much he wants Melania Trump to mediate saving 1,500 people in Oleshky, Putin continues to kill civilians 10 minutes away from my house, continues to bomb Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia,” he told the Daily Beast.

“Now Putin will be a ‘humanitarian’ for moving people from Oleshky to Russia," he said. "The Oleshky operation is truly the greatest victory of Russian propaganda.”

The first lady hosted an event at the White House on Thursday with delegations from both Russia and Ukraine in attendance, where both sides praised her efforts to achieve peace.

She said she had “acted immediately” to secure a ceasefire in Oleshky and described herself as the “exclusive intermediary” between the hostile nations. The event lasted about 15 minutes, and the first lady did not take questions from the press.

Nearly 800 people were evacuated from Oleshky, according to the first lady. The frontline Russian-occupied city in the Kherson region has been trapped in a horrific war zone since 2022, with residents facing months of severe food shortages.

Andrushchenko was even more blunt about the propaganda surrounding the operation.

“Using Donald Trump and Melania as their façade, Russian propaganda is building a campaign in order to blame Ukraine, put the ‘genocide,’ hunger in Oleshky on our shoulders,” he said.

“They are allowing American journalists in; they have brought a bunch of dubious reporters from Moscow. Not sure how Ukraine is supposed to react.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky has awarded the first lady the Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, for her humanitarian work supporting Ukraine, including efforts to bring Ukrainian children home.

The Daily Beast reports that Ukrainians have mixed feelings about Melania’s involvement in the Oleshky evacuation. It helped people escape Oleshky while Russian strikes continued elsewhere, including Dnipro. It may have set a precedent for more truces on the frontline, but critics said it also handed Russia a propaganda coup. The report also raised concerns that moving Ukrainians out of occupied territory contributed to ethnic cleansing.

“Melania Trump brokered a ceasefire without a single independent monitor in the room, and Russia used that gap to stage exactly the picture it wanted the world to see,” Lyudmyla Yankina of the Ukrainian human rights group Civil Fortis told the Daily Beast.

Special envoy Steve Witkoff came under fire from U.S. lawmakers and Ukraine for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” following Russia’s release of U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard on October 21.

title: Arab bloc signals willingness to back coalition seeking to oust Netanyahu
content:
A veteran Arab lawmaker in Israel says his bloc is willing to break with decades of precedent and join forces with Jewish-led parties in a shared bid to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long rule.

We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government, Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Arab Joint List, told The Associated Press.

But any such partnership could be politically fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israels wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Netanyahus opponents, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israel's policies, but reject its identity as a Jewish state.

RELATED STORY | Israel's elections are running to a new scramble to build coalition government

After historic voter turnout delivered Arab-led parties a record share in Israel's parliament, Tibi said the Joint List is willing to support an anti-Netanyahu government without joining it. That could reassure Jewish-led factions that view them with suspicion and satisfy their own constituents. It would still give the Joint List major influence.

Only one Arab party has ever served in an Israeli government, in 2021. But that party, Raam, is much more conciliatory than the Joint List and held fewer seats. Raam is willing to join another anti-Netanyahu government as a partner, but any such arrangement would still need the support of the Joint List.

If the Jewish-led parties reject such a partnership, then it would prove Israel is an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens, Tibi said.

The Joint List's positions put it at odds with most Israelis

Most of the Palestinian population in what is now Israel fled or was expelled during the 1948 war surrounding its creation. Those who remained were granted citizenship, including the right to vote, and today they and their descendants make up some 20% of the population.

Many Jewish Israelis have historically viewed Arab-led political parties with suspicion. That distrust has been reinforced by lawmakers who have defended or praised Israel's enemies.

The Joint List, a coalition of three left-wing and nationalist parties, rejects what it refers to as the racist Zionist consensus in Israel. It calls for partnering with Jewish Israelis who support a Palestinian state in the West Bank, Gaza and east Jerusalem, territories occupied in the 1967 Mideast war. It rejects Israels identity as a Jewish state, calling for equal rights for all its citizens.

Many Jewish Israelis see that as support for the countrys enemies at a time of war. Netanyahu has encouraged such sentiments, lodging unproven accusations of electoral fraud against the Arab-led parties and portraying them as a threat to national security.

A dilemma for Netanyahu's opponents

That creates a dilemma for Netanyahus main opponents, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot.

In the campaign, they portrayed Netanyahu as a corrupt leader who failed to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack and then blocked a public inquiry into it. They cast the election in existential terms, saying Netanyahus far-right government threatened Israels democratic institutions.

They won 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared to 53 for Netanyahus coalition. The Joint List won 11 seats and Raam won 8, making them crucial to forming an anti-Netanyahu majority.

The Joint List could help an anti-Netanyahu bloc take power by voting for it or by abstaining to lower the threshold needed for a majority. Either arrangement could allow opposition parties to form a government without requiring the Joint List to become part of their administration. Joining could put its lawmakers in the uncomfortable position of being part of a government waging wars in Gaza and Lebanon that they oppose.

Some of Eisenkots allies welcome Arab support while others are opposed, pointing to past statements by Joint List leaders they argue deny Israels legitimacy or support its enemies.

Tibi said he was under no illusions that a partnership with Netanyahus opponents would end the wars or bring about a Palestinian state. But he said a repair government would improve the lives of Palestinian citizens, by ending Netanyahus rule and also potentially addressing local issues like a wave of violent crime in Arab communities.

It's unclear what conditions would be required

Eisenkot has said Arab-led parties must meet certain conditions in any partnership, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.

Tibi said the conditions do not apply to parties like the Joint List that want to provide outside support.

The Joint List and Raam have denounced the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack and any violence against civilians. But they have refused to brand Hamas a terrorist group or call for its destruction, saying that doing so would justify Israels devastating military campaign in Gaza.

Tibi said both the Oct. 7 attack and Israels response to it were immoral.

RELATED STORY | Trump reverses course on Israel aid amid Tuesday's midterm election

The veteran lawmaker has long been a lightning rod for right-wing attacks on Arab parties. During Israels 2019 elections, Netanyahu, popularly known as Bibi, campaigned on the slogan Bibi or Tibi? to warn voters that opposing him meant relying on Arab-led parties to form a government.

Tibi said Tuesday that the election result had turned the slogan on its head.

When he said Bibi or Tibi, he incited against Arabs, he said. Now, its Tibi, because Arab voters went in a very massive way to take part in the elections. Its definitely our story this time.

They won 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared to 53 for Netanyahus coalition. The Joint List won 11 seats and Raam won 8, making them crucial to forming an anti-Netanyahu majority.

The Joint List could help an anti-Netanyahu bloc take power by voting for it or by abstaining to lower the threshold needed for a majority. Either arrangement could allow opposition parties to form a government without requiring the Joint List to become part of their administration. Joining could put its lawmakers in the uncomfortable position of being part of a government waging wars in Gaza and Lebanon that they oppose.

Some of Eisenkots allies welcome Arab support while others are opposed, pointing to past statements by Joint List leaders they argue deny Israels legitimacy or support its enemies.

Tibi said he was under no illusions that a partnership with Netanyahus opponents would end the wars or bring about a Palestinian state. But he said a repair government would improve the lives of Palestinian citizens, by ending Netanyahus rule and also potentially addressing local issues like a wave of violent crime in Arab communities.

It's unclear what conditions would be required

Eisenkot has said Arab-led parties must meet certain conditions in any partnership, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.

Tibi said the conditions do not apply to parties like the Joint List that want to provide outside support.

The Joint List and Raam have denounced the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack and any violence against civilians. But they have refused to brand Hamas a terrorist group or call for its destruction, saying that doing so would justify Israels devastating military campaign in Gaza.

Tibi said both the Oct. 7 attack and Israels response to it were immoral.

RELATED STORY | Trump reverses course on Israel aid amid Tuesday's midterm election

The veteran lawmaker has long been a lightning rod for right-wing attacks on Arab parties. During Israels 2019 elections, Netanyahu, popularly known as Bibi, campaigned on the slogan Bibi or Tibi? to warn voters that opposing him meant relying on Arab-led parties to form a government.

Tibi said Tuesday that the election result had turned the slogan on its head.

When he said Bibi or Tibi, he incited against Arabs, he said. Now, its Tibi, because Arab voters went in a very massive way to take part in the elections. Its definitely our story this time.

title: Sixty Years on, UN Is Finally Interpreting Freedom of Association
content:
The Palais des Nations, Geneva, Switzerland. Credit: Mathias Reding on Unsplash

By Sigrid Lipott
GENEVA, Nov 6 2026 (IPS)

 

A right under pressure

No one disputes freedom of association. It is in the Constitutions of almost every country, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 22 of the ICCPR, and in regional Articles in Europe, America, and Africa. What it has never had, at the universal level, is sincere implementation by governments.

Regional organisations and courts have filled that space in limited ways. Courts and human rights commissions have issued decisions that have not always been followed. States are left to interpret these obligations themselves for citizens and non-citizens in their jurisdiction.

Violations of the right to free association have risen 50% in two years, according to CIVICUS Monitor. The rise is not only a matter of scale. Governments are no longer relying mainly on administrative interference or political pressure to constrain civil society. They devise restrictive laws governing who can organise, on what terms, and access to resources. Restricting international funding for civil society, particularly through foreign agents’ laws, is now a global trend and poses unprecedented significant challenges. In 2025, restrictive laws affecting civic freedoms were recorded in at least 66 countries, the ninth most prevalent civic space violation worldwide.

Sigrid Lipott

The Committee is preparing to adopt General Comment No. 38 on Article 22 of the ICCPR, which guarantees everyone the right to freedom of association. General Comments are the Committee’s official interpretations of the Covenant. They clarify a right’s meaning and scope and set out how States may implement it. They serve as a reference point for national courts, litigators, and human rights institutions.

Rights and recognition for everyone

Article 22 clearly says everyone has the right to come together, but it does not specify who counts. On protest rights, General Comment No. 37 says all citizens and non-citizens hold the right, including migrants , asylum seekers, refugees and stateless people. Article 22 should follow the precedent.

Most of the world’s organising happens in grassroots movements, digital networks, and fluid conflict and humanitarian contexts, not with registered organisations. Restrictions fall hardest on those already excluded from decision-making and resources.

The article defines qualifications on national security, public order, and safeguards and rights of others. Without clarity, they have remained fluid since 1966. The Committee needs to clarify the scope.

States cannot be left to interpret the article. Amid rising authoritarianism and divisive politics impacting civic life and participatory governance, minorities and excluded people need strong freedom of association protection to defend their rights.

Registration is among the worst restrictions because authorities treat it as routine paperwork rather than a decision about whether a group may exist at all. The Committee should state plainly that registration means notifying the authorities, not asking permission, and that any procedure must be simple, quick, and free of official discretion. Organisations should not be required to comply with “national interest ” or meet disproportionate reporting demands. Penalties for administrative slip-ups should fit the offence, and only a court should be able to shut an organisation down, as a last resort.

Funding is critical for survival

Foreign agents’ laws have spread from a handful of states to dozens, with vague definitions of “foreign influence” and “political activity” that let officials choose their targets. These come with heavy reporting duties, frequent audits, and penalties ranging from fines to licence withdrawal and prison.

Other measures achieve the same effect without the label: prior approval for foreign grants, punitive taxes, or rules forcing funds through state-controlled accounts. Where foreign support is the only resource available, organisations will struggle to survive.

Funding is critical to securing freedom. The Committee should recognise the right to seek, receive and use resources from domestic, foreign and international sources, whether or not a group is registered.

Online and across borders

Groups now recruit, debate and organise online, so internet shutdowns and surveillance strike directly at freedom of association. Governments imposed a record 313 shutdowns in 2025, up from 304 the year before, according to Access Now, and people in 100 countries have lived through one since tracking began. Blanket shutdowns are disproportionate, even in conflict zones.

Governments increasingly pursue critics abroad through surveillance, harassment of relatives back home, misuse of Interpol and stripping of nationality, cutting exiles off from organisations at home. This transnational repression is also a restriction on association and should be named.

No justification without limits

In dozens of countries, counter-terrorism laws criminalise people for exercising basic freedoms. A government’s own definition of “security” cannot override its treaty obligations, and none of these grounds justifies criminalising organisations for lawful work. Emergency powers follow the same pattern.

At least 50 states restricted freedom of association during the pandemic, and many of those measures outlasted the crisis, as independent UN human rights experts warned they might. The Committee should set out categories of emergency and the limits each can justify, matching the real scale of the threat.

Enabling environment without

Governments must also create the conditions for civil society to thrive, including laws that meet international standards, access to information, a real say in decisions and lasting access to resources. A good law achieves little if officials publicly smear the groups it protects.

That means protecting people from intimidation, arbitrary arrest, smear campaigns, travel bans and reprisals for cooperating with the UN. Freedom of association cannot be separated from freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. According to the CIVICUS Monitor, just 7% of the world’s population lives in countries where these civic freedoms are broadly respected.

Building on regional courts

The European Court of Human Rights has built a rich body of case law treating freedom of association as essential to a pluralist democracy. In 2020, the EU’s Court of Justice struck down Hungary’s 2017 law on foreign-funded organisations as incompatible with freedom of association. The African and Inter-American human rights commissions have also set progressive standards.

But these rulings apply only within their regions, and even there, groups defending minority rights or exposing sensitive issues still come under attack. A universal standard would give everyone, everywhere, something to invoke.

Sixty years, one opportunity

Article 22 has waited, and the wait has had consequences. Restrictive laws survive because the standard is vague enough to accommodate them: a registration regime is presented as administration, a funding restriction as transparency, a ban as security. At the global level, nothing has tested those claims.

General Comment No. 38 can change that. It can give parliaments, courts and governments the detail they need to draft laws, interpret them and respect the limits of their power, at a moment when restrictions are spreading faster than the standards meant to contain them.

Freedom of association is a right that makes other freedoms enforceable. The Covenants turn sixty this year. At this critical juncture, the Committee must give it the clarity it deserves.

Sigrid Lipott is an international treaties specialist and the UN adviser at CIVICUS. Based in Geneva, Switzerland, she leads CIVICUS’s engagement with UN human rights mechanisms. CIVICUS is a global alliance of more than 17,000 civil society organisations and activists from 175 countries working to strengthen citizen action and defend civic freedoms worldwide.

IPS UN Bureau

 

 

 

 

Excerpt:

The UN Human Rights Committee (the Committee) will adopt its first interpretation of Article 22 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). It has a unique opportunity to set what the right to freedom of association requires of States. Sixty years after the UN General Assembly adopted it, that provision remains without an authoritative interpretation, while restrictive legislation tests its limits worldwide.

title: Israel's elections are running to a new scramble to build coalition government
content:
Eyes worldwide are still on the electoral race in Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a new challenge in parliament.

President Isaac Herzog wrapped up consultations earlier Thursday on forming a new government. Neither Netanyahu nor challenger Gadi Eisenkot won a parliamentary majority in the elections, setting off a scramble for coalition partners.

So where do things stand now? And what does this mean moving forward?

Scripps News spoke with Ruth Eglash, the senior Israel correspondent for the Jewish Telegraph Agency.

"President Herzog has been meeting with the representatives of the 11 parties that passed the electoral threshold and that do have a place in Israel's parliament," Eglash said. "He's met with most of the parties. He still has to meet with the two main parties, which is Netanyahu's Likud party and, as you mentioned, his challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party."

RELATED STORY | Netanyahu bloc falls short of majority as Israel enters coalition talks

"It's looking pretty clear that the president will ask Gadi Eisenkot to begin the process of trying to put together a coalition. Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot have a clear path to forming that coalition. Any coalition in Israel needs a minimum of 61 seats in order to have a majority in the Israeli parliament and there's no clear path for either party to reach that number."

Watch the full interview with Eglash in the video above.

title: Bomb threats hit more than a dozen European flights, forcing diversions and emergency landings
content:
A wave of bomb threats Thursday forced flight diversions and emergency landings across Europe after more than a dozen flights were targeted.

One plane headed from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military base in France, with all 157 people on board safe. Authorities say security sweeps have so far found no explosives or suspicious materials.

The incident follows several similar hoax threats earlier this week. Airports in Madrid, Milan, Bucharest, Warsaw and London were among those targeted.

Some flights arrived at their destination safely but were ultimately searched by experts, while others had to be diverted. For example, four flights headed to Prague were threatened with some kind of explosive device being on board. But once they all arrived, they were searched and no explosive devices were found.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat

UK Secretary of State for Transport Heidi Alexander has described the threats as a malicious hoax. Heathrow Airport has also dismissed that it was the subject of a bomb threat, saying it didn't believe it was a credible threat. As a result, no actions were taken to shut down airport operations in any way.

It remains unclear exactly who is behind these threats or how long they may continue. European Union transport chief Apostolos Tzitzikostas said it's also unclear whether all of the bomb threats this week are linked, or whether there is one group behind all of the same threats.

The UK Department of Transport has made it clear that London's Metropolitan Police Aviation Section is working with its international counterparts to try to figure out exactly what is happening and where these threats are emanating from.

There has been one claim made in Italy by a group which says it is an anti-feminist organization that wanted to make the skies turn red. However, that has not been verified as a credible claim, so it remains unclear whether these threats are coming from an individual, a group, a hostile state, or none of the above.

title: I Also Accuse
content:
This is the second article in a four-part series. The remaining two will follow.
I wish to warn distinguished readers that a distorted and unauthorized version of my first article, 'I Accuse', has been posted on the [https://www.thenewyorkernews.com] site.
The original version, published by IPS, is available at [https://www.ipsnews.net/2026/11/i-accuse/].

By Saber Azam
GENEVA, Nov 5 2026 (IPS)

Following my first article with a similar title, I must note that many actors have contributed, and continue to contribute, to the world’s current appalling state and the calamities that may await future generations. When historical injustices committed by colonial powers and their ramifications are ignored; when the drums of war sound in many corners of the world; when international institutions remain powerless; when vulgarity permeates politics and diplomacy; and when heads of state in rich and “poor” countries, along with the leadership of the United Nations (UN), are unable or unwilling to address issues affecting humanity’s destiny, I also declare:

Saber Azam

I Accuse Other Leaders

At the national level, leaders are elected, selected, or imposed with firm claims that they will lead their nations toward a more secure, peaceful, and prosperous future and serve their people with dedication, honesty, and vision. I do not argue here about their accession to power, but rather about their “obligation” to protect their nations’ interests without prejudice toward any constituent group and in concert with other nations, all naturally pursuing similar objectives. Yet bigotry has become a preferred tool and strategy for many leaders seeking to gain or retain power, even in societies considered “democratic.” Moreover, the wealth of a few too often determines the destiny of the many.

Most leaders of countries commonly referred to as “poor or developing” have failed their people. Mired in incompetence, many neglect their duties, serve other interests, and misuse national treasuries to amass personal wealth and property. At the same time, despite possessing enormous natural resources, their populations still lack access to basic social services, their infrastructure lies in ruins, and their economies remain in disarray, requiring support from foreign countries or financial institutions at high interest rates. In contrast, powerful countries appear entrenched in strategies of lip service. The clearest example is so-called “development aid,” often used as a guise to pressure “the needy to submit to the will of the rich.” Like multilateral development initiatives, bilateral aid has produced limited tangible results despite decades of existence and trillions of US dollars spent.

As a standard operating procedure, some states use proxy groups to sow insecurity and to circumvent international law. In both technologically advanced and less developed countries, politics often seems driven by short-term personal or party interests.

International cooperation has lost much of its meaning and substance, becoming “international competition.” While powerful countries may have the military and economic might to pursue this political philosophy, it harms the welfare of less powerful or technologically disadvantaged nations. Honest and sincere cooperation therefore remains elusive. The mighty seek to impose their vision of the world, bullying the less powerful, who often lack the courage to free themselves from dependency and compromise. Many leaders in both groups of countries therefore bear responsibility for the world’s lack of equitable peace, stability, and progress.

I Accuse the UN Leadership

Article 97 of the UN Charter establishes the Secretariat, comprising the Secretary-General and such staff as the Organization may require. Article 99 provides that the “Secretary-General may bring to the attention of the Security Council any matter which in his opinion may threaten the maintenance of international peace and security.” Article 100 further states that “in the performance of their duties, the Secretary-General and the staff shall not seek or receive instructions from any government or from any other authority external to the Organization. They shall refrain from any action which might reflect on their position ….” Article 101 emphasizes that “the paramount consideration in the employment [recruitment] of the staff and in the determination of the conditions of service shall be the necessity of securing the highest standards of efficiency, competence, and integrity.”

When judging the performance of UN Secretaries-General, their senior management teams, and the heads of UN agencies, few have truly met the required standards. This is also a major reason the Organization has failed to fulfill its duties and obligations. Many factors have contributed to UN leadership’s shortcomings in serving humanity. Political and funding pressure from powerful countries seeking to impose their views and preferred candidates—mostly former politicians, ministers, or other prominent figures—for senior UN positions has been a significant obstacle. Such individuals have often proved more loyal to their countries’ policies or political alliances than to the “world-loving” spirit and the principles of impartiality and fairness outlined in the UN Charter. Furthermore, the desire to secure a second term, remain in senior roles for as long as possible, or work in prestigious headquarters such as New York, Geneva, Paris, or Vienna—where political prominence and financial remuneration are most attractive—has left parts of the Organization’s leadership willing to compromise on key principles. As a result, powerful member states have turned such positions into “bargaining chips.” The willingness of some of the most senior UN leaders to yield to external pressure has seriously damaged the Organization’s efficiency and reputation.

The Secretary-General, senior Secretariat officials, and agency heads are expected to uphold international morality and law. They must unequivocally denounce violations of human rights and lawlessness by any state, organization, business, or individual and take decisive action. Leaders who resist political pressure to fulfill their duties have been pushed out. Inefficiency and a lack of accountability are other trademarks of some senior UN managers. In the worst cases, behind-the-scenes deals appear to be the preferred solution because “scandals tarnish the image of the organization.” The internal justice system frequently appears to protect senior managers while being applied more readily to junior staff.

Almost all development agencies, especially the UN Development Program, have failed to meet expectations despite decades of operation and trillions of US dollars spent. Many agencies have overlapping mandates, prompting competition for relevance and funding and leaving them vulnerable to exploitation. No Secretary-General has dared to suggest shutting down some of these agencies, or at least replacing them with more effective bodies and streamlining their mandates. Likewise, reform efforts have amounted to little more than superficial fixes, allowing senior managers to remain in place and the status quo to persist. Therefore, since its inception more than eighty years ago, UN leadership has also played a significant role in the world’s deplorable situation by remaining silent, yielding to external pressure, and accepting unacceptable compromises on crucial issues of peace, security, human rights, and development.

[To be continued]

Saber Azam is a former United Nations official who served at UNHCR and UN-DPKO. He is the author of Soraya: The Other Princess and Hell’s Mouth: A Journey to the Heart of West African Jungles. His third book, Nowhere to Go, will be published soon.

title: More than 600,000 rally across France to demand higher wages and school funding
content:
Frances Interior Ministry said more than 600,000 people rallied Thursday across France, including in Paris, to demand higher wages and support the student protest movement, piling fresh pressure on the beleaguered government.

After more than a month of large, recurring protests across France, major rallies took place again in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and elsewhere, most of which were peaceful. The Interior Ministry said the figures were still provisional.

RELATED STORY | French protesters defy heavy police presence in new demonstrations

The Paris march proceeded peacefully Thursday afternoon, drawing a massive crowd, including students carrying signs reading, Inequalities seriously jeopardize our future and We cant spend our whole lives just trying to make a living. Workers and retirees also joined, demanding higher wages and pensions.

About a third of Frances high schools were closed or unable to operate, some because of student blockades and others because teachers were on strike. Public transportation was disrupted in some areas. The Eiffel Tower was also closed.

Police are prepared but tensions flare again

Interior Minister Laurent Nuez said that 70,000 police officers were deployed, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters. Police have been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics.

Many demonstrations in recent weeks have been marred by violence, which authorities blamed on masked far-left radicals seeking to incite insurrection and others intent on looting.

Authorities in the western region of Brittany said masked individuals tried to block roads in Rennes. They said young people, often accompanied by adults, committed serious acts of violence, including throwing steel balls at police.

Authorities also reported tensions, scuffles and other incidents in the cities of Lyon, Nantes, Pau, Orlans, Rennes and Toulouse.

Unions aim to send a warning

Frances main unions warned that the country is on the brink of recession and that layoff plans are multiplying. Fuel, food products, rent, gas, electricity everythings going up except wages and pensions, they said in a joint statement.

France is mired in debt and is one of the worst economic performers in Europe, along with Italy and Belgium.

We need to give every single children here in this country a proper future, said Garance Blaise, a 21-year-old university student taking part in the Paris march.

It's all about the way we dont know whether well get a job or not. And our parents, they know that and they agree with us and they also have things to ask for, she said. So I think the movement is already global, it is already all over Europe and its not just students, its the whole population.

Corinne Cucchini, from the Private Healthcare Federal Union, joined the Paris demonstration to denounce staff shortages and a lack of equipment at the private hospital in Paris where she works. Our demands focus on raising wages and the working conditions, she said.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | France wakes up to wreckage of a night of rioting after protests turned violent

Fabien Villedieu, national secretary of the SUD-Rail union, took aim at President Emmanuel Macron 's centrist government and the national rail company, SNCF.

When the government is not reasonable, when the head of the SNCF is not reasonable we simply do what weve always done in France, which is to go on strike, he said at the Gare de Lyon station in Paris.

Before the strike action, the government had been negotiating with unions a familiar scenario in French politics in hopes of limiting the protest movement, which has resulted in France's most violent civil unrest in years.

Protests are drawn into election campaigning

The movement began in September with a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris and spread nationwide. It drew students demanding more education funding and then broadened to workers seeking better pensions and help with soaring fuel prices and other costs.

Thursday's demonstrations come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political leaders seeking to capitalize on the movement. Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Far-right contender Marine Le Pen is the favorite to win.

Some candidates participated in the Paris march, including veteran far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mlenchon, Green leader Marine Tondelier and Raphal Glucksmann, who represents the moderate left.

There is a sense of absolute frustration at the governments failure to operate, said Paul Smith, an associate professor of French history and politics at the University of Nottingham in England. Whoever wins the presidential election is going to have a stack of problems to cope with.

Its very difficult to see exactly where things go, he said.

Fabien Villedieu, national secretary of the SUD-Rail union, took aim at President Emmanuel Macron 's centrist government and the national rail company, SNCF.

When the government is not reasonable, when the head of the SNCF is not reasonable we simply do what weve always done in France, which is to go on strike, he said at the Gare de Lyon station in Paris.

Before the strike action, the government had been negotiating with unions a familiar scenario in French politics in hopes of limiting the protest movement, which has resulted in France's most violent civil unrest in years.

Protests are drawn into election campaigning

The movement began in September with a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris and spread nationwide. It drew students demanding more education funding and then broadened to workers seeking better pensions and help with soaring fuel prices and other costs.

Thursday's demonstrations come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political leaders seeking to capitalize on the movement. Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Far-right contender Marine Le Pen is the favorite to win.

Some candidates participated in the Paris march, including veteran far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mlenchon, Green leader Marine Tondelier and Raphal Glucksmann, who represents the moderate left.

There is a sense of absolute frustration at the governments failure to operate, said Paul Smith, an associate professor of French history and politics at the University of Nottingham in England. Whoever wins the presidential election is going to have a stack of problems to cope with.

Its very difficult to see exactly where things go, he said.

title: GOP insiders say one official is about to quit and point the blame at Trump
content:
On Thursday, new bombshell reporting revealed that one of President Donald Trump's top Cabinet officials may be preparing to resign. According to GOP insiders who spoke with the Independent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio appears to be leaving the administration in order to protect himself from midterm blowback as he ramps up a 2028 presidential run.

As the Independent explains, "Even before the disastrous midterm results — when the Republicans lost both the House and the Senate — senior party sources in the US and senior figures in the UK government told the Independent that Mr Rubio could quit his senior role in President Donald Trump’s administration. The sources doubled down on the expectation after the midterms gave a damning indictment of the Trump presidency, with the Democrats seizing Republican strongholds such as Kansas and Texas. Mr Rubio is one of up to five members of Mr Trump’s current Cabinet who are thought to be preparing to 'run for the hills' in the aftermath of the midterms humiliation. One Washington insider told the Independent that Mr Rubio needs to 'distance himself from the Iran war and pin that one on Trump.'" Sources say that Trump may also lay the blame on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — whose impeachment is being called for even by members of his own party — with Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also targeted as potential scapegoats.

As one insider, an ally of Rubio, elaborated, "It makes complete sense for him to step down and leave the administration. Rubio is the leading candidate at the moment to be the [Republican] nominee. He’s definitely ahead of [Vice President JD] Vance. But he cannot run while he is still secretary of state and being tied to the administration will only harm his prospects anyway.” Immediately after the GOP's midterm massacre, Vance was quick to blame the war in Iran in a clear effort to distance himself from it. “The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone … The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," wrote Vance in his scathing remarks. "Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Meanwhile, many have noted that Rubio has played a "quieter" role in the war, with others helming negotiations despite the fact that his position makes him the country's top diplomat.

One senior UK government source told the Independent, “We are looking to see what he will do after the midterms. It seems unlikely that he will stick around. He would make a strong presidential candidate and we expect him to run.” Another Republican source asserted, “Rubio will be gone after the midterms. There will be about four or five them running for the hills." As this source noted, “The country has completely turned against Trump. People cannot even say where Iran is on a map and do not get this war. The cost of gas has really p—— people off.” They added: “Once the Democrats control the House and Senate we are just going to see attempts at impeachment and nobody wants to stick around for that.”
